Good morning. Yes, let's start. I re-read both fixes in the code before answering, so everything below is from the real kernels.

You are mostly right. One correction up front: the bug triggers when one loss call has more than 65,536 **rows** (B × T tokens), not only when the context length is above 65,536. 16k × 8 rows = 131,072 also hit it.

# Part 1: The loss bug

## Words first
- **Row:** one token position of the micro-batch. A micro-batch of B rows × T tokens has n = B × T rows. At 128k with B = 1, n = 131,072.
- **Thread:** one small worker on the GPU. **Block:** a group of threads (here 256 or 512) that can share a small fast memory. **Grid:** all the blocks of one launch. `<<<blocks, threads>>>` means "start this many blocks, each with this many threads".
- **Partial sum:** the sum of a small piece, which still has to be added to the other pieces.

## What the loss forward does: 3 launches (`LossKernels.cu`)

**Launch 1: the loss of every row.** `blocks = batch_size`, 512 threads each. One block per row. The block's 512 threads go together over that row's 49,280 vocabulary values: they find the max, add up the exponentials, and compute loss = log(sum) − logit of the correct token. The result goes into `losses[row]`.
- A prompt or pad row (label 65535) gets loss 0.
- **So n is ALL rows (B × T), not the trained-token count.** Untrained rows are in the list; their value is just 0.

**Launch 2 (pass 1): add the losses in groups of 256.**
- `reduce_blocks = (batch_size + 256 − 1) / 256` blocks, 256 threads each. That is already the rounded-up count you suggested, (n + 255)/256, not n/256. Pass 1 was always correct.
- Each thread takes ONE row's loss. The block adds its 256 values in its shared memory and writes one partial sum.
- Example: n = 131,072 gives 512 blocks and 512 partials.

**Launch 3 (pass 2): add the partials into one number.**
- `<<<1, 256>>>`: one block of 256 threads.
- **This is where the bug was.** The old code had each thread read exactly ONE partial: thread 0 read partial 0, thread 1 read partial 1, …, thread 255 read partial 255. Then it added those 256.
- So only partials 0–255 were ever added, which is 256 × 256 = 65,536 rows. Partials 256 and above were never read.
- At n = 131,072, partials 256–511 (rows 65,536–131,071) were silently dropped. The loss came out about half as big.
- Real case: val loss at 81,920 tokens printed **1.3007** before the fix and **1.6068** after; numpy says 1.6063.

So your description of pass 2 is exactly right: one block of 256 threads, each taking one partial. It works up to 256 partials and drops the rest after that.

## What was affected
Only the **loss number we read**: the printed train loss and the val loss.

The **gradients were correct**. The backward kernel (`sparseCENormalize_from_stats_inplace`, line 918) takes each row's saved max and sum, the incoming gradient and the denominator. It never reads this summed loss, so training itself learned correctly. The wrong part was the numbers we used to judge it.

## The fix (10-30, commit `6aac3bf`)
In `sum_reduction_kernel`, each thread now **loops** when there are more values than threads. Thread t adds value t, then t + 256, then t + 512, and so on, until the end of the list. After that comes the same block-level add as before.
- At n = 131,072, pass 2 sees 512 partials, so each of the 256 threads adds 2.
- At n = 1,000,000 there are 3,907 partials, so each thread adds 15 or 16.

Two details:
- When the threads already cover everything (≤ 256 partials, i.e. ≤ 65,536 rows), the old one-value path still runs. So results up to 65,536 rows are **bit-identical** to before. The loop only switches on when needed, because an always-on loop cost about 0.3 µs per call on the H200.
- Tested: 154 of 154 cases pass (16 failed before the fix), and the trainer val loss now matches numpy.

**Why not just launch more threads in pass 2?** Pass 2 must end with ONE number. Two blocks in pass 2 would produce two partials again, which then need a pass 3 or atomics. So the choices are: loop inside one block, or do more passes.

## How other libraries do the same sum
- **PyTorch** (`F.cross_entropy` → `nll_loss`, `aten/src/ATen/native/cuda/Loss.cu`): the launch is `<<<1, nthreads>>>` (line 392), one block only. Each thread loops over all rows: `for (i = threadIdx.x; i < nframe; i += blockDim.x)` (line 242). Then the same block-level add. There is no pass 1 at all; it's the same loop as our fix, applied to all n rows.
- **CUB, NVIDIA's reduction library** (`cub/device/dispatch/dispatch_reduce.cuh`):
  - **Pass 1** uses a *limited* number of blocks, `max_blocks = occupancy × SM count` (lines 750–755), and each block loops over many groups.
  - **Pass 2** is `DeviceReduceSingleTileKernel<<<1, …>>>` (lines 235 and 665): one block that loops over all partials. Same shape as ours.
- **atomicAdd:** each block adds its partial straight into the result, so one launch is enough. But the order of additions changes from run to run, so the result is not bit-reproducible. We avoid that.
- **More passes:** repeat pass 2 until one number is left. Also correct, but it needs extra launches.

**Is our fix optimal? Yes, for this job.** The sum reads only n floats (131,072 × 4 bytes = 0.5 MB, a few microseconds). Launch 1 reads all the logits (12.9 GB at 128k, milliseconds), so the sum is not where time goes. Our fix is correct for any n, adds in a fixed order (same result every run), and changes no bit for ≤ 65,536 rows. It's the same pattern PyTorch and CUB use.

# Part 2: The RoPE table bug (fixed 10-31, commit `d067e89`)

This is a **different kind of bug**. The loss launch ran but did too little. The RoPE launch was refused completely.

## Words first
- **The table:** for every position `pos` (0 to T − 1) and every pair `i` (0 to 63, since head_dim 128 has 64 pairs), angle = pos × inv_freq(i). The table stores cos(angle) and sin(angle). It is a [T × 128] array, built once and then used to rotate q and k.
- **Grid x and grid y:** a launch can arrange its blocks in two directions. **CUDA allows up to 2,147,483,647 blocks in x, but only 65,535 in y.**

## Old code (`RoPEKernels.cu`)
```
grid  = ( (64 + 127) / 128 = 1 ,  T )    → x = 1 block, y = T blocks
block = 128 threads
pos = blockIdx.y   (one block per position)
i   = threadIdx.x  (one thread per pair; only 64 of the 128 threads had work)
```

## The bug
- At T = 65,536, grid y = 65,536, one more than the 65,535 limit.
- The GPU **refuses the whole launch** ("invalid configuration"), so the kernel runs zero times. Not even position 0 is written.
- The old code never checked for launch errors, so nothing stopped. The table memory stayed unfilled.
- So every rotation at T ≥ 65,536 used garbage values, for **all** positions, not just the ones above 65,535.
- At T = 32,768, grid y = 32,768 is under the limit, which is why it never showed before.

To your question: it is not like the loss bug's "only 256 blocks" case, where some values were computed and the rest skipped. Here nothing was computed at all. What the two share is a size of about 65,536 that nobody had tested past.

## The fix
- **Flat grid:** n = T × 64 entries, one thread per entry, blocks of 256 threads, all in grid **x**. Thread e works on `pos = e / 64`, `i = e % 64`.
- **Capped grid plus a loop:** at most 2^20 (1,048,576) blocks; if there are more entries, each thread loops (e, e + stride, …). So any T works.
- **Same formula,** so every value is computed exactly as before.
- **Every launch is checked** (`rope_check_launch`): if the GPU ever refuses a launch, the run stops with an error instead of continuing with empty data.
- **Same fix in the per-token RoPE kernels,** which also had the token in grid y; they now use grid x. And no more idle half-blocks: before, 64 of the 128 threads in each block did nothing.
- **Tested:** the trainer's table matches a numpy reference at 4k–131k.

So the loss bug was "the launch was too small"; the fix was a loop. The RoPE bug was "the launch was too big in the y direction"; the fix was to put the work in x and check every launch. Both only show above about 65,536, which is why the long-context tests found them.

What would you like to start on today? Per our notes, next is the 889 `cudaFree` calls in the normal training path.

### CLAUDE [2026-11-02 12:39 IST]

Two quick checks, so the numbers I give are exact: how many threads PyTorch's single block uses, and how many threads per row our *training* loss kernel uses (the training path uses the "save stats" version).
> tool `Bash`: Check PyTorch's thread count, its log_softmax step, and our training loss kernel's launch

Not quite: neither of them does a tree over all B×T values directly. One block can have at most 1,024 threads, so a tree over 131,072 values in one block is impossible. Both designs first **loop**, then do a small tree. Here are both at 128k (n = B×T = 131,072 rows).

**PyTorch: one launch, one block**
- Threads: `nll_loss_threads` (Loss.cu:148-149) gives 2^round(log2(131,072/16)) = 8,192, capped at **1,024 threads**.
- **Step A (loop):** each thread adds 131,072 / 1,024 = **128 values, one after another**. Thread 0 adds rows 0, 1,024, 2,048, …. That leaves 1,024 sums.
- **Step B (tree):** 1,024 → 512 → 256 → … → 1, which is 10 halving steps.
- So the tree is only over the 1,024 thread sums, not over B×T.

**Ours (and CUB, same shape): two passes**
- **Pass 1:** 512 blocks × 256 threads. Each thread takes 1 value; each block does a tree 256 → 1 (8 steps). That leaves 512 partials.
- **Pass 2:** 1 block × 256 threads. Each thread adds 2 partials (the loop from the fix), then a tree 256 → 1.
- CUB is the same, except pass 1 uses a fixed number of blocks (about SM count × occupancy), and each block loops over many groups before its tree.

**Which is better? Both are correct and both are fine at our sizes.**

| | one block (PyTorch) | two passes (ours / CUB) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| launches | 1 | 2 (each costs a few µs to start) |
| who reads the n values | 1 SM of the 132 | all SMs, in pass 1 |
| good for | small n | large n (millions and up) |

At our n (65k–131k floats, 0.25–0.5 MB), either takes a few microseconds. That's an estimate from arithmetic; I haven't timed the two side by side. Launch 1 takes milliseconds, so the sum is about 0.1–0.3% of the loss forward. Changing the sum method would save nothing worth measuring.

**Launch 1, as you said, with numbers:**
- **Grid:** `blocks = batch_size` = B×T, `threads = 512` (the training kernel `sparse_ce_forward_kernel_vec_save_stats`, LossKernels.cu:1111-1112). One block per row, and all B×T rows get a block.
- **Per row:** the block's 512 threads go through that row's 49,280 logits together, about 96 each. They find the max and the sum of exponentials, and write one loss value for the row (saving max and sum for the backward). An untrained row gets loss 0.
- **Cost:** this launch reads every logit, 12.9 GB of bf16 at 128k, which is where the time goes.

PyTorch's version of this step is different. `F.cross_entropy` first runs `at::log_softmax` over the whole [N, V] (LossNLL.cpp:514), which writes a full [N, V] log-prob tensor. Only then does `nll_loss` read one value per row and sum. That extra full write is one reason our loss is faster and uses less memory.

### CLAUDE [2026-11-02 12:51 IST]

**1. RoPE table: yes, the whole table was in danger, at T ≥ 65,536.**

- At T ≥ 65,536 the GPU refused the whole table launch, so not a single entry was written, not even position 0. Every position's cos/sin was whatever happened to be in that memory, and q and k were rotated wrongly at every position, not only above 65,535.
- At T < 65,536 (4k, 8k, 16k, 32k) the launch was accepted and the whole table was correct.

**2. Launch 1: B×T blocks, but they don't all run at the same moment.**

- **Blocks issued:** at 128k with B = 1, B×T = 131,072 blocks of 512 threads are issued in one launch.
- **How many run at once:** an H200 SM can hold at most 2,048 threads at a time, so up to 4 blocks of 512 per SM. With 132 SMs that is up to about 528 blocks running at once. Registers could lower that number; I haven't checked this kernel's register count.
- **The rest wait:** blocks are not synchronized and run in no fixed order. When a block finishes, the GPU starts the next waiting block on that SM. 131,072 blocks ÷ ~528 ≈ 250 rounds.
- **Independence:** each block works only on its own row and never waits for the others.

**3. PyTorch's first step is different, and CUB has nothing to do with launch 1.**

- **Ours, launch 1:** computes the loss of each row directly (max, sum of exponentials, loss) and writes **one number per row** (131,072 numbers at 128k), plus max and sum for the backward.
- **PyTorch, `F.cross_entropy`:**
  1. `at::log_softmax` also finds each row's max and sum of exponentials. But then it writes log_softmax for **every vocabulary entry** of every row: a full [N, 49,280] tensor, the same size as the logits (12.9 GB at 128k in bf16). It does not compute the loss yet.
  2. `nll_loss` picks the one value at the correct token in each row, negates it, and sums (the one-block loop + tree from before).

  So PyTorch makes an extra full-size write and read that we skip.
- **CUB** is a general "add up a list" library. It doesn't compute losses. Only our **sum step** (launches 2–3) has the same two-pass shape as CUB. Launch 1, the per-row loss, is our own kernel; its job matches PyTorch's log_softmax + nll pair, but done in one step.

So the steps are:

| step | ours | PyTorch | CUB |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| per-row loss | launch 1 (one value per row) | log_softmax (full [N, V] write) + nll pick | — |
| sum of the row losses | 2 passes | 1 block (loop + tree) | 2 passes (generic sum) |

On the H200, registers do not lower the number of blocks: it stays at **4 blocks of 512 per SM, 528 at once**. Here is how I got that.

**1. The kernel's real resource use on the H200.** I compiled the training loss kernel (`sparse_ce_forward_kernel_vec_save_stats<bf16, uint16>`) for `sm_90a`, with the same flags the Makefile uses:

| | value | proof |
| --- | --- | --- |
| registers per thread | **32** | `ptxas info: Used 32 registers` and `cuobjdump: REG:32` |
| register spills | 0 | `0 bytes spill stores, 0 bytes spill loads` |
| shared memory per block | 1,024 B static + 12,288 B dynamic | `cuobjdump: SHARED:1024`; launch `6 × 512 × 4` (LossKernels.cu:1124) |

**2. How many blocks fit on one SM.** H200 limits per SM (compute capability 9.0): 2,048 threads, 65,536 registers, 228 KB (233,472 B) shared memory, 32 blocks. One block here is 512 threads = 16 warps.

| limit | calculation | blocks per SM |
| --- | --- | --- |
| threads | 2,048 ÷ 512 | 4 |
| registers | 32 regs × 32 threads = 1,024 per warp; × 16 warps = 16,384 per block; 65,536 ÷ 16,384 | 4 |
| shared memory | 1,024 + 12,288 + 1,024 reserved = 14,336 per block; 233,472 ÷ 14,336 | 16 |
| block cap | — | 32 |

The smallest is **4**, so 4 × 132 SMs = **528 blocks at once**. That is 64 warps per SM, 100% occupancy.

Registers and threads both allow exactly 4. The kernel sits right at the edge: with 33 or more registers per thread, a block would need more than 16,384 registers and only 3 would fit.

**3. Proof that this formula is the one CUDA uses.** There's no H200 here, so I ran CUDA's own occupancy calculator (`cudaOccupancyMaxActiveBlocksPerMultiprocessor`) on this exact kernel on the RTX 3060:

```
GPU NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3060 sm_86 | SMs 28 | max threads/SM 1536 | regs/SM 65536 | smem/SM 102400 B | reserved smem/block 1024 B
kernel: regs/thread 40 | static smem 0 B | dynamic smem 12288 B
CUDA occupancy API: 3 blocks of 512 threads per SM -> 84 resident on the GPU
```

Same formula with the 3060's numbers:
- threads: 1,536 ÷ 512 = 3;
- registers: 40 × 32 = 1,280 per warp, × 16 = 20,480 per block, 65,536 ÷ 20,480 = 3.2 → 3;
- shared: 102,400 ÷ 13,312 = 7.

The minimum is 3, and the API also says 3.

On the 3060 the compiler uses 40 registers instead of 32, because the build is for a different architecture. For the H200 I used the compiler's `sm_90a` output (32 registers) and the published 9.0 limits. When we next have an H200, I can run the same test there for a direct API proof.

**4. At 128k:** 131,072 rows ÷ 528 ≈ **249 rounds**, if every block took the same time. In practice, untrained rows finish almost immediately, so the rounds aren't even.

Saved in `profiling_reports/long_context_kernels_2026_10_31/loss_kernel_occupancy_2026_11_02/` (the test program and the compiler output), and written down as plan Q&A 191.

## Ready (CPU side)
- **Data:** all 3 mixes × 22 template versions, 274 train/val folders (56 GB). All have T = 4,096 and `vocab_rows` 49,280, which matches the new loader check, and none contain split-chat pieces.

## Blockers

**1. The trainer can't be built for Ada as it stands.**
- The trainer links `dist`. `dist` puts BluCCL's `multimem.red` code in two files, and that instruction needs sm_90. dist/Makefile:299-302 says it: "On a pre-Hopper card this will fail at ptxas". I hit exactly this error on the 3060 last night.
- We can't just build all of `dist` for sm_90, because `dist` also has kernels the trainer runs on any GPU: `ZeroKernels.cu`, `dist_grad_norm_kernels.cu`, the TP kernels.
- **Fix:** compile only the 2 BluCCL files for sm_90 and everything else for sm_89. With NCCL on one GPU, BluCCL kernels never run.

**2. The embedding backward has to change on Ada.**
- `BLU_EMB_BWD=segmented` (what `run_sft.sh` sets, the same as pretraining) uses BluCCL's `EmbeddingBwdFused`, which is in that same sm_90-only file.
- **Fix:** use the library's `cooperative` mode on Ada: fp32 sums, no atomics, deterministic. All 198 runs would use it, so the comparison between versions stays fair. But it isn't the H200 production setting.

**3. The scripts assume an H200:**
- `run_sft.sh:71` and `gpu_free` in `fmt_screen.sh` require ≥ 60 GB free. An Ada has 48 GB, so nothing would ever launch.
- `run_sft.sh:75` looks up the library path with `SM_ARCH=90`.
- **Memory:** the study takes about 26 rows per step, and `plan()` allows micro-batches up to 16 rows. That gives 13 rows × 4,096 tokens ≈ 49 GB, using the H200 memory model (8.4 GB + 0.757 MB per token). Too big for 48 GB, so the micro-batch needs a cap (about 6–8 rows), with the same rows per step through accumulation.

**4. Kernels never validated on sm_89.**

| part | what runs on Ada | status |
| --- | --- | --- |
| all GEMMs (layers, lm_head, Muon) | BluBLAS's **sm_89 branch**: `128x128_32_6` when M, N ≥ 1024, else `256x128` / `128x256` / `256x64` (Bgemm_dispatcher.cu:206-283) | **never tested on sm_89**. On the 3060, its sm_86 sibling gave wrong rows. Every trainer shape must be checked against cuBLAS first |
| attention (packed, chat plan, hd 128) | generic kernels (GQA_fwd/bwd_generic.cu, tensor cores) | correct on the 3060 only (1 known case at 1.049× the error limit). **Slow:** 0.9 TFLOP/s on the 3060; the faster rewrite is a future item |
| RMSNorm | Ada's own sm_89 kernels (LayerNormKernels.cu:420-439) | never run in our tests |
| q/k norm + RoPE | `fused_rms_rope_bf16` (generic) | tested on the 3060: bit-identical, 44/44 |
| loss | generic | matched fp64 on the 3060 last night |
| SwiGLU, embedding forward | generic | fine; include them in the check |

**On bf16 vs fp32:** the study runs bf16, the same as the H200 runs, and Ada has bf16 tensor cores. Every part above has a bf16 path, so the question is whether the sm_89 paths are correct, which the tests answer. The fp32 path isn't more ready: its fused RoPE kernels are Hopper-only files.

### CLAUDE [2026-11-02 14:43 IST]

You're right in principle. This study asks which chat template and special-token setup trains the best model. That is a data question, not a kernel question, so any correct SFT trainer can answer it, as long as **all 198 runs use the same trainer and the same recipe**. Using PyTorch or TRL on the Ada node is a valid choice.

One correction: "numbers are numbers, anything will be the same" only holds if the recipe matches. A different framework with its own defaults (packing, optimizer, loss averaging, model details) gives different numbers. For a ranking study that's fine *inside* one framework, but:
- don't mix frameworks within the 198 runs;
- the final production SFT runs in BluTrain, so after the study, re-run the top 2–3 versions in BluTrain on the H200 to confirm the ranking holds there.

## What has to match our recipe
1. **Model:** our 135M multiplies embeddings by √512 (`EMBED_SCALE=1`) and ties the lm_head to the embedding. Stock HF Qwen3 does neither, which is why our HF export is untied and "eval-only". A training replica needs the scale plus tied weights; that's a small model change.
2. **Data:** our pre-packed rows (the files are built), with per-chat attention and positions restarting at 0 for each chat. FlashAttention-2 handles that through `position_ids` / varlen, and it supports Ada.
3. **Loss:** the sum over trained tokens divided by the step's total trained-token count. TRL does this already (`num_items_in_batch`, which we read in its code on 10-31).
4. **Optimizer:** Muon for the weight matrices plus AdamW for the rest, LR 1e-4, cosine, 3% warm-up, about 128 chats per step, 1 epoch. TRL doesn't include Muon, so it has to be added (PyTorch's own Muon in recent versions, or the reference implementation), with the same settings as ours.

## Options

| option | setup effort | how close to our recipe |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Plain PyTorch + HF model code** (FA2 varlen, a ~300-line training loop reading our row files) | medium | **closest**: our exact rows, loss rule, Muon + AdamW split, tied + scaled embedding |
| **HF TRL SFTTrainer** (+ Liger, FA2, padding-free) | fastest | it repacks the data unless we feed our rows; no Muon by default; needs the custom model for tie + scale |
| torchtune / torchtitan | high | no Muon; overkill for a 135M |
| Unsloth | medium | fast on one GPU, but awkward with our custom model |

**My recommendation: plain PyTorch with the HF model code.** It trains on exactly the rows we already built, with our loss rule and optimizer split. It can write the HF folder directly, which the evaluation step already expects. TRL is the fallback if we accept its packing and optimizer.

## What it takes
1. **Trainer:** write it (about 300 lines). Load each version's start weights from `init_fmt/<v>` (the converter exists), read our row files, train, export to HF.
2. **Checks on one Ada GPU before the grid:**
   - the study gate: step-0 val loss must equal the numpy reference within 0.2%;
   - the first ~50 steps compared with one of our 10-28 H200 runs on the same data, which should match at the noise level;
   - one smoke run for speed and memory.
3. **Hook it into `fmt_screen.sh`:** only the trainer command changes; stop/resume, the `READY` marker and evaluation stay as they are.
4. **Software on the Ada node:** PyTorch, flash-attn 2, optionally Liger, plus the evaluation stack.

How long the 198 runs would take on Ada I won't guess. The smoke run measures it, and we size the grid from that.

Which way do you want? I can also still fix our own framework for Ada instead (dist build, embedding mode, scripts, then the sm_89 GEMM and attention checks). That's quicker to set up, but its speed on Ada is unknown because of the slow generic attention.

The **9× is the measured slowdown** (3.8 s ÷ 0.42 s). The **5× was an estimate** of how much slower the Ada hardware itself is, from published specs. Two of my earlier numbers need correcting, and one of them was wrong:

| spec | H200 | RTX 6000 Ada | H200 ÷ Ada |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| memory bandwidth | 4.8 TB/s (HBM3e) | **960 GB/s** (GDDR6, confirmed below) | **5×** |
| bf16 tensor math (dense) | ~989 TFLOPS | **~364 TFLOPS**, not the 182 I said earlier | **~2.7×** |
| number of SMs | 132 | 142 | — |

**The correction:** NVIDIA lists **1,457 TFLOPS for FP8 *with sparsity*** for the Ada. Without sparsity that's 728 for FP8, and bf16 runs at half the FP8 rate, so **~364 for bf16**. My earlier 182 halved one time too many. The search results didn't contain a direct bf16 figure, so 364 is that derivation, not a quoted number.

**What this means:**
- **SM count** doesn't explain it: the Ada actually has *more* SMs. Each H200 SM does more bf16 math, and the H200's memory is 5× faster.
- **Our 135M model** (d = 512) is small, so much of its time is memory-bound (norms, casts, attention, the 49,280-wide loss). The fair hardware gap is therefore **somewhere between 2.7× and 5×**, so good code should take roughly **1.1–2.1 s per step** on the Ada.
- **Before:** 3.8 s (9×), so about half the time was our own overhead.
- **Now with compile:** about **2.1 s (≈ 5×)**, at the slow end of that range. Most of the overhead is gone; further gains are possible but smaller.

The compiled re-checks are running now: the gate on GPU 4 and 30 parity steps on GPU 5. I'll report them next.

Several things to check before answering: what the study's evaluation scripts actually use, the live state of every run, and the AnyDesk ID. Gathering them now, read-only:

Here's everything you asked, with the live numbers.

## Evaluation tools

| tool | what it is | made by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **vLLM** | an inference **engine**: generates text fast. It doesn't score anything | vLLM project (started at UC Berkeley) |
| **lm-eval** (lm-evaluation-harness) | an evaluation **harness**: prompts, tasks (IFEval, MMLU, …) and metrics; uses vLLM or HF to generate | **EleutherAI**, not Hugging Face |
| **lighteval** (your colleagues) | also an evaluation **harness**, similar to lm-eval; can also use vLLM | **Hugging Face** |

So it's not "vLLM vs lm-eval vs lighteval": vLLM is the engine underneath, and lm-eval and lighteval are two harnesses on top of it.
- **Our study (designed 10-30) uses lm-eval 0.4.12 on vLLM**, through our class `vllm-fmt` in fmt_lm_eval.py. That class feeds the model the *exact token ids training used*. Plain harnesses render the template to text and re-tokenize it, which gives different ids for several of our 22 versions.
- **lighteval** is what HF used for the published SmolLM numbers. It's useful if we want results comparable to HF's. For ranking our own 22 versions against each other, lm-eval with exact ids is the right tool. Switching would mean porting that exact-id logic.
- **Missing on the node:** `lm_eval` isn't installed yet (vLLM is). I'll set up a separate environment for it before the evaluation stage, with your OK.

| --- | --- | --- |
| BluTrain, H200, 32 rows (16-row micro-batches) | **0.41–0.44 s** | 58 GB |
| our PyTorch copy, Ada, **same 32 rows** (4-row micro-batches) | **2.18 s** (5× slower) | 17.4 GB |
| our PyTorch copy, Ada, study shape (24 rows) | 1.58–1.62 s training, **1.75 s including validation** | 18.6 GB |

## Where the logs are (on the node)

All paths are under `/mnt/volgrp03/3rd_floor/gautam_fmt/`:
- `logs/status_fmt`: the grid's timeline, one line per run start and end.
- `runs_fmt/<run>/run.log`: each run's log, one line per step (train, val, norm, clip, dt) plus `[val]` lines.

## AnyDesk

2. Get this server's **AnyDesk address** (a 9–10 digit number) and its **access password** from whoever set it up. It's also shown in the AnyDesk window on the server's own screen. I tried reading the ID from our account; it printed nothing.

## Pause and resume for your colleagues
- **One run is the unit** (about 25 minutes). The trainer saves no mid-run checkpoints: for a 25-minute run it isn't worth it, and the most that can be lost is about 25 minutes of one GPU. A stopped run restarts from step 0 later. Finished runs (`READY`) are never redone.
- **Gentle hand-over:** remove the GPU numbers from `logs/gpus.txt`. The run on each finishes (≤ 25 minutes) and nothing new starts there. Nothing is lost.
- **Immediate hand-over:** also run `bash code/fmt_screen_torch.sh stop-gpu <i>` for each GPU, which kills our run there now (it gets redone later). Remove the GPU from `gpus.txt` first, or the grid starts a new run there.
- **Stop everything:** `bash code/fmt_screen_torch.sh stop`.
- **Resume:**
  - **grid still running:** put the GPU numbers back in `gpus.txt`;
  - **grid stopped:** restart it with `GPUS_FILE=logs/gpus.txt setsid nohup bash code/fmt_screen_torch.sh grid logs/runs.txt &`. It skips finished runs, leaves running ones alone, and redoes stopped ones from the start. It also makes a second pass over the list, so runs stopped mid-way get picked up again.

## Monitoring: widening it now
The current watcher only alerts on failures, intruders, a stopped grid, and finished rounds. As you asked, I'm adding training-health checks:
- NaN/inf in any log;
- skipped Newton–Schulz updates;
- val loss going **up** between checks;
- train-loss spikes;
- gradient norm above 5;
- step time above 2.5 s;
- a run whose log hasn't changed for 5 minutes (stuck);
- disk under 100 GB or RAM under 50 GB.

Each finished round also gets a table of final val losses, so we can compare the template versions.

The new watcher is running. It checks the node every minute and alerts me if any of these happens:
- **Grid and runs:**
  - the grid loop stops;
  - a run fails;
  - a run's log stops updating for 5 minutes (stuck).
- **GPUs:** a GPU gets a second process, or a process that isn't ours.
- **Training health:**
  - NaN or inf appears;
  - a Newton–Schulz update is skipped;
  - val loss goes up between checks;
  - train loss spikes above 1.6× its recent median;
  - gradient norm goes above 5;

Yes. When the training runs and then the evaluations are done, this study tells us which chat template and special-token setup works best for our 135M model. But we're comparing **22 versions, not 198**. Each version is trained **9 times**, which makes 198 runs.

## Where 198 comes from: 22 versions × 3 data mixes × 3 seeds

**1. The 22 versions (what we're comparing).** The same chat content, wrapped in a different structure each time (chat_formats.py):

| versions | template style | markers are… | after each answer |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| v1 / v2 / v3 | Tülu (`<|system|>`, `<|user|>`, `<|assistant|>`) | **plain text** | id 0 / id 2 / id 2 between turns + 0 at the end |
| v4 / v5 / v6 | Tülu | **special ids** (49152–49154) | same three choices |
| v7 / v8 / v9 | ChatML (`<|im_start|>`, `<|im_end|>`) | plain text | same three choices |
| v10 / v11 / v12 | ChatML | special ids (1, 2) | same three choices |
| v13 / v14 | = v11 / v12, but ids 1 and 2 start as they are in the base | special ids | — |
| v15 | **no markers at all** (only blank lines) | — | id 0 |
| v16 / v17 / v18 / v19 / v20 / v21 | the formats other teams use: Cohere / Phi-3 / GLM-4 / Zephyr / Llama 3 / Mistral (system merged into the user turn) | mixed | each team's own rule |
| v22 | a default system message | — | — |

The questions they answer:
- Plain-text markers vs real special tokens?
- Which end token after an answer?
- Which other team's style works best for a model this small?
- Does a default system prompt help?

**2. 3 data mixes (does the answer depend on the data?):**
- **m1_smol:** mostly multi-turn chats.
- **m2_tulu:** single-turn, a lot of math and code.
- **m3_smol_math:** the third, math-leaning mix.

If one version wins on one mix and loses on another, we report that separately and never average it away (plan rule 4.48).

**3. 3 seeds (is a difference real or noise?):** the same chats in 3 different shuffled orders (`train_screen`, `_s2`, `_s3`). Two runs that differ only in order differ by some amount, and that is the noise. A version only counts as better if its lead is bigger than that.

**So:** 22 × 3 × 3 = **198 runs**. The grid runs seed 1 for all 66 version/mix pairs first (rounds 1–9), so we get a first full look after about 66 runs, then seeds 2 and 3.

## How "best" is decided
Not by training loss. The versions put different structure tokens around the same content (plain-text markers add tokens, end tokens differ), so their raw train and val losses aren't directly comparable. After each run, the evaluation stage (fmt_evalq.sh) tests the exported model with the exact token ids it was trained with:
- **Our own measurements** (fmt_measure.py):
  - **m1:** loss per *answer* token only, so it is comparable across versions;
  - **m2:** whether the model **stops** correctly;
  - **m3 / m3b:** whether it **uses earlier turns**;
  - **m7 / m7b:** robustness to injected markers and hidden instructions;
  - **m9:** refusals on safe vs unsafe prompts (XSTest).
- **Standard benchmarks** through lm-eval on vLLM: IFEval, GSM8K, ARC-Easy/Challenge, HellaSwag, MMLU, PIQA, Winogrande.

The best version is the one that wins on these, beyond the seed noise and consistently across the 3 mixes. The plan then re-checks the top versions at other learning rates, and in BluTrain on the H200.

### CLAUDE [2026-11-02 16:30 IST]

Short answers first, then the reasons.

**1. Can we use the winner for all our models?** Yes, as the **default** template, and one standard template across models is a good idea: one data pipeline, one evaluation setup. Two things to keep in mind:
- **Model size:** the study runs on the 135M. Small models are usually *more* sensitive to format than big ones, so a difference we see at 135M may shrink at 1.7B+. Before fixing it for a bigger model, re-run only the **top 2–3 versions** on it, on one mix. That's a small check, not the full study.
- **Tokenizer:** the decisions carry over (special ids or plain-text markers, which end token, which structure). The **exact ids don't**. Ids like 49152–49155 exist only in the 135M tokenizer's extension. Another model, such as the 1.7B on tiktoken, gets the same tokens added to its own tokenizer.

Fixing a template causes no problem, as long as each model keeps the **same template everywhere**: SFT, evaluation, DPO, serving. Changing it after SFT means training again.

**2. Tool and function calling later:** yes, keep it in the decision.
- **Room for new tokens:** the 135M has **128 spare embedding rows** (49,280 rows against 49,152 tokenizer ids). The study uses only 4 (49152–49155), so there's room for tool tokens like `<tool_call>`, `</tool_call>` and `<tool_response>`.
- **Prefer a template with real role markers:** ChatML-style templates (Qwen and Hermes use `<|im_start|>tool`) and Llama 3 (an `ipython` role plus `<|eom_id|>`) already have a natural place for a tool role. When two versions are close, choose the one that extends cleanly to tools.
- **Not tested yet:** the study doesn't include tool calling. When we add it, that needs tool-call SFT data and a short check of its own. I'll note this as a future item.

**3. Will the format matter much?** The study is designed to tell us, without guessing. The 3 seeds give the noise level, and any difference smaller than that counts as "no real effect".
- **Benchmarks:** I also expect IFEval, MMLU and the like to differ only a little between versions, when each model is used with its own template.
- **Where bigger differences are likely:** what our extra measurements look at:
  - whether the model **stops** at the right place;
  - whether it **leaks structure tokens** into answers;
  - whether **typed fake markers** can hijack it. With plain-text markers, a user can type `<|assistant|>` into a message; with special ids they can't.
  - how well it **uses earlier turns** in multi-turn chats.
- **If everything is within noise:** we choose for engineering reasons (special ids for safety, room for tools) and record that the format didn't matter at this size. That's a useful answer too.

**4. Which labs' formats are in the 22?** Each lab's *structure* is rebuilt with our tokenizer's ids:

| lab / model | version |
| --- | --- |
| AllenAI Tülu (`<|system|> <|user|> <|assistant|>`) | v1–v6 (plain text and special ids, 3 end choices) |
| OpenAI ChatML, used by Qwen, Hermes and HF's SmolLM2/3 | v7–v14 |
| Cohere Command-R | v16 |
| Microsoft Phi-3 | v17 |
| Zhipu GLM-4 (no end token between turns) | v18 |
| HF Zephyr (end token after every turn) | v19 |
| Meta Llama 3 (header markers + end-of-turn) | v20 |
| Mistral v0.1 (system merged into the first user turn) | v21 |
| no markers at all / a default system message | v15 / v22 |

**Not in the 22:** Google Gemma, DeepSeek, Llama 2 (`<<SYS>>`), and OpenAI's newer Harmony format (gpt-oss). If you want any of them included, they can be added as extra versions. That would be new data builds and 9 runs each.

Mostly yes, on all three. Details:

**1. Testing on the small model:** agreed, it's the right place. If the format matters anywhere, it's at 135M, and whatever wins carries over as a **strategy**: special ids or plain text, which end token, how the system message is handled. If a future model has a different tokenizer, we add the same special tokens and use the same structure there.

**2. The parser** (the tokenizer's "special-token switch"): it lives in **our encoding code, not in the model**. The model only ever sees ids. Our pipeline (chat_formats.py, the same code that built the training data) uses it like this:

| piece | switch | why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| message **content** | **ON** | so the base's own special ids 3–16 inside text (e.g. code) stay as in pretraining. Any chat whose content contains a **structure name** (`<|endoftext|>`, `<|im_start|>`, `<|im_end|>`, our new role names) is **dropped** before tokenizing, so training data never has typed marker text inside content |
| template **pieces** (markers, role words, newlines) | **OFF** | marker text can't turn into a special id by accident; the special ids are inserted by number |

- **At serving time (default):** user text is encoded so that typed marker text can **never** become a structure id. That means the switch is OFF for the structure names, or they are removed.
- **In the tests:** measurement **m7** tests both on purpose. Switch OFF is the correct product; switch ON is a careless product. That shows how badly each version can be hijacked when someone gets it wrong.

**3. Gemma, Llama 2, OLMo, DeepSeek:** our 10-28 survey (plan file) rendered the real templates of:
- Llama 3.1, Qwen2.5, Qwen3, SmolLM2;
- Tülu 3, OLMo 2, OLMo 3 Instruct and Think;
- Hermes 3, OpenAssistant, Vicuna;
- **Llama 2**, Zephyr, Mistral v0.1 / v0.3, **Gemma**, Phi-3;
- gpt-oss "harmony", OpenHermes.

**DeepSeek was not in it.** The 22 versions test the *strategy choices* those templates are built from, so most labs are covered in substance:

| lab template | its strategy | covered by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **OLMo 2** Instruct | exactly the Tülu format: plain-text markers, end = endoftext | **v1, directly** |
| **OLMo 3** Instruct / Think | ChatML special ids, plain role words, `im_end` between turns + `endoftext` after the last answer | **v12, directly** |
| **Gemma** | "ChatML's shape under other names": special start id + plain role word (`model`) + special end id; no system role | **v11** (shape) + **v21** (system merged); only the word `model` differs |
| **Llama 2** | plain-text `[INST] … [/INST]`, system inside the first user turn (`<<SYS>>`), end token after answers | plain-text marker families (**v1–v3, v7–v9**) + system merged (**v21**); the exact `[INST]` strings aren't tested |
| **DeepSeek** V3/R1 (not surveyed) | one special id per role (`<｜User｜>`, `<｜Assistant｜>`, no newline), system as plain text at the start, end only after answers | closest: **v4** (role special ids, end 0) / **v18**; the "no newline after the role id" detail isn't tested |

So every **strategy dimension** these labs use is in the 22:
- markers as plain text or special ids;
- a single role id, or a start id plus a role word;
- which end token, and whether there's an end between turns;
- system message separate, merged, or a default.

What isn't tested is each lab's exact marker strings (`[INST]`, `model`, `<｜User｜>`). The model only sees ids, so those strings matter much less than the strategy. If you want exact replicas of Gemma, DeepSeek or Llama 2 as well, I can add them as v23+: new data builds, then 9 runs each, about 30 GPU-minutes per run on these Adas.

**1. lm-eval, vLLM and lighteval.** You're right that they're different things:
- **vLLM is the engine.** It generates text fast and runs underneath either harness.
- **lm-eval (EleutherAI) and lighteval (Hugging Face) are the two harnesses.** Each defines the tasks, prompts and scoring. So the real comparison is lm-eval vs lighteval, not either of them against vLLM.

| | lm-eval (EleutherAI) | lighteval (Hugging Face) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| tasks | the largest task library; the most-used harness in papers; HF's Open LLM Leaderboard ran on it | HF's own task set and prompts |
| used for | our study (with our exact-token-id class built on top) | HF's published SmolLM numbers; what your colleagues use |
| engine | vLLM or HF | vLLM, HF, nanotron |

**Neither is "better" in general.** For ranking our 22 versions against each other, **lm-eval with exact training ids** is the right tool, and it's already built. Numbers from the two harnesses aren't directly comparable: different prompts and scoring give different scores for the same model. ### CLAUDE [2026-11-02 19:38 IST]

**Ctrl+C won't work.** The grid was started detached from any terminal (`setsid nohup`), so there's no window to press Ctrl+C in. Use these commands instead, run on the node from `/mnt/volgrp03/3rd_floor/gautam_fmt`:

**1. Pause now (fastest):**
```bash
cd /mnt/volgrp03/3rd_floor/gautam_fmt
bash code/fmt_screen_torch.sh stop
```
This stops the grid loop and the 8 running trainings. Finished runs (`READY`) are safe. The 8 half-done runs are lost, up to about 25 minutes each, because a run has no mid-run checkpoint; they redo from step 0 when you resume.

**2. Resume (from where it stopped):**
```bash
cd /mnt/volgrp03/3rd_floor/gautam_fmt
GPUS_FILE=logs/gpus.txt setsid nohup bash code/fmt_screen_torch.sh grid logs/runs.txt > logs/grid_stdout.txt 2>&1 < /dev/null &
```
It skips every finished run, redoes the stopped ones, and carries on with the rest.

**3. Gentle pause (nothing lost):** empty the GPU list.
```bash
echo "" > logs/gpus.txt
```
The 8 running trainings finish (up to about 25 minutes) and nothing new starts. To resume, put the list back: `echo "0 1 2 3 4 5 6 7" > logs/gpus.txt`. The grid loop is still alive and picks the GPUs up again on its own.

**4. Give only some GPUs to a colleague,** e.g. 0–3:
```bash
echo "4 5 6 7" > logs/gpus.txt          # no new runs on 0-3
bash code/fmt_screen_torch.sh stop-gpu 0  # optional: free GPU 0 right now (its run is redone later)
```

**If someone just kills the processes:**
- **Only the 8 Python trainings killed:** the grid loop sees them end, starts new runs on the free GPUs, and redoes the killed ones at the end. The watcher alerts me in this case.
- **Everything killed, grid loop included:** nothing is lost except the half-done runs. Run command 2 to continue.

Either way, finished results are never touched. The v23 build on the laptop is separate and unaffected.

I've worked out the stall, and I have a measured test to back it. One honest caveat first: the test shows the stall is real, but it does not yet show it is what made the trainer slower. I haven't fixed anything; I'm waiting for your go.

## How it works today

1. When the trainer calls a matmul, the CPU puts the work into a queue for the GPU and moves on right away. Normally the CPU stays ahead and the GPU always has work waiting. All our trainer work goes through one queue: stream 0 ([DeviceCore.cpp:63](../BluTrain_push/Tensor-Implementations/src/device/DeviceCore.cpp#L63)).
2. A matmul's output is cut into tiles, and the BluBLAS kernel works through them in some order.
   - For **tall** outputs (many more tile rows than tile columns), it reads that order from a small table in GPU memory.
   - The table is built on the CPU and kept in a **16-slot cache**, looked up by the tile-grid size ([Bgemm_sm90_warpspecialized_template.cuh:1681-1725](../BluTrain_push/Tensor-Implementations/BluBridge-BLAS/src/level3/batched_gemm/BF16/SM90/Bgemm_sm90_warpspecialized_template.cuh#L1681-L1725)).
3. When a grid size is **not** in the cache, BluBLAS:
   - builds the table on the CPU;
   - calls `cudaMalloc`;
   - copies the table to the GPU with a plain `cudaMemcpy`. **This copy waits until every piece of GPU work already queued has finished.** The CPU stops right there.
   - Once the cache is full, it also calls `cudaFree` on the oldest slot.
4. For tall grids the table is just plain row order: tile i is (i / grid_n, i % grid_n). Nothing in it needs the CPU.

## What changed with trained rows

- The lm_head dX matmul is `[M_t, 49280] × [49280, 512]`. That is a tall grid of `M_t/128 × 2` tiles.
- Before, M = B×T never changed: one cache miss at the start, then hits.
- Now M_t changes every micro-batch: a new grid size every time, so a miss and a full wait every time.

## What we observed in the trainer (10-31 nsys, 10 steps, one run each)

| run | micro-batches | extra `cudaMalloc` | extra `cudaMemcpy` | time the CPU sat inside those copies |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 4k | 20 | +19 | +19 | 10 → 565 ms |
| 128k | 10 | +10 | +10 | 17 → 1,556 ms |

That is exactly one miss per micro-batch. At 4k, one value of M_t happened to come twice.

## Controlled test (P032 GPU 1, checked free before every run)

It makes the same BluBLAS call as the trainer, on stream 0, and runs cuBLAS the same way.

**Test 1:** give the GPU 20 ms of queued work, then make one dX matmul call. Each column is how long that single call keeps the CPU stuck (median of 20 calls).

| library | same M | new M, GPU busy | new M, GPU idle |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| BluBLAS | 3 µs | **20,014 µs** (all 20 calls) | 12 µs |
| cuBLAS | 9.5 µs | 95 µs (7 of 20 calls waited ~20 ms) | 100 µs |

- **BluBLAS:** the cost is the wait for the queue, not the CPU work.
- **Same 20 M values run twice:**
  - BluBLAS waited on all 40 calls. With 20 shapes and 16 slots evicted in turn, each shape is thrown out before it comes back.
  - cuBLAS waited on 7 of the first 20 calls and none of the second 20. Its wait is `cuKernelSetAttribute` the first time it loads a new kernel: once per kernel, not once per shape.

**Tests 2 and 3:** a training-like loop of 33 iterations, M fixed vs a new M each iteration (same average size). Numbers are wall time per iteration, three repeats.

| loop | BluBLAS fixed | BluBLAS new M | cuBLAS fixed | cuBLAS new M |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| test 2 | 63.5 / 62.8 / 63.6 ms | 63.7 / 62.8 / 62.8 ms | 61.3 / 61.3 / 60.8 ms | 62.8 / 62.5 / 63.6 ms |
| test 3 (more CPU work in backward) | 64.4 / 64.3 / 63.3 ms | 64.3 / 63.4 / 63.4 ms | 61.3 / 62.0 / 61.3 ms | 64.3 / 63.3 / 62.0 ms |

- BluBLAS held the CPU about 9.5 ms per iteration, yet the loop got no slower. The GPU stayed the slower side, so the CPU caught up after waiting. GPU idle grew only 0.4 ms per iteration.
- nsys of the new-M run: 35 `cudaMalloc`, 35 blocking `cudaMemcpy`, 22 `cudaFree` for 33 new shapes. The 2 extra misses are fixed model shapes that got evicted and had to be rebuilt.

## What is proven and what is not

- **Proven:** a new M_t makes BluBLAS wait for all queued GPU work, and the cache thrashes once more than 16 shapes are in use.
- **Not proven: that this is what slowed the trainer.**
  - The wait only costs time when the work after it can't let the CPU get ahead again.
  - At 4k the trainer was blocked about 56 ms per step and the step got 52 ms slower, which fits.
  - But that is one run each. The trainer's own `cudaFree` time jumped 2.1 → 5.6 s (4k) and 7.9 → 19.9 s (128k) between the two runs. One 128k step took 12.1 s in one run and 6.5 s in the other.
  - The kernel gain was only 9 ms per step (22 ms at 128k), and noise that size hides it.
- **To prove it:** fix the cache, then run the trainer with the switch off and on for more steps, several times. The allocator stalls (the 889 `cudaFree` calls task) also need understanding first.

## Your other questions

- **Memory caching or metadata caching?** Metadata: it caches tile-order tables. Its miss path does memory work (`cudaMalloc`, a blocking copy, `cudaFree`), and that is what stops the CPU. The trainer's own allocator stalls are a separate problem.
- **What CUTLASS does** (checked in the 4.5.1 source): it computes each tile's position on the GPU from the tile number (`static_tile_scheduler.hpp:169-243`). There is no table, no allocation and no copy, and the basic scheduler needs no extra memory.
- **cuBLAS** (closed source): the library file contains the settings `CUBLASLT_HEURISTICS_CACHE_CAPACITY` and `CUBLAS_AUTOTUNING_CACHE_CAPACITY`, which point to a CPU-side cache of which kernel to use for a shape. The measurement matches: a new shape costs only CPU time, and it waits only the first time a new kernel is needed.
- **MoE:**
  - CUTLASS grouped GEMM keeps each expert's size in GPU memory, and the kernel reads it there (`sm90_tile_scheduler_group.hpp:283`).
  - DeepGEMM does the same (`__ldg(grouped_layout + group_idx)` in `scheduler.cuh`).
  - BluBLAS has no grouped GEMM. An MoE built on it would call the normal matmul once per expert, with a new size every step, so most calls would miss. The expert counts would also have to be copied back to the CPU first, which is another wait.
- **Does this fix the sm_86 wrong rows? No, it's a different bug.**
  - The sm_86 kernels never use a tile map.
  - Their tile-order formula ([Bgemm_core_template.cuh:77-79](../BluTrain_push/Tensor-Implementations/BluBridge-BLAS/src/level3/batched_gemm/BF16/SM89/Bgemm_core_template.cuh#L77-L79)) groups tile rows in 8s and skips tiles when the number of tile rows is not a multiple of 8.
  - Running that formula by itself reproduces 11-01 exactly: M = 6464 / 6528 / 6656 skip 576 tiles starting at row 6144 (291 wrong trained rows), while 8192 skips none.
  - It can hit any matmul on those GPUs with such a size. It needs its own small fix.
- **B300 is worse:** its templates keep a single slot per kernel config and rebuild the table whenever the grid size differs from the previous call's, for every shape.

## Fix options (none applied)

1. **Tall grids:** compute the row order inside the kernel, the way CUTLASS does. No table, no cache, no CPU work.
2. **Square grids:** compute the Hilbert order on the GPU too, or keep one table per GPU, never freed during a matmul, copied with `cudaMemcpyAsync` on the matmul's stream.
3. **B300 and cluster templates:** the same change.
4. **sm_86:** fix the last group so the formula covers every tile.

For each: check the outputs are bit-identical, time the matmul before and after, then rerun the trainer with the switch off and on several times.

Everything is written up in work doc §45.133 and plan Q&A 196. Test scripts, results and nsys reports are in `profiling_reports/long_context_kernels_2026_10_31/tilemap_stall_2026_11_02/`.

P032 GPU 1 is released. The format study is at 83/208, all runs fine, and the watcher is running.

But that is one run each. The trainer's own cudaFree time jumped 2.1 → 5.6 s (4k) and 7.9 → 19.9 s (128k) between the two runs. One 128k step took 12.1 s in one run and 6.5 s in the other.
The kernel gain was only 9 ms per step (22 ms at 128k), and noise that size hides it.
To prove it: fix the cache, then run the trainer with the switch off and on for more steps, several times. The allocator stalls (the 889 cudaFree calls task) also need understanding first.
Your other questions
Memory caching or metadata caching? Metadata: it caches tile-order tables. Its miss path does memory work (cudaMalloc, a blocking copy, cudaFree), and that is what stops the CPU. The trainer's own allocator stalls are a separate problem.
What CUTLASS does (checked in the 4.5.1 source): it computes each tile's position on the GPU from the tile number (static_tile_scheduler.hpp:169-243). There is no table, no allocation and no copy, and the basic scheduler needs no extra memory.
cuBLAS (closed source): the library file contains the settings CUBLASLT_HEURISTICS_CACHE_CAPACITY and CUBLAS_AUTOTUNING_CACHE_CAPACITY, which point to a CPU-side cache of which kernel to use for a shape. The measurement matches: a new shape costs only CPU time, and it waits only the first time a new kernel is needed.
MoE:
CUTLASS grouped GEMM keeps each expert's size in GPU memory, and the kernel reads it there (sm90_tile_scheduler_group.hpp:283).
DeepGEMM does the same (__ldg(grouped_layout + group_idx) in scheduler.cuh).
BluBLAS has no grouped GEMM. An MoE built on it would call the normal matmul once per expert, with a new size every step, so most calls would miss. The expert counts would also have to be copied back to the CPU first, which is another wait.
Does this fix the sm_86 wrong rows? No, it's a different bug.
The sm_86 kernels never use a tile map.
Their tile-order formula (Bgemm_core_template.cuh:77-79) groups tile rows in 8s and skips tiles when the number of tile rows is not a multiple of 8.
Running that formula by itself reproduces 11-01 exactly: M = 6464 / 6528 / 6656 skip 576 tiles starting at row 6144 (291 wrong trained rows), while 8192 skips none.
It can hit any matmul on those GPUs with such a size. It needs its own small fix.
B300 is worse: its templates keep a single slot per kernel config and rebuild the table whenever the grid size differs from the previous call's, for every shape.
Fix options (none applied)
Tall grids: compute the row order inside the kernel, the way CUTLASS does. No table, no cache, no CPU work.
Square grids: compute the Hilbert order on the GPU too, or keep one table per GPU, never freed during a matmul, copied with cudaMemcpyAsync on the matmul's stream.
B300 and cluster templates: the same change.
sm_86: fix the last group so the formula covers every tile.
For each: check the outputs are bit-identical, time the matmul before and after, then rerun the trainer with the switch off and on several times.

Everything is written up in work doc §45.133 and plan Q&A 196. Test scripts, results and nsys reports are in profiling_reports/long_context_kernels_2026_10_31/tilemap_stall_2026_11_02/.

P032 GPU 1 is released. The format study is at 83/208, all runs fine, and the watcher is running.

### CLAUDE [2026-11-02 21:06 IST]
> tool `Bash`: Read the existing feedback memory about explaining setup first
> tool `Bash`: Record the feedback that each test must be explained from zero

You're right. Here it is again from zero, with every term defined and every test explained step by step.

---

## Part 1: The words

- **CPU:** the processor that runs our program's code (the C++ trainer). It does not do the matrix math.
- **GPU:** the H200. It does the math.
- **Kernel:** one piece of GPU work, for example "multiply these two matrices". The CPU tells the GPU to run a kernel; this is called a *launch*.
- **Queue (stream):** when the CPU launches a kernel, the kernel goes into a line. The GPU takes kernels from this line one after another. Our trainer uses a single line, called stream 0.
- **The CPU does not wait after a launch.** It puts the kernel in the line and goes straight to its next line of code. So in normal running, the CPU is ahead: it has already put many kernels in the line while the GPU is still working on older ones. That is good, because the GPU never has to wait for new work.
- **A waiting call:** a few CUDA functions make the CPU stop until the GPU has finished every kernel already in the line. While the CPU is stopped, it adds nothing new. When the GPU finishes the last kernel, the line is empty and the GPU has nothing to do until the CPU adds the next kernel.
  - `cudaMemcpy`, a plain copy from CPU memory to GPU memory, is one such waiting call.
  - `cudaFree`, which gives GPU memory back, is another.
- **ms and µs:** 1 ms = 1,000 µs (microseconds). 20,014 µs = 20.0 ms.
- **nsys:** NVIDIA's profiler. It records every CUDA call the CPU makes and every kernel the GPU runs, with start and end times.

## Part 2: How a matmul is split into tiles

- A matmul output is a big table of numbers. The lm_head dX output, for example, has M_t rows × 512 columns.
- The GPU cuts this output into small blocks called *tiles*. With BluBLAS's choice here, each tile is 128 rows × 256 columns. So 512 columns = 2 tiles across, and M_t rows = M_t / 128 tiles down.
- The H200 has 132 compute units. Each one takes a tile, computes it, then takes the next one.
- The order in which tiles are handed out does not change the result. It only changes speed, because neighbouring tiles share input data that is already in the fast memory.

## Part 3: BluBLAS's tile-order list and its 16 slots

1. For some output shapes, BluBLAS writes down the tile order as a list in GPU memory. One of those shapes is *tall*: many more tile rows than tile columns. Our dX output is tall: for example 166 tile rows × 2 tile columns.
2. The CPU builds this list.
3. To avoid rebuilding it every call, BluBLAS keeps up to 16 lists, one per output shape. This is the "cache" ([Bgemm_sm90_warpspecialized_template.cuh:1681-1725](../BluTrain_push/Tensor-Implementations/BluBridge-BLAS/src/level3/batched_gemm/BF16/SM90/Bgemm_sm90_warpspecialized_template.cuh#L1681-L1725)).
4. On every matmul call, BluBLAS checks whether a list for this exact shape is already there.
   - **If yes:** use it. This takes a few µs.
   - **If no:** build the list on the CPU, reserve GPU memory for it (`cudaMalloc`), and copy it to the GPU with a plain `cudaMemcpy`. **That copy is a waiting call: the CPU stops until the GPU has finished everything already in the line.**
   - **If all 16 slots are full:** it also throws out the oldest list with `cudaFree`, which is another waiting call.
5. For tall shapes, the list is just "tile 0, tile 1, tile 2… row by row". The kernel could compute that itself. The list is not needed at all.

## Part 4: What the trained-rows switch changed

- **lm_head** is the last matmul. It turns each token's 512 numbers into 49,280 scores, one per vocabulary word. In the backward pass there is a matching matmul, *dX*, with output M × 512.
- **Before the switch:** lm_head ran for all tokens in the micro-batch (a micro-batch is the group of rows processed in one forward + backward). That is B × T tokens, the same number every micro-batch, so the dX output shape never changed. The list was built once at the start and reused forever.
- **With the switch:** lm_head runs only for tokens that have an answer label (the *trained rows*, M_t). M_t is different in every micro-batch, for example 21,248 in one and 24,832 in the next. So the dX output shape is different each time, there is never a list for it, and **every micro-batch, the CPU stops and waits for the whole line to finish**.

## Part 5: What we saw in the real trainer (10-31), and why it wasn't enough

- **Setup:** the 135M trainer under nsys, 10 steps with the switch off, then 10 steps with it on. At 4k context (20 micro-batches) and at 128k context (10 micro-batches).
- **Columns:** "extra" means calls in the switch-on run minus calls in the switch-off run. The last column is the total time the CPU was stopped inside those copies.

| context | micro-batches | extra `cudaMalloc` | extra `cudaMemcpy` | CPU stopped in copies, off → on |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 4k | 20 | +19 | +19 | 10 → 565 ms |
| 128k | 10 | +10 | +10 | 17 → 1,556 ms |

- **One new list per micro-batch:** the extra calls match that exactly. (At 4k, one M_t value happened to appear twice, so 19 instead of 20.)
- **Speed:**
  - The lm_head math got faster: 9 ms per step at 4k, 22 ms per step at 128k.
  - But the median step time got slower: 462 → 514 ms at 4k, 1160 → 1256 ms at 128k.
- **Why this didn't settle the question:** those runs also had large random delays from the trainer's own memory calls.
  - The trainer's own `cudaFree` time was 2.1 s in one run and 5.6 s in the other.
  - One 128k step took 12.1 s in one run and 6.5 s in the other.
  - With noise in the seconds, you can't tell what a 9–22 ms gain or loss came from.
- **So I wrote a small separate program** that runs only matmuls, with nothing else, to measure the list problem alone. I ran it on P032 GPU 1.

## Part 6: Test 1, "does a new shape make the CPU stop?"

**Why:** to see the stop directly, in isolation.

**What the program does, step by step:**
1. Puts one kernel in the line that does nothing except wait until 20 ms have passed. Now the GPU is busy for exactly 20 ms. The CPU is not stopped; it just added a kernel.
2. Immediately calls one dX matmul (output M × 512, like the lm_head backward).
3. Reads the CPU clock before and after that one call. That difference is how long the call kept the CPU stuck.
4. Waits until the GPU is done, then repeats. 20 times in total.

**Cases:**
- **Same M:** all 20 calls use M = 12,288. The list was built once before the test, so every call should find it.
- **New M:** each call uses a different M (8,448, 8,704, …), as with trained rows. No call finds a list.
- **New M, GPU idle:** same as new M, but without the 20 ms kernel. This shows the cost of building the list by itself, with nothing to wait for.
- **All three cases with BluBLAS, and again with cuBLAS** (NVIDIA's own matmul library) for comparison.

**What I expected:**
- If a call does not wait, it returns in a few µs.
- If it waits for the line, it returns only after the 20 ms kernel is done, so about 20,000 µs.

**Result:** median time one call kept the CPU stuck, out of 20 calls.

| library | same M | new M, GPU busy | new M, GPU idle |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| BluBLAS | 3 µs | 20,014 µs (= 20 ms), all 20 calls | 12 µs |
| cuBLAS | 9.5 µs | 95 µs; but 7 of the 20 calls took ~20 ms | 100 µs |

**What it means:**
- **BluBLAS, new M:** every call waited for the full 20 ms. With the GPU idle, the same call took only 12 µs. So building the list costs almost nothing; **the whole cost is the waiting.**
- **cuBLAS, new M:**
  - Usually about 0.1 ms. That is CPU time spent choosing a kernel for the new shape, with no waiting.
  - 7 calls did wait. In the nsys record, those 7 were the first time cuBLAS needed a kernel it had never used before in the program. Loading a new kernel made it wait (the waiting CUDA call was `cuKernelSetAttribute`).

**Extra check: the same 20 M values, twice in a row.**
- **Why:** to see whether a shape's cost is paid once or every time.
- **cuBLAS:**
  - First 20 calls: 7 waits.
  - Second 20 calls: 0 waits, all 8–46 µs.
  - So cuBLAS pays once per new kernel, then never again.
- **BluBLAS:**
  - Waited on all 40 calls.
  - The reason: 20 different shapes but only 16 slots. Each list is thrown out before its shape comes back, so every call misses again.

## Part 7: Test 2, "does the stop actually make training slower?"

**Why:** a CPU stop only costs time if the GPU runs out of work because of it. Test 1 proves the stop happens. Test 2 checks whether it costs time in a loop shaped like our training.

**What one iteration does (a fake training step):**
1. **Forward:** 37 layers. Each layer has 4 matmuls with our 135M model's sizes on 16,384 tokens, one 0.2 ms kernel standing in for attention (the attention time I took from the 10-31 profile at 4k), and 40 tiny kernels standing in for small ops such as norms and adds.
2. **lm_head:** its forward, dX and dW matmuls, with M_t rows.
3. **Backward:** 37 layers. Each has 8 matmuls, one 0.57 ms kernel for attention backward, and 50 tiny kernels.
4. **Optimizer:** 1,000 small matmuls and 2,000 tiny kernels.

**Cases:**
- **Fixed M_t:** 12,288 in every iteration.
- **New M_t:** a different value every iteration: 33 values from 8,192 to 16,384. Their average is also 12,288, so the GPU does the same total math in both cases, and any time difference comes only from the waiting.
- Each case with BluBLAS and with cuBLAS, 3 times each. Repeating shows how much identical runs differ (about 1 ms), so we know which differences are real.

**What is measured:**
- CPU clock time for 33 iterations, divided by 33: the time per iteration.
- One extra run under nsys, to measure **GPU idle time**: the time when no kernel was running on the GPU.

**Result:** time per iteration, three runs.

| | BluBLAS fixed | BluBLAS new M | cuBLAS fixed | cuBLAS new M |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| time per iteration | 63.5 / 62.8 / 63.6 ms | 63.7 / 62.8 / 62.8 ms | 61.3 / 61.3 / 60.8 ms | 62.8 / 62.5 / 63.6 ms |

**What it means:**
- BluBLAS with new M stopped the CPU about 9.5 ms in every iteration, but the iteration got no slower (the differences are within the 1 ms run-to-run noise).
- Why, step by step:
  1. The CPU puts the forward kernels in the line. It needs less time to add them than the GPU needs to run them, so it gets ahead.
  2. The CPU reaches the dX call and stops until the GPU finishes the forward. That is the ~9.5 ms of waiting.
  3. Now the line is empty and the GPU is idle.
  4. The CPU adds the next kernel within µs, and the GPU starts again.
  5. The backward kernels take the GPU longer to run than the CPU needs to add them, so the CPU is quickly ahead again.
- **nsys:** GPU idle was 6.47 ms per iteration with fixed M and 6.86 ms with new M. The stop added only 0.4 ms.
- **nsys also counted:** 35 list builds for 33 new shapes. The 2 extra builds are 2 of the model's own fixed shapes that were thrown out of the 16 slots and had to be rebuilt.
- **When the stop does cost time:** when, after the stop, the CPU needs longer to add kernels than the GPU needs to run them. Then the GPU sits idle, and the time the CPU spent waiting is lost.

## Part 8: Test 3, trying to create that bad case

**Why:** to see whether the stop costs time when the backward is heavy for the CPU, the way a framework spends some CPU time on every small op.

**What changed from test 2:** before each of 60 small kernels per layer in the backward, the CPU first spends 10 µs doing CPU work. That adds about 22 ms of CPU time per backward.

**Result:** still no difference. BluBLAS fixed was 64.4 / 64.3 / 63.3 ms, new M 64.3 / 63.4 / 63.4 ms.

**What it means:** the GPU's backward work (about 37 ms) was still longer than the CPU's 22 ms, so the CPU still caught up. **Test 3 did not reach the bad case, so it proves nothing new.** It only showed that my fake backward was not CPU-heavy enough.

## Part 9: What is proven and what is not

- **Proven:**
  - With trained rows, BluBLAS stops the CPU on every micro-batch until the whole line is finished.
  - The 16-slot cache cannot keep up with shapes that keep changing.
- **Proven:** when the GPU is the slower side after the stop, the stop costs almost nothing (0.4 ms per iteration in test 2).
- **Not proven:** that this stop is why our real trainer got slower.
  - The 4k numbers fit: the CPU was stopped about 56 ms per step, and the step got 52 ms slower.
  - But that is one run each, with seconds of random delay from the trainer's own memory calls.
- **To prove it:**
  1. Fix the list problem.
  2. Run the real trainer with the switch off and on, with more steps and several times each.
  3. Also look into the trainer's own memory calls (the 889 `cudaFree` task); otherwise their noise hides everything.

## Part 10: Your other questions

- **Memory caching or metadata caching?**
  - *Metadata* means helper information about how to run the matmul, here the tile-order list. It is not the matrices themselves.
  - The cache stores these lists, so it is a metadata cache.
  - The trouble is what happens on a miss: reserve memory, a copy, and (when full) a free. The copy and the free make the CPU wait.
  - The trainer's own memory calls (889 `cudaFree` per 10 steps) are a different problem.
- **What CUTLASS does:** I read its source (version 4.5.1). The kernel itself calculates each tile's position from the tile number: row = number ÷ tiles-across, column = remainder, with an optional reordering formula (`static_tile_scheduler.hpp:169-243`). Nothing is built on the CPU, nothing is copied, nothing is freed.
- **What cuBLAS does:** its code is closed, so I measured it (test 1). A new shape costs about 0.1 ms of CPU time to choose a kernel, with no waiting. It waits only the first time it loads a new kernel, then never again for it. The library file also contains the setting names `CUBLASLT_HEURISTICS_CACHE_CAPACITY` and `CUBLAS_AUTOTUNING_CACHE_CAPACITY`; those are its CPU-side "which kernel for this shape" cache.
- **MoE (your colleagues):**
  - In MoE, each token is sent to a few experts. Each expert has its own weights.
  - How many tokens each expert gets changes every step, for example 3,000 for one and 500 for another.
  - A *grouped GEMM* does all the experts' matmuls in one kernel.
  - In CUTLASS (and in DeepGEMM), the list of per-expert token counts stays in GPU memory and the kernel reads it there, so the CPU never needs those counts and never waits.
  - BluBLAS has no grouped GEMM. On BluBLAS you would call the normal matmul once per expert, each with a new token count, so most calls would miss the list cache and wait, for every expert, every step.
  - The CPU would also first need the token counts, which means copying them from the GPU to the CPU: another wait.
- **Does this fix the sm_86 wrong-rows bug? No, it's a separate bug.**
  - sm_86 (RTX 3060 / A100-class GPUs) uses completely different kernel code, with no list.
  - Its tile-order formula ([Bgemm_core_template.cuh:77-79](../BluTrain_push/Tensor-Implementations/BluBridge-BLAS/src/level3/batched_gemm/BF16/SM89/Bgemm_core_template.cuh#L77-L79)) hands out tile rows in groups of 8.
  - **Example, M = 6656:** 6656 ÷ 256 rows per tile = 26 tile rows. That is groups of 8, 8 and 8, then 2 left over.
    1. The formula treats the last group as if it had 8 rows.
    2. In that group, 6 of every 8 blocks get row numbers 26–31, which don't exist, so they quit.
    3. Only about a quarter of the column tiles in rows 24–25 get computed.
    4. 576 tiles are never written, so everything from row 6144 (= 24 × 256) onward is wrong.
  - **M = 8192:** 32 tile rows = 4 full groups, so nothing is skipped.
  - I checked this by running that exact formula by itself for each M (no GPU needed). It matches 11-01 exactly: 6464 / 6528 / 6656 wrong from row 6144, and 8192 correct.
  - It can hit any matmul on those GPUs whose tile-row count isn't a multiple of 8.
- **B300:** its kernels keep only 1 list per kernel type and rebuild it whenever the shape differs from the previous call, for all shapes. So it would stop even more often.

## Part 11: The fix (not done yet)

- **Tall shapes:** remove the list. The kernel calculates row = tile number ÷ tiles-across and column = remainder, the way CUTLASS does. No CPU work, no copy, no waiting.
- **Square shapes** (they use a curve order called Hilbert): calculate that on the GPU too, or keep one list per GPU that is never freed during a matmul and copied without waiting.
- **B300 and the other templates:** the same change.
- **sm_86:** fix the last group so every tile is computed.
- **Checks for each:**
  - the output is bit-for-bit the same as before;
  - the matmul time before and after;
  - the real trainer with the switch off and on, several runs.

Tell me which part is still unclear. When you say go, I'll start the fix.

## Your questions, answered with what I could prove so far

How I read the scope: B300 stays out. The SM90 tall-shape fix, the square-shape fix and the sm_86 fix are all in, to be analyzed, fixed and tested now, with every normal matmul checked too. Tell me if you meant something else.

### 1. Won't computing the order inside the kernel (the CUTLASS way) add GPU overhead?

**What the kernel does today for a tall grid:** before computing each tile, the GPU threads read that tile's row and column from the table in GPU memory, and they must wait for that read to come back.

**What it would do instead:** compute row = tile number ÷ tiles-across and column = remainder, with about 20–30 simple integer instructions.

- **This code already exists and already runs in normal training.** Wide grids, which are most of our matmuls, already compute their order like this on every call (`sm90_decode_tile_supergrouped`). The tall fix calls that same code with group size 1. That is check 1 above: the order is identical to the table.
- **Same order means the same output.** Each tile is computed by exactly the same instructions on the same data, so the result must be bit-for-bit identical.
- **The cost is once per tile, and tiles are long.**
  - A dX tile (K = 49,280) takes roughly 0.4 ms of math.
  - A 135M layer tile (K = 512) takes a few µs.
  - Either a table read or a few dozen instructions is a tiny fraction of that.
  - My expectation is "same or slightly faster", but that is an expectation, not proof. Adding a parameter can change how many registers the kernel uses, and that can change speed. So it must be measured (tests below).

### 2. Does the problem only happen for matmuls whose shape changes?

- **Yes, with one exception: more than 16 table-using shapes in one process.**
- **Proof:** in the 10-31 runs with the switch off, `cudaMalloc` was 43 and `cudaMemcpy` 58 at both 4k and 128k. The totals are identical, so all of those happened at start-up and none per step.
- **Our 135M trainer has 6–7 fixed table-using shapes**, from the eviction counts: 4k gives 6 + 19 − 16 = 9 evictions. With fewer than 16, after step 1 every call finds its table.
- **The exception:** if a process uses more than 16 different tall or square shapes, even fixed shapes start getting thrown out and rebuilt. That can happen with a bigger model, extra validation shapes, MoE, and so on. In my test 2, 2 fixed shapes were evicted this way.
- **Pretraining today:** fixed shapes, fewer than 16, so it doesn't hit this.

### 3. Who else computes logits only for trained tokens, and which matmul do they use?

**Apple Cut Cross-Entropy (CCE):** yes, only the trained rows. I read their GitHub source.
- **Picking the rows:** it builds the list of non-ignored positions with `valids = (targets != ignore_index).nonzero()` (`utils.py`).
- **Launch grid:** sized by the number of valid rows: `B = valids.numel()`, grid = `cdiv(B, BLOCK_B) * cdiv(V, BLOCK_V)` (`cce_lse_forward.py`).
- **Inside the kernel:** it loads each row's position from that list (`offs_b = tl.load(Valids + ...)`).
- **Matmul:** their own Triton kernels, with the matmul fused into the loss. Not cuBLAS.
- **Tile order:** computed inside the kernel, in groups of 8, and the last, partial group is handled: `group_size_b = min(num_pid_b - first_pid_b, GROUP_B)`. That is exactly the sm_86 fix.
- **Tuning:** autotuning is off by default (`CCE_AUTOTUNE` defaults to `"0"`), so a new row count needs no re-tuning.
- **One wait per loss call:** `.nonzero()` on a GPU tensor makes the CPU wait for the GPU, because PyTorch must know how many positions there are. Our switch builds the row list on the CPU from labels the CPU already has, so it doesn't need that wait.

**Unsloth:** its fused loss calls CCE (`unsloth_zoo/loss_utils.py`: `from cut_cross_entropy import linear_cross_entropy`). Same method.

**Liger:** does not do this. It runs the matmul on all rows, ignored ones included, in fixed-size chunks with `torch.mm` (cuBLAS), and the ignored rows only get masked in the loss ([fused_linear_cross_entropy.py:157-168, 187-198](../sft_research/Liger-Kernel/src/liger_kernel/ops/fused_linear_cross_entropy.py#L157-L168)).

**Plain Hugging Face:** cuBLAS on all rows.

So the ones that skip untrained rows use their own Triton matmul, with the order computed in the kernel. Those that use cuBLAS run it on all rows, and cuBLAS handles changing shapes without waiting (my test 1).

### 4. Compute the order for all tall shapes, or only the ones that change?

All tall shapes.
- The kernel cannot know which shapes will change later. Deciding on the CPU would need the same kind of bookkeeping that causes the problem.
- The order is identical (check 1), so results are identical.
- One code path is simpler and also removes the table memory and start-up copies for fixed shapes.
- The condition: the measurements show no slowdown on fixed tall shapes. If any shape gets slower, we decide again for that case.

### 5. Do the other fixes add overhead to normal cases?

- **sm_86:** where the current formula already works, the fixed one gives the identical order (check 2: 532 of 532 grids). So normal cases get the same tiles in the same order, giving the same output.
  - The only added instruction is a `min` per block.
  - Still to measure: speed on the laptop RTX 3060 (the only sm_86 GPU we have). **Is it OK to use the laptop GPU for that test?**
- **Square shapes (Hilbert order):** computing this inside the kernel is not a simple formula when the grid size is not a power of 2. The table skips curve points that fall outside the grid, so "the k-th tile" needs a search.
  - So for square shapes I propose to keep the table, with the kernel unchanged (zero GPU overhead), and fix only how the table is stored and copied:
    - one set of tables per GPU;
    - copied with `cudaMemcpyAsync` on the matmul's own queue, so the CPU does not wait;
    - never freed during a matmul.
  - To measure: no change in square-shape speed or output.

### 6. Your decision rule

If any normal matmul gets slower beyond measurement noise, we drop the logits optimization. Agreed, and it will be decided by the measurements below.

  - A tall table depends only on the number of tile columns, so one table per GPU and column count serves every M.
  - It grows only a few times per run, is copied without the CPU waiting, and is never freed.
- **The sm_86 bug fix** (laptop RTX 3060, 29 cases):
  - Normal cases: bit-identical and same speed.
  - Broken cases: correct now; before, up to 25 million output values were never written.
  - The same bug was in 3 files: BF16 and FP16 in groups of 8, and FP32 in groups of 16. H200 training never used those kernels.
- **What other libraries do:**
  - Apple CCE computes logits only for trained rows, in its own Triton kernels, with the tile order computed inside the kernel and the last partial group handled.
  - Unsloth uses CCE.
  - Liger and plain Hugging Face run cuBLAS on all rows.
