No, not pakka in all directions. CP=2 is proven correct for the cases we ran, but several real-use cases have never been run. I checked this against the result files and the run logs.

### What was tested (11-07, 2× H200, GPUs locked)

Each test ran the same data and the same start weights for 30 steps, once with CP off (the whole row on 1 GPU) and once with CP=2 (each row split over 2 GPUs).
- **Step-0 val loss** checks the forward pass.
- **Step-0 grad norm** checks the backward pass.
- **Noise** is the gap between two identical CP-off runs. A CP difference smaller than the noise means CP is correct.

| Case | Step-0 val loss, off → CP=2 | Grad norm, CP=2 vs off | Noise | Speed | Memory per GPU |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 135M, 4k, B 4 | 1.424576 → 1.424576 | +0.000% (3.0473 both) | 0.000% | 55.9 → 49.7 ms | 23.4 → 21.6 GB |
| 135M, 64k, B 1 | 3.216672 → 3.216672 | −0.019% | 0.56% | 250.7 → 158.2 ms | 61.5 → 36.3 GB |
| 135M, 128k, B 1 | 3.216672 → 3.216672 | +0.18% | 0.24% | 492.9 → 297.9 ms | 111.0 → 62.2 GB |
| 1.6B, 4k (random init) | 11.232169 → 11.23217 | +0.017% | – | 480.0 → 274.5 ms | 66.7 → 42.4 GB |
| 1.6B, 64k | 1 GPU runs out of memory | no reference possible | – | 861 ms | 96.6 GB |
| **Control: CP=2 with the old TI (no fix)** | same | **−6.9%** | | | |

- The control run shows the test does catch the bug.
- The train loss over the 30 steps also stayed within noise in every case.
- What those runs actually used: Muon, segmented embedding, ZeRO-1 with the reduce overlap on, bf16 logits, packed rows, grad clip, and validation at step 0.

### What was NOT tested

| # | Case | Risk | How to test | GPUs, time |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **CP + data parallel**, e.g. 4 GPUs = 2 CP × 2 DP | **High.** The loader split, the token counts (divided by U) and the gradient sum over 4 ranks have never run | 4 GPUs: CP=2×DP=2 vs DP=4 vs 1 GPU | 4 GPUs, ~10 min |
| 2 | **Checkpoint save + resume under CP** | **High.** The save interval was 1000, so nothing was ever saved in 30 steps | Save at step 10, resume, compare with a run that didn't stop | 2 GPUs, ~10 min |
| 3 | **Gradient accumulation > 1 under CP** | Medium. Every test used GRAD_ACCUM 1 | GRAD_ACCUM 2, CP=2 vs off | 2 GPUs, ~5 min |
| 4 | **A long run** (hundreds of steps) | Medium. Only 30 steps were compared | Several hundred steps, CP=2 vs off, compare the loss curves | 2 GPUs, ~15-30 min |
| 5 | **U = 3 or 6 on the 1.6B** (18 q / 6 KV heads allow it) | Medium. Only U=2 has run | U=3 on 3 GPUs, U=6 on 6 | 3-6 GPUs, ~10 min |
| 6 | overlap_refresh ON with CP | Low-medium. The tests had it off | One 30-step run | 2 GPUs, ~2 min |
| 7 | Validation in the middle of a run | Low. Only step 0 ran, but it's the same code | Set the val interval to 10 | inside test 4 |
| 8 | AdamW instead of Muon | Low. CP doesn't touch the optimizer | One 30-step run | 2 GPUs, ~2 min |
| 9 | A CP rank whose half of the row has 0 trained tokens | Low. The loss divides by the global count, but it was never checked on purpose | A row with all trained tokens in the first half | inside test 1 |
| 10 | GPUs other than H200 (generic attention) | Unknown | Only if CP is needed there | – |

### Limits by design (refused with an error, not bugs)

- U must divide the KV heads. So CP=4 is impossible on the 135M (2 KV heads), and on the 1.6B the options are 2, 3 or 6. Going further needs Adhitya's ring + Ulysses hybrid.
- The trained-rows switch is refused with CP.
- At 4k, CP is slower than plain data parallel (49.7 vs 38.4 ms). Use CP only when one row doesn't fit on one GPU.
- The 1.6B 64k result only shows that it runs; there's no reference to compare against. Its correctness is inferred from the 1.6B 4k match and the 135M 64k match.

**My view:** CP=2 itself is correct. Before a real long-context SFT run, tests 1, 2 and 3 are needed: data parallel, checkpoint resume, and gradient accumulation. That's about 25 minutes on 4 GPUs. Test 4 is worth adding if a long run is planned. I'll prepare the scripts on the CPU first, and I won't run anything until you give the GPUs and say go.

**Symmetric test:** **75 of 75 pass**. 7 come out "mirrored" and 68 "same as OFF". "Same as OFF" doesn't by itself mean the flag was ignored: when the normal full GEMM is already exactly symmetric, the mirrored result equals it bit for bit. The log's "OFF itself asymmetric" count tells the two apart, and the speed stage will show whether tiles were really skipped. Pulling the S log to check each case:
> tool `Bash`: Pull the S log and list each case's mode and asymmetry

Every case is correct. "Same as OFF" is explained by the last column:

- **All X·Xᵀ / Xᵀ·X cases and the addmm cases with alpha 1:** the normal full GEMM (OFF) is already exactly symmetric ("OFF itself asymmetric 0"), so a mirrored result must equal it bit for bit. Whether those calls really skipped tiles will show in the speed stage, which is running now.
- **The real Newton-Schulz addmm, `B = b·A + c·A@A` with the per-batch bias:** here the full GEMM is off by the last bit in 1-13 elements, so the mirror is visible. All 7 such cases (n 256 / 512 / 768 / 2304, batch 1 / 5 / 37) come out **mirrored**: lower half bit-identical to OFF, upper half an exact copy, error under the bound. So the combined path that neither line had ever tested (per-batch bias + symmetric) works.

**Speed results (ms per call, median of 7 rounds of 20 calls, H200 GPU 7).** "ON/OFF" below 1 means the symmetric mode is faster. "null" is OFF compared with a second OFF run; it stays within about ±2%, so differences larger than that are real.

| Model, matrices | n | A = X·Xᵀ ON/OFF | B = b·A + c·A@A ON/OFF |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1.6B q/o (52) | 2304 | **0.706** (1.77 → 1.25 ms) | **0.687** (2.05 → 1.41) |
| 1.6B gate/up (52) | 2304, K 6144 | **0.627** (4.70 → 2.95) | **0.691** |
| 1.6B down (26) | 2304, K 6144 | **0.617** | **0.696** |
| 1.6B k/v (52) | 768 | 0.873 | 1.039 (4% slower) |
| 135M q/o (74) | 512 | **1.270 (27% slower)** | 1.058 |
| 135M k/v (74) | 256 | **1.376 (38% slower)** | 1.293 |
| 135M gate/up (74) | 512, K 1408 | 0.992 | 1.057 |
| 135M down (37) | 512, K 1408 | 0.902 | 0.966 |

So Aparna's mode is a **30-38% saving on the 1.6B's big Newton-Schulz products** (n = 2304), but it **slows the 135M's small ones** by up to 38%. On small matrices the extra mirror launch and the shorter tile list cost more than the skipped tiles. This confirms that phase 2 needs a size threshold: turn it on only from about n ≥ 768-2304, never at 256/512. The timing changes also prove the shortened tile list really runs in the X·Xᵀ calls. The SFT A/B is running now.

### CLAUDE [2026-11-11 18:52 IST]

Your worry is right to check, but the push can't slow down the 135M or any small model. The symmetric mode is **off by default**, and nothing on our line, `preproduction-135M` or `madhu_post-training` turns it on. With it off, the merged library is the same code as today. The tests show this directly:

- every existing kernel is byte-identical;
- the 84 real 135M SFT GEMM shapes give bit-identical results;
- the 135M SFT step time is the same: 104.9 ms vs a6d4292's 104.2-105.1 ms.

So pushing the merge changes nothing for our trainers. The slowdown only happens if some caller switches the mode on for small matrices.

**Where it could hurt:** Aparna's own caller (TI `coconut`, her compiler line) switches it on for every Newton-Schulz matrix regardless of size. She only measured the 1.5B. Even then, the absolute cost for a 135M is small. This is an estimate from the per-call times we measured (5 Newton-Schulz iterations, all matrices on 1 GPU), not a trainer run with the mode on:

| | Mode off | Mode on | Per optimizer step (5 iterations) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 135M: X·Xᵀ + addmm, all matrices, one iteration | 0.334 ms | 0.352 ms | about **+0.09 ms slower** (~0.1% of a 110 ms step) |
| 1.6B: same | 14.2 ms | 9.5 ms | about **−24 ms faster** |

The large relative slowdowns (up to 38%) are on GEMMs that only take 0.01-0.05 ms each, so the total is tiny. The large gains are on the big 1.6B products.

**What hasn't been tested yet:**
1. a trainer run with the mode **on**, because no caller on our line uses it yet (that's phase 2);
2. a fine sweep to find the exact size where it starts to pay off (we know 2304 gains, 768 is mixed, 512 and below lose);
3. other GPUs: on B300 and Ada the flag is ignored, which is correct but gives no gain.

### CLAUDE [2026-11-11 21:00 IST]

Short answer: yes, we already use PTX in our hot kernels, the same way DeepSeek does. "DeepSeek used PTX" isn't the secret by itself. The setup first, then what they did, then us.

**What PTX is**

Every CUDA kernel goes through these steps when it's compiled:

| Step | What it is | Who writes it |
|---|---|---|
| CUDA C++ | the normal kernel code | us |
| **PTX** | NVIDIA's intermediate assembly (a virtual instruction set, the same across GPU generations) | made by `nvcc` from C++, or written by hand with inline `asm volatile("...")` |
| SASS | the real machine code for one GPU (sm_90a for H200, sm_103a for B300) | made by `ptxas` from PTX; NVIDIA gives no official way to write it |

So every CUDA kernel is PTX at some point. "Using PTX" means writing some instructions by hand, inside a CUDA C++ kernel, because C++ doesn't expose them or the compiler doesn't use them well.

**What DeepSeek actually did** (V3 report, DeepEP and DeepGEMM repos, from memory)
- **Communication kernels (DeepEP):** for MoE all-to-all between GPUs, they used customized PTX instructions. One of them is a load NVIDIA doesn't document for this use (`ld.global.nc.L1::no_allocate.L2::256B`). The point was to use only about 20 of the 132 SMs for communication and keep the L2 cache clean, so training compute runs at the same time.
- **FP8 GEMM (DeepGEMM):** CUDA C++ with inline PTX (wgmma, TMA). They even patched the compiled SASS afterwards ("FFMA SASS interleaving").
- **Why they needed it:** their H800s have reduced NVLink bandwidth, so they had to squeeze communication.

Videos and blogs turned this into "DeepSeek bypassed CUDA". They didn't: they wrote CUDA C++ with hand-written PTX inside, exactly the pattern you describe.

**Can a whole kernel be written in PTX?** Technically yes: PTX is a full language, and a `.ptx` file can be loaded with the driver API. Almost nobody does it for real kernels. The normal way, used by CUTLASS, FlashAttention-3, DeepGEMM and us, is **CUDA C++ for the structure, inline PTX for the critical instructions**. Even then `ptxas` makes the final choices (register allocation, instruction order). We saw that ourselves: the wgmma wait-order trick, and the R2UR count in the SASS.

**What we already use** (in BluBLAS SM90 and our SM90 attention)
- `wgmma.mma_async` (Hopper tensor-core matmul);
- TMA (`cp.async.bulk.tensor`);
- `mbarrier`;
- `cp.async` with commit/wait groups;
- `griddepcontrol` (PDL);
- `ldmatrix` / `stmatrix`.

We also tried `setmaxnreg` (parked), and we read and count SASS (the instruction-excess and R2UR work). So for GEMM and attention we work at the same level. The older Tensor-Implementations kernels (for example `matmul_bf16_optimized`) are plain CUDA with `wmma`. That's the C++ API, not hand-written PTX.

**The downsides of PTX**
1. **Tied to one GPU generation.** `wgmma` exists only on Hopper (sm_90a); Blackwell uses `tcgen05`. That's why BluBLAS has separate SM103 kernels.
2. **Easy to get subtly wrong.** Several of our 13 GEMM bugs on 11-05 were exactly this kind: a `cp.async` commit inside an `if`, a gemv thread returning before the barrier. They gave silently wrong results.
3. **Undocumented behaviour can break** on a new driver or GPU (DeepEP's load is "out of spec" by their own words).
4. **More code to maintain and test.**

**So what is special about DeepSeek?** Mainly the system design around those kernels:
- FP8 training with fine-grained scaling;
- DualPipe, which overlaps communication with compute;
- MLA attention;
- MoE load balancing without the auxiliary loss;
- kernels shaped to their hardware limits.

PTX is one tool they used for that. Our gap versus them is at that system level (FP8 training, communication at MoE scale), not "PTX or no PTX".

**Short answer:** every SFT run we have done used the same scheduler: a linear warm-up over the first 3% of the steps, then cosine decay down to one tenth of the peak LR. The other three schedulers are in the trainer but I found no run recorded with any of them, so the comparison between the four was never done.

## What we used in the runs

| Runs | Scheduler | Warm-up | End LR |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1.6B SFT (from step 8000, Oct 6 onward) | cosine | 3% | peak ÷ 10 (2e-5 → 2e-6) |
| 135M stage-1 grid (Oct 28, LR × chats per step) | cosine | 3% | peak ÷ 10 |
| 135M format-study screen | cosine | 3% | peak ÷ 10 |
| 135M before/after and CP runs (Nov 6 onward) | cosine | 3% | peak ÷ 10 |

Cosine is the default in both the trainer (`BLU_SFT_SCHEDULE`) and the launcher (`SCHEDULE` in `sft/run_sft.sh`), so any run that did not set it got cosine.

## The four schedulers in the trainer

They were added on Oct 28 for stage 2 of the 135M grid, in [bluscript_sft.cpp:1600](../BluTrain_push/train/production_zero/bluscript_sft.cpp#L1600). All four start with the same linear warm-up.

| `BLU_SFT_SCHEDULE` | After the warm-up | Who uses it for SFT |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `cosine` (default) | LR falls along a cosine curve to peak ÷ 10 | SmolLM2 (with 10% warm-up) |
| `linear` | LR falls in a straight line to peak ÷ 10 | Tülu 3 (warm-up 3%), Moonlight (linear to 0) |
| `constant` | LR stays at the peak until the end | no published SFT recipe we read |
| `wsd` | LR stays at the peak, then cosine decay over the last 20% of the steps (`BLU_SFT_DECAY_FRAC`) | no published SFT recipe; it is our pretraining shape |

## What the research found

- **Published SFT recipes use only cosine or linear.**
  - Tülu 3 uses linear with warm-up 0.03 (its Table 11).
  - Moonlight uses linear to 0.
  - SmolLM2 uses cosine with 10% warm-up.
  - The Qwen2.5-7B test in our optimizer doc uses cosine from 2e-5 to 2e-6.
- **Nobody uses WSD or constant for SFT.** This was the colleague's point, and we recorded it in the work log on Oct 28. We kept WSD as one arm only, because it is the shape our pretraining used (3.5e-4 → 3.5e-5).
- **Our first plan said linear.** The early plan (research doc §3.11) copied Tülu 3, but the trainer was built with cosine and all runs used it. The work log already notes that the settings table still says "linear" while we use cosine.
- **Warm-up correction.** One chat answer on Oct 30 said "10% warm-up", but the launcher used 3%. This is correction 20 in the plan file.
- **Yano et al. (arXiv 2603.16127) is a separate question.** It is about the pretraining schedule: a base pretrained without LR decay fine-tunes better (1B: 54.4 vs 53.4; 8B: 55.0 vs 53.9). For us that is the 750B vs 900B checkpoint test (side experiment X2), which has not been run.

## What is still open

- **Stage 2 never ran.** The plan was the best LR and batch × 4 schedulers × 2 arms. Stage 1 was stopped on Oct 28 at 14:55 for the 8192 benchmarks, and the work then moved to the format study.
- **The schedule is still undecided in the plan.** It is factor 8 in `plan_grid_search_sft.md`, grouped with LR, chats per step and epochs (factors 6-9).
- **Linear, constant and WSD are compile-checked only.** I found no run with them, so they have no result and no correctness check on a real run.

### CLAUDE [2026-11-12 18:17 IST]

**WSD = Warmup, Stable, Decay.** The LR rises (warm-up), stays at the peak (stable), then falls (decay).

There is no angle setting in any of them. The fall is fixed by three numbers: the peak LR, the end LR, and how many steps the fall has. The end LR is peak ÷ 10 for every schedule that decays, including WSD (it can be changed with `BLU_SFT_MIN_LR`).

Example with the 135M stage-1 run: 6,996 steps, peak 1e-4, end 1e-5, warm-up 3% = 210 steps.

| Schedule | Steps 0-209 | After the warm-up | LR at the last step |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| cosine | rises 0 → 1e-4 | falls along the cosine curve over the remaining 6,786 steps | 1e-5 |
| linear | same | falls in a straight line over the same 6,786 steps | 1e-5 |
| wsd | same | stays at 1e-4 for 5,387 steps, then falls along the cosine curve over the last 1,399 steps (20% of 6,996) | 1e-5 |
| constant | same | stays at 1e-4 | 1e-4 |

**Linear:** the slope comes out of those numbers: (1e-4 − 1e-5) ÷ 6,785 = about 1.3e-8 lower per step, the same amount every step.

**Cosine:** it also goes from the peak to peak ÷ 10 with nothing extra to set. Only the shape of the fall differs from linear: slow at the start, fastest in the middle, slow again at the end.

| Point in the fall | Cosine LR | Linear LR |
| --- | --- | --- |
| start | 1.00e-4 | 1.00e-4 |
| 25% | 8.68e-5 | 7.75e-5 |
| 50% | 5.50e-5 | 5.50e-5 |
| 75% | 2.32e-5 | 3.25e-5 |
| end | 1.00e-5 | 1.00e-5 |

So cosine keeps the LR higher than linear in the first half and lower in the second half; they meet in the middle and at both ends.

**WSD:** the 20% is how long the fall lasts and the 10% is where it ends, so both apply. It falls along the same cosine curve, only squeezed into the last 20% of the steps, and it stops at peak ÷ 10, not at 0.

### CLAUDE [2026-11-12 18:49 IST]
> tool `Edit`: /home/blu-bridge016/Downloads/Neural_Networks_exp_1926/work_docs(mark-down - (.md) files ) /learning_rate_schedulers.md

**Position** is the step's place inside the fall only, as a number from 0 to 1. It is not its place in the whole run: the warm-up steps are not counted.

    position = (step − first step of the fall) ÷ (steps in the fall − 1)

In the 135M stage-1 run the fall is steps 210 to 6,995:

| step | position |
| --- | --- |
| 210 (first step of the fall) | 0 |
| 1,906 | 0.25 |
| 3,603 (middle) | 0.50 |
| 5,299 | 0.75 |
| 6,995 (last step) | 1 |

**Why "1 + cos" and the 0.5:** the formula needs a factor that starts at 1 (full peak) and ends at 0 (end LR). The cosine alone goes from +1 to −1, so it is corrected in two small moves:

| piece | position 0 | position 0.5 | position 1 | why |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| π × position | 0 | π/2 | π | takes exactly half a cosine wave, top to bottom, so it only falls |
| cos(π × position) | +1 | 0 | −1 | the plain cosine |
| 1 + cos(…) | 2 | 1 | 0 | adding 1 makes it end at 0 and never go negative |
| 0.5 × (1 + cos(…)) | 1 | 0.5 | 0 | halving makes it run from 1 to 0 |

Then `LR = end + factor × (peak − end)`. Factor 1 gives the peak, factor 0 gives the end LR.

One step by hand, at position 0.25 with peak 1e-4 and end 1e-5:

- cos(π × 0.25) = 0.707
- 1 + 0.707 = 1.707
- 0.5 × 1.707 = 0.854
- LR = 1e-5 + 0.854 × 9e-5 = 8.68e-5

**Why a cosine at all:** it is flat at its top and flat at its bottom, so the LR leaves the peak slowly and arrives at the end LR slowly. It is a common choice, not something proven best; linear is used just as much.

**If your "0.1" meant the end LR (peak ÷ 10):** that is not part of the cosine formula. It is only our trainer's default for where the fall ends, the same ratio as our pretraining (3.5e-4 → 3.5e-5). It can be changed with `BLU_SFT_MIN_LR`; Tülu 3 and Moonlight end at 0.

I added all three to the document as Q11, Q12 and Q13.

### CLAUDE [2026-11-12 19:05 IST]
> tool `Edit`: /home/blu-bridge016/Downloads/Neural_Networks_exp_1926/work_docs(mark-down - (.md) files ) /learning_rate_schedulers.md

This is the actual formula from the trainer's code (`get_lr`), for a step in the fall:

    decay_ratio = (step − (warmup + stable)) ÷ ((max_steps − (warmup + stable)) − 1)
    coeff       = 0.5 × (1 + cos(π × decay_ratio))
    lr          = min_lr + coeff × (max_lr − min_lr)

So it is not `min + cos(…) × (peak − min)`. The cosine first becomes a factor from 1 to 0 (the `coeff` line), and that factor is what multiplies `(peak − min)`.

Each line answers one question:

| line | question | range |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `decay_ratio` | how far through the fall is this step? | 0 (start) to 1 (end) |
| `coeff` | how much of the drop is still left to do? | 1 (all of it) to 0 (none) |
| `lr` | what is the actual LR for that? | peak down to min LR |

**Why `(peak − min)`:** the LR has to go from the peak down to the min LR, not down to 0. So the total amount it has to lose is peak − min. With peak 1e-4 and min 1e-5, the whole drop is 9e-5.

**Why `min +`:** the LR must never go below the min LR. So the min LR is always there, and only the drop part is scaled by the factor:

    lr = min LR + (the part of the drop that is still left)
       = min LR + factor × (peak − min)

| factor | min LR + factor × drop | LR | meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 1e-5 + 1 × 9e-5 | 1e-4 | nothing dropped yet: the peak |
| 0.854 | 1e-5 + 0.854 × 9e-5 | 8.68e-5 | 85.4% of the drop still left |
| 0.5 | 1e-5 + 0.5 × 9e-5 | 5.5e-5 | half of the drop done |
| 0.146 | 1e-5 + 0.146 × 9e-5 | 2.32e-5 | 14.6% of the drop still left |
| 0 | 1e-5 + 0 × 9e-5 | 1e-5 | whole drop done: the min LR |

**What goes wrong without these two pieces:**

- `lr = factor × peak`: at factor 0 the last step gets LR 0, not the min LR.
- `lr = min + factor × peak`: at factor 1 the start gets peak + min, which is above the peak.
- Only `min + factor × (peak − min)` gives exactly the peak at factor 1 and exactly the min LR at factor 0.

**The cosine only decides the factor.** Linear uses the same last line; only the factor differs:

| schedule | factor | LR |
| --- | --- | --- |
| cosine | 0.5 × (1 + cos(π × position)) | min + factor × (peak − min) |
| linear | 1 − position | min + factor × (peak − min) |

Both factors go from 1 to 0. The linear factor loses the same amount every step. The cosine factor loses little at the start, most in the middle, and little at the end.

I added this to the document as Q14.

### CLAUDE [2026-11-12 19:13 IST]
> tool `Edit`: /home/blu-bridge016/Downloads/Neural_Networks_exp_1926/work_docs(mark-down - (.md) files ) /learning_rate_schedulers.md

Yes, both are right: cos(0) = +1 gives factor 1 and the peak LR, and cos(π) = −1 gives factor 0 and the min LR.

It is one formula. The code only writes it on three lines so it is readable. On one line:

    lr = min_lr + 0.5 × (1 + cos(π × (step − first step of the fall) ÷ (steps in the fall − 1))) × (peak − min_lr)

All three pieces are needed, because each one does a different job:

| piece | job | what breaks without it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| position (step → 0 … 1) | gives the cosine an input that runs from 0 to π over exactly the steps of the fall | the curve would not start at the first step of the fall or finish at the last step |
| 0.5 × (1 + cos) | cos gives +1 … −1; this turns it into 1 … 0 | the factor would go negative |
| min + factor × (peak − min) | turns the factor into an LR between the peak and the min LR | the LR would end at 0 or start above the peak |

And yes, this is how everyone writes it:

- **The paper it comes from** (Loshchilov and Hutter, "SGDR", 2017): `η = η_min + 0.5 × (η_max − η_min) × (1 + cos(π × T_cur ÷ T_max))`.
- **PyTorch `CosineAnnealingLR`:** the same expression, with `eta_min` as the min LR.
- **Hugging Face `get_cosine_schedule_with_warmup`:** `0.5 × (1 + cos(π × progress))` times the peak LR. That is the same formula with min LR = 0, so it ends at 0.

So ours is the standard cosine formula, with the min LR set to peak ÷ 10. I quoted the three outside formulas from memory, not from their sources today.

| --- | --- | --- |

| 65,536 (B 1) | out of memory at 143.1 GB | 96.6 GB per GPU |

My estimate from these numbers is that one 32,768-token row would need roughly 95 to 100 GB on one GPU, so it should fit on an H200 (143.8 GB). That is a calculation, not a run. It needs one short run to confirm.

I read the whole paper (Balestriero and LeCun, 29 Oct 2026, 35 pages with the appendix). Some of what you assumed is not right, so I start there.

## Your questions

**1. What are CLIP and DINO?** Neither is an audio or video model, and neither generates anything. Both are encoders: an image goes in, one vector comes out.

| model | what it is | trained on | size (from my memory, not from the paper) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| DINOv2 | image-only encoder, never sees text | crops of the same photo | ViT-S 22M, ViT-B 86M, ViT-L 300M, ViT-g 1.1B |
| CLIP | two encoders, one for images and one for text, trained together | 400M image-caption pairs (the ViT-H one: LAION-2B) | ViT-B/32 about 150M in total, ViT-H image side about 630M |

The main comparison uses DINOv2 ViT-B. There is no audio in the paper. Video appears only in one small test (MSR-VTT, 7k clips).

**2. What is the 109M model?** A BERT-base encoder (12 layers, bidirectional, max 64 tokens) trained from scratch on image captions only. It cannot generate text or predict the next word. A caption goes in, one vector comes out.

**3. "Beats Qwen2.5-72B" in what?** Only in one thing: how similar its embedding space is to the image model's embedding space. It is not a benchmark of answers, reasoning or generation.

The score is mutual 10-NN, measured like this:
- Take 1,024 Wikipedia image-caption pairs (WIT).
- For each image, find its 10 nearest images in DINOv2's space.
- For its caption, find the 10 nearest captions in the text model's space.
- Count how many of the 10 are the same pairs, then average over all pairs.

A score of 0.184 means about 1.8 of 10 neighbours agree. For Qwen, the caption vector is the mean of the hidden states, and the best layer is taken.

## What the paper claims

- **Theory:** if two models are trained separately on two modalities, and their "positive pairs" are two observations of the same scene, both learn the same embedding up to one rotation.
- **Good views:** two different captions of one image, or two photos of one scene.
- **Bad views:** two corruptions of one sample, such as two maskings of one caption or two crops of one photo.
- **Next-token prediction:** they show it has the form of a bad-view JEPA (prefix and its continuation, from one document). So it spends embedding dimensions on wording and style, which an image model cannot match.

## Main numbers

All three of "ours" are the same 109M BERT, the same texts (captions of 940M web images) and the same 900M samples. Only the objective differs. Columns: mutual 10-NN on WIT with DINOv2 ViT-B, then with CLIP ViT-H, then on 5,000 COCO pairs with DINOv2 ViT-B.

| text model | WIT, DINOv2 | WIT, CLIP-H | COCO |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ours, good views | .184 | .230 | .161 |
| ours, next-token | .111 | .146 | not measured |
| ours, bad views | .088 | .116 | not measured |
| Qwen2.5-72B | .154 | .210 | .108 |
| Llama-3-70B | .151 | .206 | .113 |
| CLIP text encoder | .124 | .159 | .132 |
| all-mpnet-base-v2 | .118 | .159 | .156 |

Other results:
- **Sample efficiency:** good views reach .109 with 21.6M samples; next-token needs 900M for .111 (42 times more).
- **Captioning:** frozen DINOv2 + one linear map fitted on 30k pairs + a text-only decoder gives CIDEr .838 on COCO.
- **No pairs at all:** 64.4% top-5 on ImageNet-100, against 47.6% for Qwen3-8B with the same method.

## My analysis

**Solid part:** the same-texts, same-encoder comparison (good .184, next-token .111, bad .088). It holds at every data size, every seed and every vision model they tried.

**Weaker part: the "beats 72B" headline.**
- **Image information leaks into the training text.** Two of the three texts per image were written by LLaVA, which looks at the image through CLIP. With no image captioner (alt-text plus a text-only paraphrase), good views reach .060 instead of .107 at the 2M-image scale. The authors say the comparison with LLMs relies on these texts.
- **The grouping is paired information.** Good views need to know which texts describe the same image.
- **One setting was selected on the test benchmark.** A seed with twice the SIGReg weight scored .121, not .184; they kept the other weight after seeing this. All four seeds average .168, still above Qwen-72B's .154.
- **The benchmark is small.** At smaller scales the authors say the differences from LLMs are within noise.
- **The comparison is not like for like.** Qwen is trained to generate all kinds of text, and its embedding is a mean of hidden states it was never trained to make useful. The JEPA is trained only on captions, and the test is captions.
- **As a text encoder it is not the best.** On sentence similarity (STS-B) it scores .632, above BERT-base (.551) but below all-mpnet (.834).

**What it means for us:** nothing in it says next-token prediction is worse for language modelling. It says next-token prediction is an inefficient way to get embeddings that match a vision model. It matters if we ever want a text encoder to join with an image encoder; it does not change pretraining or SFT of a generative model.

The proofs are for an idealised case (finite world, perfect optimum), and the authors state that no experiment meets those conditions exactly.

### CLAUDE [2026-11-12 21:59 IST]

No, neither model ever gets an image.

**How the 109M model is trained:** on text only. For each web image it gets three texts about that image (the alt-text and two captions). Two of these texts are a positive pair. The image itself is never given to the model. The image is used only to know which texts belong together.

**Qwen2.5-72B:** the normal text-only next-word model, not multimodal. It also never gets an image.

**How the test works** (1,024 image-caption pairs from Wikipedia):

| step | what goes in | which model | what comes out |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | the 1,024 images | DINOv2 (image-only model) | 1,024 image vectors |
| 2 | the 1,024 captions | the 109M text model | 1,024 text vectors |
| 3 | the same 1,024 captions | Qwen2.5-72B (mean of its hidden states) | 1,024 text vectors |

So the images go only to DINOv2, and the captions go to the text models.

**What is compared:** the vectors themselves are not compared, and they are not the same. They even have different sizes (DINOv2 768, the 109M model 768, Qwen much larger). What is compared is the neighbours:

- For image number 5, DINOv2 gives its 10 nearest images, say numbers 12, 40, 77 and so on.
- For caption number 5, the text model gives its 10 nearest captions.
- The score is how many of these 10 numbers are the same in both lists, averaged over all 1,024.

Result with DINOv2 ViT-B: the 109M model shares 1.84 of 10 neighbours on average (score .184), and Qwen2.5-72B shares 1.54 of 10 (score .154).

So the claim is that the 109M text model arranges captions more like DINOv2 arranges the images than Qwen does. That is the only place where it beats Qwen.

One correction to my last message: I said two of the three texts were written by LLaVA, "which looks at the image through CLIP". That part is still true, and it is the one indirect way image information reaches the 109M model: through the caption text, not through pixels.

### CLAUDE [2026-11-12 22:07 IST]

Three corrections first, then how it works.

- **No video.** It is images (DINOv2) and text.
- **The 1,024 images and captions are only the test.** No model is trained on them.
- **"Similar" is weak.** The best score is 1.84 shared neighbours out of 10. Chance is 0.1 out of 10. So it is far above chance, but most neighbours still differ.

## How an image model reads an image

Text is also only numbers to a model (token ids). An image model does the same kind of thing with pixels:

1. The image is cut into small squares (patches) of 14 x 14 pixels. A 224 x 224 image gives 256 patches.
2. Each patch (its pixel numbers) goes through one linear layer and becomes one vector. This is the same role as a token embedding in text.
3. These 256 vectors go through transformer layers with attention, the same as tokens do.
4. One vector comes out for the whole image.

So a patch plays the role of a token. The architecture is nearly the same as a text model.

## How DINOv2 is trained without any text

- Take one photo and make two different crops of it.
- Train the model so both crops give nearly the same vector.
- Add a term that stops all images collapsing to one vector.

After this, photos with the same content (dog on a beach) end up close together, because their crops share the same patterns. No label or caption is used.

## How the 109M text model is trained

- Take two different captions of the same image.
- Train the model so both give nearly the same vector.
- The same anti-collapse term.

After this, captions about the same content end up close together.

## Why the two come out similar

Neither model understands the other, and their vectors are different numbers. What is similar is only which items are near which.

- Both data sets describe the same world. A photo of a dog on a beach and a caption "a dog runs on the beach" come from the same scene.
- Both training rules say the same thing: two observations of the same scene must be close.
- So in both models, which items are neighbours is decided by the scenes, not by pixels or words. Dog-on-beach photos are near other dog-on-beach photos; dog-on-beach captions are near other dog-on-beach captions.

That is what the test measures: for image 5 and caption 5, are the neighbours the same items.

The paper's theorem says this exactly: if both sides use the same rule for which scenes are positives, the two solutions are the same up to one rotation. That holds only in their idealised setting; in the real runs the agreement is partial (1.84 of 10).

## Why Qwen scores lower on this

Qwen's training pair is a prefix and its next word, from one document. So its vectors also keep wording and writing style. An image model has nothing that matches wording or style, so that part of Qwen's space cannot agree with DINOv2.

### USER [2026-11-13 11:53 IST]

so currently we used 37 layers righ ? so in each step , in each forward and backward pass , we usually goes through , those 37 transfromer blocks right ?per each step  or what ?

### CLAUDE [2026-11-13 11:53 IST]

Yes, for the 135M model. It has 37 transformer blocks (the 1.6B has 26), and every forward and every backward goes through all of them.

One correction on "per step": the full pass happens per micro-batch, not once per optimizer step.

**One micro-batch:**
1. Forward: embedding, then block 1 to block 37 in order, then the final norm, the lm_head (logits) and the loss.
2. Backward: the same path in reverse, from the loss through the lm_head, then block 37 down to block 1, then the embedding.

**One optimizer step:**
- If gradient accumulation is N, the step runs N micro-batches. So it is N forwards and N backwards through the 37 blocks, with the gradients added up.
- Then the gradient clip and one optimizer update (Muon or AdamW) of all weights.
- With more than one GPU, each GPU does this on its own micro-batches, and the gradients are combined before the update.

**Inside each of the 37 blocks**, both directions pass through:
- the attention part: norm, the q / k / v projections, QK-norm and RoPE, the attention kernel, the output projection, then the residual add;
- the MLP part: norm, gate_up, the activation, down, then the residual add.

So per micro-batch the attention kernel runs 37 times forward and 37 times backward, while the lm_head and loss run once each way.

> tool `Bash`: Find how the SFT trainer assigns weights and learning rates to Muon and AdamW
> tool `Bash`: Locate the SFT trainer source and launcher on the laptop
> tool `Bash`: Show the Muon and AdamW learning rate lines in the current trainer and launcher
> tool `Read`: /home/blu-bridge016/Downloads/BluTrain_push/train/production_zero/bluscript_sft.cpp
> tool `Read`: /home/blu-bridge016/Downloads/BluTrain_push/train/production_zero/bluscript_sft.cpp

Yes, it is possible. Our trainer already has separate learning rates for the two; our SFT launcher just sets them to the same value.

**What decides Muon or AdamW**

It is decided per weight, by the weight's shape, once at the start. The gradient has the same shape as its weight, so it is the same thing either way.

| weight | optimizer |
| --- | --- |
| 2-D matrices inside the blocks (q, k, v, output projection, gate_up, down) | Muon |
| 1-D weights (RMSNorm scales, QK-norm q_gamma / k_gamma) | AdamW |
| token embedding and lm_head | AdamW, even though they are 2-D |

So "2-D is Muon" has one exception: the two vocabulary matrices are excluded on purpose ([bluscript_sft.cpp:2134-2140](../BluTrain_push/train/production_zero/bluscript_sft.cpp#L2134-L2140)).

**The learning rates**

There are two pairs, one per optimizer:

| setting | for | default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `BLU_SFT_LR` | AdamW peak | 2e-5 |
| `BLU_SFT_MIN_LR` | AdamW end | AdamW peak ÷ 10 |
| `BLU_SFT_MUON_LR` | Muon peak | none; it must be given |
| `BLU_SFT_MUON_MIN_LR` | Muon end | Muon peak ÷ 10 |

Both use the same schedule (same warm-up steps, same curve). The trainer calls the schedule function twice per step, once with each pair. So the shape over time is the same and only the scale can differ.

**What we did**

Our launcher [run_sft.sh:87](../BluTrain_push/sft/run_sft.sh#L87) passes `BLU_SFT_LR=$LR BLU_SFT_MUON_LR=$LR`. So in every SFT run of ours both had the same peak (5e-5 on the 1.6B, 1e-4 on the 135M) and the same end (peak ÷ 10). We never tested different values in SFT.

To use different values today, the trainer needs no change. Only the launcher line needs a separate variable for the Muon value, or the trainer can be started with the four settings directly.

**Why the two can be equal, and why someone would make them differ**

- Muon's update is normalised: the trainer scales it so its entries have about the same size as an AdamW update. So the same learning rate means about the same step size for both. That is why equal is a reasonable first choice.
- They are still different weights with a different update rule, so the best value for each need not be the same. In pretraining our own defaults already differ: the code comment says the Muon rate is set about 4 times the AdamW rate, because Muon tolerates 2 to 4 times more.

So what your colleague did in DPO is normal and supported. Whether different rates help our SFT is not known; it would need a test.

### CLAUDE [2026-11-13 12:30 IST]

That top-left thing is the workspace indicator. The white bar is the workspace you are on, and the grey dot is a second, empty workspace.

**What a workspace is**

It is only a way to arrange windows on the screen. It is not a second desktop computer and not a second system. All windows in all workspaces are normal programs on the same laptop, under the same Linux kernel.

**CPU threads**

Nothing is halved. Using the second workspace does not reserve or split any threads.

- The Linux scheduler gives CPU time to each program's threads when they have work, no matter which workspace their window is in.
- A program that is idle uses almost nothing, in either workspace.
- If two programs both want all cores at the same time (for example two `make -j$(nproc)` builds), they share the cores and each gets slower. That is the same whether they are in one workspace or two.

So it is dynamic, by current need.

**The remote GPU box from both workspaces**

The GPU is not in the laptop, so the workspace has no effect on it at all. If you open a terminal in each workspace and ssh to the same box:

- Both connect to the same machine with the same IP address. They are two login sessions of the same user on that box.
- Both see the same files, the same GPUs and the same running processes.
- It is the same as opening two terminals in one workspace.

**If both sessions run something on the same GPU**

From the GPU's side it is two processes on one GPU:

- Memory: each process takes its own memory from the same total (about 143 GB on an H200). If the two together need more, the second one fails with out of memory.
- Compute: by default the GPU switches between the two processes in time slices. Both run, and each is slower than when alone.
- On P015 the GPUs are set to Exclusive_Process mode. There, a second process on the same GPU is refused and fails at start. I recorded this for P015 on 11-11; I have not checked which mode P032 uses.

**What this means for our work**

- Two sessions on one box are fine for things like editing, building in one and watching logs or `nvidia-smi` in the other.
- Two GPU runs on the same GPU at the same time make every timing number wrong, so not for benchmarks or before/after runs.
- Two runs on different GPUs of the same box (for example `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0` in one and `=1` in the other) do not share GPU compute or memory. They still share the box's CPU cores and disk.

### USER [2026-11-13 12:57 IST]

"On P015 the GPUs are set to Exclusive_Process mode. There, a second process on the same GPU is refused and fails at start. I recorded this for P015 on 11-11; I have not checked which mode P032 uses." exclusive process mode means ?

### CLAUDE [2026-11-13 12:58 IST]

It is a setting on each NVIDIA GPU called the compute mode. It decides how many processes may use that GPU for compute at the same time.

| compute mode | what it allows |
| --- | --- |
| Default | any number of processes can use the GPU together; they share its memory and take turns on the compute |
| Exclusive_Process | only one process can hold the GPU at a time; a second process that tries to use it gets an error at start |
| Prohibited | no process can use the GPU for compute |

**In Exclusive_Process mode:**

- The first process that creates a CUDA context on the GPU owns it until that process ends.
- Any other process that tries to use the same GPU fails right away with an error like "CUDA-capable device(s) is/are busy or unavailable". It does not wait and it does not run slowly; it just does not start.
- One process can still use many threads on that GPU. The limit is on processes, not threads.
- `nvidia-smi` still works, because it only reads status and does not compute.

**Why a box is set this way:** on a shared box it stops two people's jobs from landing on the same GPU by accident, which would slow both or run one out of memory.

**How to see it** (reading only, changes nothing):

```
nvidia-smi --query-gpu=index,compute_mode --format=csv
```

The mode is changed with `nvidia-smi -c`, which needs root, and on a shared box that is the admin's decision, not ours.

**What it meant for us on P015 (11-11):** when someone else's process was already on a GPU, our test could not start on that GPU at all. That is why the lock script skipped GPUs that had a holder.

### CLAUDE [2026-11-13 12:59 IST]

No, we did not set it. On P015 it was already set on all GPUs when we started on 11-11. Our lock script only checked which GPUs already had a process and skipped those; it never changed the compute mode.

**What is the normal default**

- The NVIDIA driver's default is Default mode (many processes allowed).
- The setting is not saved by the driver. After a reboot or a driver reload every GPU goes back to Default, unless something sets it again at start-up.
- So a fresh rented instance normally comes in Default mode. Our Verda H200 boxes behaved this way: on 10-21 we ran several libraries' processes on the same GPU in our benchmarks, which would not be possible in Exclusive_Process.

**So on P015**

Someone with root set it, most likely through a start-up script, because P015 is a shared box with many users. Who set it and when, I do not know; it is not in our records. The box admin would know.

**Two different "locks", to keep them apart**

| thing | who made it | what it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Exclusive_Process compute mode | the box admin (root), on the GPU itself | the driver refuses a second process on that GPU |
| our `lockrun_h200.sh` | us, a plain script | looks for GPUs that already have a process, skips them, and runs our tests one at a time; changes no setting and kills nothing |

For P032 or any new box, the one-line `nvidia-smi --query-gpu=index,compute_mode --format=csv` check tells which mode it has.

### CLAUDE [2026-11-13 13:09 IST]
> tool `Bash`: Read our lock script to see what it does

I read the script again to answer exactly. Two parts of what you said are not right: it never kills anything, and the lock is weaker than "no one can run".

**What our script does**

1. Waits until the GPUs we named are free: no process on them and under 1,500 MiB used. It checks twice, 20 seconds apart.
2. If they are not free within 90 minutes, it runs nothing and exits.
3. Starts one small "holder" process on each of our GPUs (64 MB, no compute).
4. Runs our tests one after another.
5. Stops the holders at the end.

**It never kills**

There is no kill of anyone's process anywhere in it. If someone is on the GPU it only waits. That is by design, from your rule: never kill anyone else's process.

**What the holder really does (a box in Default mode)**

- It does not block anyone. In Default mode another person can still start a job on that GPU while our holder is there.
- It is only a sign: anyone who looks at `nvidia-smi` sees a process on that GPU and knows it is in use.
- It is also how our script tells "ours" from "someone else's" when it checks whether the GPU is free.

So if someone starts a run by mistake on our GPU in Default mode, their job runs alongside ours and our timings are disturbed. The script does not stop that and does not detect it after the start.

**On P015 (Exclusive_Process mode)**

- The script starts no holders there, because a holder would block our own tests (this happened in the first run: 228 test groups failed with "device busy").
- While one of our test processes is running, the driver refuses everyone else on that GPU. That part is a real lock, but it comes from the box setting, not from our script.
- Between two of our test processes the GPU is free for a moment. Someone could take it then. In that case our next test fails with a "busy" error in the log; it would not give wrong results.

| box mode | is the GPU really locked for us? |
| --- | --- |
| Default | no; the holder is only a visible sign |
| Exclusive_Process | yes while one of our processes runs; not in the gaps between them |

"Chat layout" only means **the list of chat lengths inside one packed row**. We have tested the same idea since 12/10/2026 under other names. Three parts of their study are new to us.

## What the document is

- **The kernel tested:** "ours" in the doc is the Nova build (`nova-opt dff63defe56f`). I read that as the compiler-made attention kernel, not our hand-written kernel on lottn; confirm this with your colleague.
- **The test:** forward only, one row (B=1), 18 query heads / 6 KV heads, head dims 64 and 128, row lengths 2,048 to 131,072, against FA3, FA4 and cuDNN on P032 GPU 7.
- **The four layouts:**

| Name | Chats in the row | What it tests |
|---|---|---|
| one1 | one chat filling the whole row | plain dense causal attention |
| pk1 | chats of 300–1,500 tokens | normal SFT packing |
| sh1 | chats of 32–160 tokens | very short chats, mostly one small chat per tile |
| edge1 | one-token chats and lengths at 63/64/65, 127/128/129 and so on | correctness at tile edges; not run in this study |

## What they found

- **Correctness:** all 42 cases pass.
- **Head dim 128:** level with FA3 on one long chat and on medium chats, but 1.28–1.44x slower than FA3 on short chats.
- **Head dim 64:** behind FA3 on every layout, 1.03–1.71x.
- **Their four causes:**
  1. One tile per query head, so short chats give many half-empty tiles. FA3 packs the 3 query heads of a KV head into one tile.
  2. At head dim 64 the tile is 128 rows with 2 compute groups; FA3 and FA4 use 192 rows with 3.
  3. The kernel that builds the chat list is slow at B=1 (up to 66 µs).
  4. At 131,072 with one chat they are 11% behind FA3. Their guess is that K/V is read 3 times; they say it is not confirmed.

## What we already did on this

| Their layout | Our matching test | Date |
|---|---|---|
| one1 | dense rows, and "one 4,096 chat per row" | 12/10/2026 onward |
| one1, long rows | dense at 4k–128k against FA3 / FA4 / cuDNN, heads 4/2 | 31/10/2026 |
| pk1 | real packed rows from our data (`real_rows_752`, the middle rows) | 12/10/2026 onward |
| sh1 (partly) | our real rows with the shortest chats (rows 1504–1511) | 12/10/2026 |
| edge1 | test loads D4 / D6 / D7: 1+4095, 4,096 one-token chats, 63/65/127/129/255/257 | in our 296-case quick and 605-case full suite |

Our results with our kernel, on a different box and date, so not directly comparable with theirs:
- **Packed forward, 4,096, 18/6 heads (19/10/2026):** 0.865x FA3's time.
- **Packed forward + backward, heads 4/2 (31/10/2026):** 0.875x FA3 at 4k, 0.993x at 131k.
- **Where we trail:** packed forward alone at 32k–128k is 0.6–2.0% slower than FA3.

## What we did not do

1. **Chats of 32–160 tokens, timed against the other libraries.** Our "shortest real rows" are much longer than sh1: about 14–15% of dense work at 4,096, against sh1's 2.8%.
2. **Head dim 64 on H200 against the other libraries.** All our scoreboards are at head dim 128.
3. **Packing query heads into one tile (PackGQA).** On 17/10/2026 we marked it "not needed" for dense 4,096 rows and never tested it on short chats, so their cause 1 may also apply to our kernel there.

## One thing to give your colleague

Section 1.6 of their doc says the chat-length histogram of our data is not measured. We measured it on 30/10/2026:

| Mix | Median | p90 |
|---|---|---|
| m1 smol | 905 | 1,364 |
| m2 Tülu | 454 | 1,264 |
| m3 smol + math | 671 | 1,346 |

So our real data looks like pk1 (median about 870), not sh1. The share of chats under 160 tokens is not in our records.

A fair comparison of the two kernels needs both run on their layouts on the same GPU; that has not been done.

### CLAUDE [2026-11-13 14:54 IST]
> tool `Bash`: Check in our forward attention kernel how work units are formed per head

**Short answer:** we do the same as their kernel on this point (one tile per query head), and their study is a benchmark to find where their kernel loses to FA3, not an ablation.

## What we do today

I checked our forward kernel ([GQA_fwd_sm90.cu:566-571](../BluTrain_push/Tensor-Implementations/src/Kernels/cuda/attention/arch/GQA_fwd_sm90.cu#L566-L571)). One work unit is one batch row, one query head and 128 query rows. So we also give every query head its own tile, and we do not pack heads.

Take a 40-token chat with 18 query heads and 6 KV heads (3 query heads share one KV head):

| | Tiles for this chat | Rows used per tile |
|---|---|---|
| ours, and their kernel | 18 (one per query head) | 40 of 128 = 31% |
| FA3 | 6 (3 query heads stacked in one tile: 3 × 40 = 120 rows) | 120 of 128 = 94% |

FA3 can stack them because the 3 query heads read the same K and V. Each tile has a fixed cost (load Q, load K/V, start, write output), so 18 tiles cost more than 6 for the same math. On a long chat every tile is full anyway, so stacking saves no tiles there.

One difference between us and their kernel is that ours has the FA3-style scheduler (a fixed set of blocks that keep taking the next unit). Their doc says their kernel launches one block per tile.

## What they are doing

They are not testing a new idea. They time their kernel against FA3, FA4 and cuDNN and look for the reason behind each loss.

The layouts are test inputs, not training modes. Each one makes one cost dominate:

| Layout | What dominates the time | What a loss there points to |
|---|---|---|
| one long chat | the main loop (the math) | tile shape, loop speed |
| medium chats | main loop plus a little edge waste | both |
| very short chats | the fixed cost per tile and per chat | too many tiles, scheduling, the chat-list kernel |

You are right that real SFT data has every length in one row. A real row's time is the sum of these costs. If they timed only real rows, they would see "5% slower" and not know which part to fix. With the extreme inputs, each part shows up alone.

## What they will change

It is still one general kernel for all lengths. Their proposed fixes (section 8 of the doc) are all general:
1. Pack the query heads of a KV head into one tile.
2. At head dim 64, use a 192-row tile with 3 compute groups.
3. Make the chat-list kernel faster.
4. Use persistent scheduling.

Nothing in the doc proposes a different kernel per chat length. Head dim and the number of KV heads come from the model, not from the chat length. What a compiler can pick is the tile shape per head dim, at compile time; FA3 does the same (192 rows at head dim 64, 128 rows at head dim 128).

## What it means for us

- Our models use head dim 128, so fix 2 does not touch us.
- Our data's median chat is 454–905 tokens, so most of our tiles are full; packing heads would help us only on very short chats, and we never measured that case.
- If you want to know, the test is our kernel on their 32–160-token layout against FA3 on one GPU.

### CLAUDE [2026-11-13 15:00 IST]

Yes, both are in their proposal list, and both copy FA3. They are two separate changes:

| Change | What it means | Where it applies |
|---|---|---|
| Pack heads | the 3 **query** heads that share one KV head go into one tile (not 3 KV heads) | all head dims; helps short chats |
| 3 compute groups | the tile grows from 128 to 192 query rows, and 3 compute warpgroups work on it instead of 2 | head dim 64 only |

- **Why packing uses query heads:** the 3 query heads read the same K and V, so one tile can load K/V once and serve all three. Different KV heads have different K/V, so they cannot share a tile.
- **Why 3 groups only at head dim 64:** at head dim 128, FA3 itself uses 128 rows and 2 groups, the same as us and them. FA3 switches to 192 rows and 3 groups only at head dim 64.

The doc lists these as proposals; nothing is built yet. They want two profiler (ncu) measurements first to confirm the causes.

Yes, we can try, but I checked our real data first and the gain for us would be small. Here is the picture.

## Where our kernel stands

- **Long and medium chats:** level with FA3 or ahead in every case we measured. The one small loss is the packed forward alone at 32k–128k, 0.6–2.0% behind FA3.
- **Very short chats (32–160 tokens):** not measured. A loss is likely, because we tile per query head like their kernel does.

## Which of their four fixes apply to us

| Their fix | For our kernel |
|---|---|
| Pack the query heads of a KV head into one tile | not in our kernel; the only one worth trying |
| 192-row tile at head dim 64 | not needed, our models use head dim 128 |
| Faster chat list | already done, we build it on the CPU once per micro-batch |
| Persistent scheduling | already done on 16/10/2026 |

## How much packing heads could give us

I counted on the laptop, using the chat lengths of our smol mix (452,974 chats), no GPU:

| Chats of 160 tokens or less | Share |
|---|---|
| of all chats | 6.25% |
| of all tokens | 0.93% |
| of all attention tiles | 1.36% |

With 3 query heads per KV head (the 1.6B model), packing would cut our total tile count by 4.9% on this data. The math stays the same; only the fixed cost of those tiles is saved. So the gain is at most a few percent of the attention forward, and less of the full step. On the 135M model (2 query heads per KV head) it would be smaller still.

Their own numbers agree: on medium chats (their pk1, close to our data) their kernel has 1.05x FA3's tiles and is already level with FA3.

## Cost of the change

Packing heads is a large kernel change: one tile then holds rows of 3 different heads, so the Q load, the causal mask, the output write and the work list all change. It must also keep "a packed chat gives the same bits as the chat alone", or our test suite rejects it.

## My recommendation

Measure before building anything. One run of about 10 minutes on one H200: our kernel against FA3 on 32–160-token chats and on a real row.
- If the loss on short chats is large and you expect SFT data with many short chats later, we build it.
- If not, we leave it as a future item.

### CLAUDE [2026-11-13 15:18 IST]

**Short answer:** packing heads helps short chats, but it is not free for other lengths, so it must be limited to the packed-rows kernel and measured. The 3-warpgroup change does not apply to us at all.

## 1. Packing 3 query heads into one tile

What changes with chat length:

| Chat length | Tiles saved | Extra cost per tile | Expected net |
|---|---|---|---|
| very short (under about 128 tokens) | many: a 40-token chat goes from 18 tiles to 6 | small against the saving | clear gain |
| medium (300–1,500 tokens) | few: only the last, partly empty tile of each chat (4.9% of all tiles on our smol data) | paid on every tile | unknown, could be a small gain or a small loss |
| long (one chat fills the row) | none, every tile is already full | paid on every tile | a small loss |

Where the extra cost per tile comes from:
- **Q load and O write:** today one tile reads 128 rows of one head, which is one contiguous block. Packed, it reads rows of 3 different heads, so the load and the write are in 3 pieces.
- **Causal mask:** today row r of a tile is token position r. Packed, 3 rows share one position, so the mask needs extra index math.

FA3 itself treats it this way. It turns packing on for varlen (chat lists) and decides per case for dense rows. In the FA3 dense run we compared against on 17/10/2026 (rows of 4,096), packing was off.

So the safe design for us is:
- **Dense kernel:** untouched. Pretraining and one-long-chat rows keep today's speed for certain.
- **Packed-rows kernel only:** gets the packing. We already keep the two as separate template modes (the L2 hints of 19/10/2026 were added to the dense kernel only, the same way).

That leaves one risk: medium chats, which are most of our real data, run in the packed-rows kernel. If the extra per-tile cost is larger than the 4.9% tile saving, our real rows get slower while short chats get faster. Only a race on real rows answers this.

One more gate: our rule "a chat in a packed row gives the same bits as the chat alone" must still hold. I think it can, because each row still sees its keys in the same order, but the test suite decides.

## 2. The 3 warpgroups

- This is a head dim 64 change: tile of 192 query rows, 3 compute warpgroups in place of 2.
- At head dim 128, FA3 and FA4 use 128 rows and 2 warpgroups, the same as us. They do not use 3 there.
- Both our models use head dim 128, so we would not build this. It affects no length in our kernel, because it is not in our kernel.

## What I recommend

1. Measure first: our kernel against FA3 on 32–160-token chats and on a real row (about 10 minutes on one H200).
2. If the short-chat loss is real and you want it fixed, build packing in the packed-rows kernel only.
3. Keep it only if the 296-case suite passes and the real-row race is not slower.
4. Then push.

Give me the box and GPU for step 1 when you want to start.

## What I found while reading our kernel

Today one work unit is one query head and two 64-row tiles, one for each compute group. When a chat has an odd number of 64-row tiles, the second group has no rows and only waits. That is every chat of 64 tokens or less, and also lengths like 129–192.

That gives a small fix, which I call MX: the idle group takes the same tile of another query head of the same KV head. Both heads read the same K/V, so the loads stay as they are.

Tile counts per call, computed on the laptop:

| Layout | Today | MX | FA3-style packing |
|---|---|---|---|
| chats 32–160 | 7,974 | −14.7% | −29.0% |
| chats 300–1,500 | 5,040 | −3.2% | −6.2% |
| one chat of 4,096 | 4,608 | 0 | 0 |
| every chat 40 | 14,832 | −33.3% | −66.7% |
| our whole smol mix | | −2.4% | −4.9% |

- **MX** changes only the work list and the unit decode. The main loop, softmax, mask, output write and the dense kernel stay the same, so long and medium chats cannot get slower in the loop.
- **FA3-style packing** saves about twice as many tiles but changes the Q load, the mask and the output write on every tile.
- With heads 4/2 (the 135M model) the two give the same tile counts.

## The order I propose

1. Stage 0 on the GPU you name. If short chats are within about 5% of FA3, we stop.
2. If we lose: build MX, test it alone.
3. Only if a real gap remains: build FA3-style packing on top of MX and test both together.

Each candidate gets the same seven checks:
1. Switch off gives the same machine code as today.
2. The dense kernel's machine code is unchanged with the switch on.
3. The 296-case suite passes.
4. A CPU model of the handshakes shows no hang.
5. A race against today's kernel on all six layouts.
6. ncu on the short-chat layout, before and after.
7. A final scoreboard against the three libraries.

Not planned, because we do not need them: other row lengths, head dim 64, 3 compute groups.

The MX candidate is now built on the laptop and all the CPU work for both stages is packed. Nothing has run on a GPU, and the master kernel files are not edited.

## The plan in simple words

1. **Stage 0: measure today's kernel.** We run our kernel and FA3 / FA4 / cuDNN on short chats, medium chats, one long chat and our real rows, about 20 minutes on one H200. This tells us if we lose on short chats and by how much.
2. **Stage 1: test MX.** Three versions run one after another in the same session, about 25 minutes:
   - **BASE:** today's kernel.
   - **MXoff:** the new kernel with the old work list. This shows what the extra decode code costs by itself.
   - **MXon:** the new kernel with the new work list. This shows what MX gains.
3. **Stage 2: FA3-style packing of 3 heads.** We build it only if MX still leaves a real gap on short chats.
4. **Keep and push** only what passes the test suite and is not slower on real rows.

## What MX is

- Today each work unit has two compute groups. For a chat with an odd number of 64-row tiles (every chat of 64 tokens or less), the second group has no rows and only waits.
- MX gives that idle group the same tile of a second query head. Both heads share one KV head, so K/V is loaded once as before.
- FA3-style packing is the bigger version of the same idea (3 heads inside one tile). MX saves about half as many tiles, with a much smaller code change.

## What I checked on the laptop

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| Switch off against the master | same machine code in both kernels (0 lines differ) |
| Switch on, dense kernel | same machine code (0 lines differ), so pretraining and one-chat rows cannot change |
| Switch on, packed kernel | 3,568 → 3,648 instructions; the 80 extra are integer decode only, the GEMM, exp, load and barrier counts are unchanged |
| Work lists, 20,000 random chats × 7 head layouts | every head and tile is computed exactly once |

- MX is switched on per run by one environment variable, so one library runs both MXoff and MXon.
- A work list built for the wrong head grouping is refused at launch.
- The old code is kept in the `#else` branches.

The speed and the 296-case suite can only be checked on the H200.

## What I need from you when you have the GPU

1. The box and the GPU number.
2. Three paths on that box: the `tva` test binary, the Tensor-Implementations tree, and the Python env with FA3 / FA4.

Then the order on the box is `stage0.sh`, then `build_mx.sh` (CPU only), then `stage1.sh`. I will give you each command to run, one at a time.

Everything is in [profiling_reports/attn_short_chats_2026_11_13/](profiling_reports/attn_short_chats_2026_11_13/):

## Locking on P032, and the kill request

I went through our lock script from 11/11/2026. P032 now has every GPU in Exclusive_Process mode, the same as P015 that day:

- **During each of our runs** the driver itself blocks everyone else. That is a real lock, stronger than our holder.
- **A holder cannot be used here.** It would be the one allowed process and would block our own tests; that is what happened on P015.
- **Between two of our runs** the GPU is free for a second or two. Someone could start there.

I did not set up a kill. If someone starts in that gap, they started on a GPU that looked free, and killing would lose their work. This also follows your standing rule from 05/11/2026: no kill of another person's process without asking you for that case. The scripts handle it this way:

- they log who it is,
- they wait up to 30 minutes without touching the process, then continue,
- our numbers cannot be spoiled, because no run of ours ever shares the GPU.

If that happens I will tell you at once with the process and its owner, and you decide.

Next, when the build finishes: stage 0 on GPU 4, the MX build, then stage 1 on GPU 5.

### CLAUDE [2026-11-13 16:18 IST]
> tool `Bash`: Check the current status of both stages

No, we do not need that overhead every time. It is there only when we use nsys, and we use nsys only for one kind of test.

**When nsys is needed**
- Only when we compare our kernel against FA3 / FA4 / cuDNN. Those libraries run from Python, and nsys is how we get the time of each kernel alone, without Python and launch gaps.
- That is stage 0.

**When it is not needed**
- When we compare our kernel against our own kernel (BASE / MXoff / MXon). Our test binary times each call itself.
- That is stage 1's race, so it has no such overhead.

**Can the nsys overhead be made smaller? Yes, in two ways, for the next time:**

| Way | What changes | Saving |
|---|---|---|
| One nsys session per layout | nsys starts once and writes its report once for all 8 runs of a layout, not 8 times | roughly 8 times less waiting |
| Start the next run while nsys writes the previous report | the CPU work of one run overlaps the GPU work of the next | roughly half |

I am not switching the running stage 0 to either of them now:
- 7 of its 54 runs are done, and changing the method in the middle would mix two methods in one table.
- Both ways need the summary script changed and tested first.

So today's stage 0 keeps its pace and ends around 17:35–17:40 IST. If you prefer, I can prepare the one-session version on the laptop while this runs, and we use it for the final scoreboard after MX.

> tool `Bash`: Watch GPUs 4, 5 and 6 every 5 seconds and report at once if a process that is not ours appears (read-only)

Yes to both. I just added a watcher for exactly that.

**Monitoring**

**Stopping and continuing in the middle**

| Action | Possible? | What happens |
|---|---|---|
| Stop | yes, any time | only the one run in progress is lost; every finished run's result is already saved |
| Continue later | yes | we start the script again for the layouts that are left; finished layouts are not repeated |
| True pause (freeze and resume the same run) | no | a half-finished timing run is not usable, so we stop between runs and restart |

- A stop touches only our own scripts, by their PID.

### CLAUDE [2026-11-13 18:14 IST]

Yes, MX makes our kernel faster than it is now, and no, MX is not a copy of FA3. We already beat FA3 without it because our cost per tile is much lower than FA3's.

## What MX does differently from today

Take one chat of 40 tokens and the 3 query heads that share one KV head. Each "pair" has two compute groups, and each group can hold 64 rows.

| Approach | How the 3 heads are placed | Pairs or tiles used | Groups doing nothing |
|---|---|---|---|
| ours today | each head gets its own pair; group 1 has the 40 rows, group 2 is empty | 3 | 3 |
| MX | heads A and B share one pair (group 1 = A, group 2 = B); head C keeps its own pair | 2 | 1 |
| FA3 | the rows of all 3 heads are mixed inside one 128-row tile (120 rows) | 1 | 0 |

- **MX changes only who works on what.** A group that sat empty now does the same tile for another head. Each 64-row tile still belongs to one head, so the main loop, the mask and the output write stay as they are.
- **FA3 mixes rows of different heads inside one tile.** That saves more tiles, but it changes how Q is loaded, how the mask is applied and how the output is written, on every tile.

So MX has the same goal as FA3's packing (fewer half-empty tiles) but is a smaller method of our own, not FA3's method.

## Why we already beat FA3

On short chats the time is roughly the number of tiles times the cost of each tile. FA3 wins on the first and loses on the second. From today's short-chat layout (chats of 32–160 tokens, 8 rows × 4,096; forward kernel time):

| | Tiles per call | Forward time | Time per tile |
|---|---|---|---|
| FA3 | 5,658 | 219.2 µs | 38.7 ns |
| ours today | 7,974 | 191.8 µs | 24.1 ns |

- FA3 has 29% fewer tiles than we do.
- But each FA3 tile costs about 1.6 times what one of ours costs, so we finish first.
- Our low cost per tile comes from the October work on what happens at the start and end of each tile. The loop itself was not the reason.
- FA3's own source says its packing "is a bit slower" per tile (`heuristics.h`, line 12), so part of its higher cost comes from the packing itself.

The tile counts are computed from the chat lengths; the times are measured.

## What MX adds on top

MX keeps our cheap tiles and removes some of them:

| Layout | Forward time with MX, against today's kernel |
|---|---|
| chats of 32–160 | −8.0% |

### CLAUDE [2026-11-13 18:52 IST]
> tool `Bash`: Check the new build's suite results and the running work on both GPUs

Yes to the plan. On your last question: no, MX is not packing 3 query heads into one tile. That is FA3's method. MX is smaller.

## What MX is, exactly

Take one chat of 40 tokens and the 3 query heads that share one KV head. One "pair" has two halves of 64 rows each.

| | Head A | Head B | Head C | Pairs used |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| today | own pair; second half empty | own pair; second half empty | own pair; second half empty | 3 |
| **MX** | first half of a pair | **second half of the same pair** | own pair; second half empty | 2 |
| FA3 packing | the rows of all three mixed inside one 128-row tile | | | 1 |

- **MX:** two query heads share one pair. Each head still has its own 64-row tile; only the half that sat empty now does work for a second head.
- With 3 heads per KV head (the 1.6B model), two heads share and the third stays alone.
- With 2 heads per KV head (the 135M model), both share, so nothing stays alone.
- It only applies to chats with an odd number of 64-row tiles (every chat of 64 tokens or less, 129–192, and so on).

FA3's packing of 3 heads into one tile saves more tiles, but it changes the loading, the mask and the output write on every tile. We did not build that. On short chats, MX alone already puts our forward at 0.80 of FA3's time.

## The plan to adopt it

Yes: adopt MX, test it from every side, benchmark again, then push. That is what is running now:

and this mx wont affect other thigns right, it benefts all , so its either benefittign or nothgin, not negative right ? pakka ?

### CLAUDE [2026-11-13 19:02 IST]

Almost, but not 100% "pakka" yet. Here is exactly what is proven, what is measured, and the one corner where it could be slightly negative.

| Case | Effect of MX | How sure |
|---|---|---|
| pretraining and any dense row | none | proven: the dense kernel's machine code is identical (0 lines differ) |
| packed rows with no shared tile (for example one long chat per row, or `BLU_GQA_MX=0`) | none | proven: these rows run today's packed kernel, identical machine code |
| backward | none in the code | proven: the backward files are not touched |
| results (the numbers the model computes) | same | tested: each chat gives the same bits as alone; 280 passed, 0 failed |
| rows of short chats | faster, −8.0% forward | measured, 4 of 4 rounds |
| rows of medium chats | faster, −2.7% | measured, 4 of 4 rounds |
| our real rows | faster, −0.4% to −1.05% | measured, but only one of three groups is certain with 4 rounds; the 8-round race running now settles it |

## The one corner that could be slightly negative

- When a row has at least one shared tile, the whole row runs the new kernel copy.
- That copy has a longer decode step. By itself it costs 0.5–1.1% of the forward on rows with many chats (we measured this as "MX code, old work list").
- On the rows we tested, the saved tiles gain more than that, so the net is positive.
- But a row where almost no chat has an odd tile count would pay the decode cost and save almost nothing. Worst case: about 0.5–1% slower in the attention forward for that row.

We can close this corner with a small rule in the work-list builder: use MX for a batch only when it saves at least about 1% of the batch's tiles, otherwise build today's list. That is CPU-side code only; the kernels stay as tested. I suggest we decide this after the 8-round race, because it shows how close our real rows are to that limit.

## Two more points

- **Whole training step:** the forward kernel is only a part of a step. The trainer test tonight (old against new, 30 steps) shows the net effect on a real step, including any small clock change in the backward. That is the final proof for "not negative".
- **Not yet run with MX:** context parallelism (it needs 2 GPUs). The code passes the right head counts there, but it has not been tested on a GPU.

what sachedulermost people useds for postrtrainign brpo ? constant lr ? or cosine/linear ?

### CLAUDE [2026-11-13 19:12 IST]
> tool `Bash`: Open our learning-rate scheduler document to answer from what we already collected
> tool `Bash`: Read the section of our scheduler document about what other labs use for SFT

Most people use a short warm-up and then a decay, either **linear or cosine**. Constant is rare for SFT.

From the recipes we read and recorded in our scheduler document (section 10):

| Source | Schedule after warm-up | Warm-up |
|---|---|---|
| Tülu 3 | linear decay | 3% |
| Moonlight (the Muon paper), SFT on the Tülu 3 mix | linear to 0 | not stated |
| SmolLM2 | cosine | 10% |
| the Qwen2.5-7B test in our optimizer document | cosine, 2e-5 down to 2e-6 | not stated |
| ours, every run so far | cosine, down to peak ÷ 10 | 3% |

- **Linear and cosine** are the two that published SFT recipes use. Both start falling right after the warm-up.
- **Constant:** none of the published SFT recipes we read uses it. Our trainer has it as an option, but we never ran it.
- **WSD** (warm-up, stable, decay) is our pretraining shape. No SFT recipe we read uses it either.
- One thing from my memory of the library, not re-checked today: the Hugging Face Trainer's default schedule is linear decay, which is one reason linear is so common.

Between linear and cosine there is no clear winner in what we read; the peak rate and the warm-up matter more. Our stage-2 plan has the scheduler comparison as an open test.

The length sweep is done (20:11 IST). It gives the full picture by chat length, and it also shows two things you should know before deciding: one small negative case, and that the gain shrinks a lot once the backward is counted.

## Length sweep: new build against today's library, forward

Every chat in the row has the same length; 8 rows × 4,096, heads 18/6, 3 rounds. Minus means the new build is faster.

**Lengths where MX can share a tile (odd number of 64-row tiles):**

| Chat length | Pairs saved | Forward | Rounds faster |
|---|---|---|---|
| 16 | −33.3% | −25.6% | 3 of 3 |
| 32 | −33.3% | −24.9% | 3 of 3 |
| 48 | −33.3% | −24.1% | 3 of 3 |
| 64 | −33.3% | −21.3% | 3 of 3 |
| 160 | −16.3% | −10.1% | 3 of 3 |
| 192 | −17.1% | −8.3% | 3 of 3 |
| 320 | −10.5% | −7.2% | 3 of 3 |
| 448 | −9.0% | −4.5% | 3 of 3 |
| 704 | −5.7% | −3.9% | 3 of 3 |
| 1,088 | −3.9% | −3.0% | 3 of 3 |
| 2,112 | −2.0% | −1.1% | 3 of 3 |

**Lengths where MX has nothing to share (even number):**

| Chat length | Forward | Note |
|---|---|---|
| 128, 256, 384, 512, 1,024, 2,048, 4,096 | −0.6% to +0.3%, not significant | no change, as expected |
| 224 | +0.2%, not significant | the row has one leftover 64-token chat |
| **96** | **+0.9%, slower in 3 of 3 rounds** | the row has one leftover 64-token chat |

## The negative case, now measured

The row of 96-token chats ends with one 64-token leftover chat. That one chat makes the whole row run the MX kernel copy, which pays its longer decode on all 344 chats and saves almost nothing. Result: 0.9% slower in the forward. This is the corner I described earlier.

It can be closed with one rule in the work-list builder: use MX for a batch only when it saves at least about 2% of the batch's units, otherwise build today's list. The kernels stay as tested; only CPU-side code changes. With that rule the 96 case goes back to 0, and every gain in the tables above stays.

## Forward and backward together

MX changes only the forward, and on short chats the backward is the bigger part of attention. The backward code is the same, but it gets about 0.1–0.3% slower in the same loop (the GPU's shared clock under the power cap, as we saw in October).

| Rows | Forward | Forward + backward together |
|---|---|---|
| every chat 16 tokens | −25.6% | about −5.3% |
| every chat 64 tokens | −21.3% | about −3.6% |
| chats of 32–160 (afternoon race) | −8.0% | about −1.2% |
| real rows group 1 (8 rounds) | −1.33% | about −0.1% |
| real rows group 2 (8 rounds) | −1.32% | about −0.25% |
| real rows group 3 (8 rounds) | −0.52% | about −0.05% |

The last column is computed from the measured forward and backward times of the same runs. It matches the trainer test: no measurable change in the step time on our real data.

## What this means for the decision

- **Safe:** results are identical, suites pass, dense and plain packed kernels are untouched.
- **Clear gain:** only on data with many short chats (64 tokens or less, and the other odd bands).
- **On today's SFT data:** neutral for the whole step.
- **One measured loss:** +0.9% forward on rows like the 96-token case, removable with the 2% rule.

My recommendation: adopt it with the 2% rule, but as "no cost on normal data, gain on short-chat data", not as a speed-up of today's training. If you would rather not add code for that, we keep it recorded as a tested candidate. Your call.

## Time

The sweep took 41 minutes, not 20, so GPU 4 is later than I said: the full suite is running now (88 checks passed so far, 0 failed), and the decision point moves to about 21:10 IST.
