Not quite. In forward and backward together we were already ahead of FA3 before MX, in every case we measured. MX makes the forward better in some cases, equal in most, and it is not the best possible for very short chats.

## Before MX: did we lose anywhere?

| Case | Today's kernel, forward + backward against FA3 | Forward alone against FA3 |
|---|---|---|
| chats of 32–160 tokens (mixed) | ahead, 0.763 | ahead, 0.875 |
| chats of 300–1,500 | ahead, 0.922 | ahead, 0.909 |
| one long chat per row | ahead, 0.959 | ahead, 0.950 |
| our real rows | ahead, 0.900 to 0.924 | ahead, 0.907 to 0.919 |
| every chat 32 tokens | not measured directly | behind: about 1.5 times FA3's time (my estimate from the sweep, not a direct race) |

So the only loss was the forward alone on very short chats. The backward is so much faster than FA3's there that the total was still ahead.

## With MX

Measured directly against FA3 (new build, MX on):

| Every chat is | Forward (ours / FA3) | Forward + backward |
|---|---|---|
| 32 tokens | 1.146 (still behind) | 0.643 |
| 64 tokens | 0.620 | 0.645 |
| 192 tokens | 0.702 | 0.771 |
| 32–160 mixed | 0.802 | 0.752 |
| real rows (3 groups) | 0.897 to 0.919 | 0.899 to 0.929 |

The lengths 128, 704 and 2,048 are still running.

## Is MX better than today's kernel in all cases?

| Case | MX against today's kernel |
|---|---|
| chats with an odd number of 64-row tiles (64 or less, 129–192, 257–320, and so on) | forward faster, from −1% (long) to −26% (very short) |
| all other lengths, dense rows, pretraining | no change (same kernel runs) |
| backward | no change in code; +0.1 to +0.3% in the same loop from the shared clock |
| our real rows, forward + backward | about equal (−0.05% to −0.25%) |
| SFT training step on real data | no measurable change |
| rows like "96-token chats plus one 64-token leftover" | forward 0.9% slower; the 2% rule removes this |

So: with the 2% rule, MX is better or equal everywhere we measured, and never worse. Without the rule there is that one small negative case.

## Is MX the best version?

It is the best we have built, not the best possible. For chats of about 40 tokens and less, FA3's forward still wins (1.146 at 32 tokens), because FA3 packs 3 heads into one tile and MX shares only 2 heads per pair. Beating FA3's forward there would need that full packing, which is a bigger kernel change. For our data it matters little: 0.49% of our chats are 64 tokens or shorter.

GPU 4 and GPU 6 are both still running; next results in about 8 minutes.

### CLAUDE [2026-11-13 21:34 IST]
> tool `Bash`: Queue the table's missing entries on GPU 4 after the 2% rule checks (MX against FA3 on medium chats; today's kernel raced directly against FA3 at four lengths), and show status
> tool `Bash`: Read the race on the 96 / 128 / 160 / 192-token rows with the 2% rule in place

Three answers.

## 1. What the 2% rule is

- The MX kernel copy has a slightly longer first step for every work unit (it has to read which heads share). By itself that costs about 0.5–1% of the forward on rows with many chats.
- When many chats can share a tile, MX saves far more than that. When almost none can, MX pays the cost and saves nothing. That is what we measured on the rows of 96-token chats: +0.9% slower.
- **The rule:** before building the work list for a batch, the builder counts how many units would share a tile. If that is less than 2% of the batch's units, it builds today's list, and the batch runs today's kernel. Otherwise it uses MX.

Two examples from our measurements:

| Batch | Units that would share | Share | Rule decides |
|---|---|---|---|
| rows of 96-token chats | 48 of 6,192 | 0.78% | today's kernel |
| real rows group 3 | 54 of 2,556 | 2.11% | MX |

The rule's test is running now on GPU 4, and the first results are in:

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| rows of 96-token chats: which kernel runs | today's kernel, 60 of 60 launches |
| short-chat layout: which kernel runs | the MX kernel, 60 of 60 launches |
| 96-token rows, forward, against today's library | −0.02% (it was +0.92% without the rule) |
| 160-token rows | −9.7%, 3 of 3 rounds (gain kept) |
| 192-token rows | −9.0%, 3 of 3 rounds (gain kept) |

So the rule does what it should: the one loss is gone and the gains stay.

## 2. Is today's optimization "2 query heads per tile, where FA3 has 3"?

Close, with one correction:

- **MX:** 2 query heads share one **pair** of tiles, and only for the last, half-empty pair of a chat. Each head still has its own 64-row tile; MX gives the half that was empty to a second head.
- **FA3:** the rows of all 3 heads are mixed inside one 128-row tile, for every tile.

So MX is the smaller form of the same idea. It is used only where a half was sitting empty, which is why it changes so little code.

## 3. The missing items in the table

They were not being tested. I have now queued them on GPU 4, right after the rule's checks:

| Missing item | Test queued |
|---|---|
| MX / FA3 on chats of 300–1,500 mixed ("not run") | new build against FA3, 2 rounds |
| current kernel / FA3 at 32, 64, 192, 704 tokens (the entries marked *, computed) | current kernel raced directly against FA3, one round each |

That is 12 runs, about 20 minutes. Expected times: rule checks done about 21:55 IST, the missing items about 22:15. I will then give you both tables again with every entry measured.

## Do the push commands include the 2% rule?

Yes. There is no separate push for it. The rule is inside one of the files in the commands (`GQA_fwd_generic.cu`, the list builder). The five files I put in the laptop tree are the version "MX + 2% rule", the same one that passed the last tests.

## What the 2% rule is

It is not a choice between MX and FA3's method. We did not build FA3's method. The rule chooses between **MX** and **our own kernel as it is today**, and it does this by itself for every batch:

| The batch | What runs |
|---|---|
| at least 2% of its work units can share a tile | the MX list and the MX kernel |
| fewer than 2% can share | today's list and today's kernel, unchanged |

- It is automatic. Nobody sets a flag during training.
- Why it exists: on a batch where almost nothing can be shared, MX costs a little (we measured +0.9%) and gains nothing. The rule sends such batches to today's kernel, so MX is never slower.
- In our real SFT batches the share is above 2%, so they use MX (the trainer test showed MX on every forward).

Two switches exist for testing only, as environment variables of the trainer:
- `BLU_GQA_MX=0`: never use MX.
- `BLU_GQA_MX_MIN_PCT=<n>`: change the 2% limit.

So you can run the push commands as they are.

The KV head count did not change. It is still 6 for the 1.6B model (18 query heads / 6 KV heads, so 3 query heads share one KV head) and 2 for the 135M model (4 / 2).

What changed is only that the trainer now **passes** that number to the function that builds the attention work list:

| | The list builder is told |
|---|---|
| before | the number of query heads only (18) |
| now | the number of query heads and the number of KV heads (18 and 6) |

The builder needs it to know which query heads read the same K and V, because only those may share a pair. The value comes from the model's own settings, as before; with context parallelism it is the count of that rank (KV heads ÷ U).

Written for: your sir and colleagues. This continues your draft right after `so what i did :`.

---first , the background in simple words , in sft we pack many chats into one row of 4,096 tokens , and in attention every token of a chat looks only at the earlier tokens of its own chat , our 1.6b model has 18 query heads and 6 kv heads , so 3 query heads read the same k and v , the attention forward kernel does not compute a whole row at once , it cuts the work into small blocks of query rows called tiles , in our kernel one work unit is one chat x one query head x one pair of tiles , a pair has two halves of 64 rows each , and inside the gpu two groups of threads work on it , one group for each half , the weak point is this , when a chat is short , for example 40 tokens , its 40 rows fill only the first half , the second half has no rows , so the second group has nothing to compute and only waits , and this repeats for every query head , fa3 (flashattention 3) does it in another way , it puts the rows of all 3 query heads of one kv head into one tile , i noticed this while reading uma mahesh's study of his nova attention kernel on short chats , the small example below shows the three ways ,,, ,

```
one chat of 40 tokens , 3 query heads (a , b , c) that read the same k and v

current kernel :  head a -> pair 1 : half 1 = 40 rows of a , half 2 = empty
                  head b -> pair 2 : half 1 = 40 rows of b , half 2 = empty
                  head c -> pair 3 : half 1 = 40 rows of c , half 2 = empty
                  -> 3 pairs , 3 empty halves

new kernel     :  head a + head b -> pair 1 : half 1 = 40 rows of a , half 2 = 40 rows of b
                  head c          -> pair 2 : half 1 = 40 rows of c , half 2 = empty
                  -> 2 pairs , 1 empty half

fa3            :  rows of a , b and c mixed inside one tile of 128 rows
                  -> 1 tile
```

---so first i measured our current kernel against fa3 , fa4 and cudnn on the p032 node (h200) , with 8 rows x 4,096 tokens per call and heads 18/6 , on rows where every chat has one length (32 , 64 , 128 , 192 , 704 , 2,048 tokens) , on mixed short chats (32 to 160) , mixed medium chats (300 to 1,500) , one long chat per row and 3 groups of our real sft rows , result , forward + backward together our current kernel is faster than fa3 in every case (it takes 0.67 to 0.96 of fa3's time) , in the forward alone it is faster than fa3 from 64 tokens per chat and above , and slower than fa3 only when every chat is very short (at 32 tokens our forward takes 1.54 times fa3's time , because fa3 fits 3 heads x 32 rows into one tile and we need one pair for each head) ,,, ,

---then the change , in a chat that has an odd number of 64 row halves (every chat of 64 tokens or less , 129 to 192 , 257 to 320 and so on) the last pair has an empty half , now that empty half is given to a second query head of the same kv head , both heads read the same k and v so nothing else has to change , with 3 query heads per kv head two heads share and the third stays alone , with 2 per kv head (the 135m model) both share , only the work list and the first step of each work unit changed , the main loop , the softmax , the mask and the output write are the same lines , and the kernel for pretraining (dense rows) and the kernel for rows without such chats are unchanged instruction by instruction (i compared the machine code , 0 lines differ) , i also added one rule , the new kernel has a slightly longer first step per unit , so on a batch where almost no chat has an empty half it was 0.9% slower than the current kernel (measured on rows of 96 token chats) , so the work list builder now counts how many units can share , and if that is less than 2% of the batch's units it builds the old list and the old kernel runs , with this rule that case is back to the current kernel's time (-0.02%) and all the gains stay ,,, ,

---results of the new kernel against the current kernel , the values are the same as before (the test suite checks that a chat inside a packed row gives the same bits as the same chat alone) , the forward is faster on every chat length that has an empty half , 21 to 26% less time than the current kernel on chats of 64 tokens or less , 8 to 10% less at 160 and 192 tokens , 1 to 7% less on longer ones , 0.5 to 1.3% less on our real sft rows , and no change on the other lengths , against fa3 the forward on 32 token chats improves from 1.54 to 1.15 times fa3's time , and on the mix of 32 to 160 token chats from 0.875 to 0.80 of fa3's time , forward + backward together it stays faster than fa3 in every case , in a full 135m sft training step on our real data the step time did not change in a measurable way (106.1 ms with the current kernel , 106.3 ms with the new one , same losses) , because the attention forward is a small part of the step and our real chats are mostly long , so with the 2% rule the new kernel is faster or equal to the current kernel in every case i measured , and the clear gain is for data with many short chats ,,, ,

---tests before pushing , the attention test suite passed on the new build (quick suite 280 of 280 with the change on , 280 of 280 with it off , 273 of 273 with heads 4/2 , full suite 333 of 333 , long rows of 8,192 tokens 69 of 69 , quick suite with the 2% rule 280 of 280) , with the profiler i checked that the test binary and the sft trainer really run the new kernel , and the 30 step trainer run gives the same step-0 loss as the current kernel (1.530339) , then i pushed to dist_side_gautam_lottn (tensor-implementations f1a7d98 , blutrain d9606c2) and checked every file on the remote , tomorrow i will continue going through the other components of the sft pipeline for optimization scope and bugs , and two things stay as future work from today , (1) for chats of about 40 tokens and less fa3's forward is still faster than ours , to pass it we need fa3's way of packing all 3 heads into one tile , (2) the same sharing idea for the backward kernel , stats below ,,, ,

### CLAUDE [2026-11-13 22:14 IST]

No, it is not only for 18/6. It works for any model where more than one query head shares a KV head, and the gain depends on that ratio.

## How it depends on the ratio

Let G = query heads per KV head (query heads ÷ KV heads). Inside each KV head, MX pairs the heads two by two; an odd one stays alone.

| G | Example heads | What MX does for a short chat | Half-empty pairs removed |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 6/6, 12/12 (no head sharing) | nothing to pair, because every query head has its own K and V | 0%; the plan and the kernel stay as before, no cost |
| 2 | 4/2 (our 135M), 16/8 | both heads share one pair | 50% |
| 3 | 18/6 (our 1.6B), 12/4 | two heads share, one stays alone | 33% |
| 4 | 16/4, 32/8 | two pairs of heads share | 50% |
| 5 | 20/4 | two pairs share, one stays alone | 40% |

So an even G gets the most, and an odd G leaves one head alone per KV head. For the same chats, 4/2 saves more pairs than 18/6: on the short-chat mix it is 22% of the pairs against 15%, and on our real smol data 3.7% against 2.4%.

The 2% rule and the choice of kernel work the same way for every ratio, because they only count units.

## What is tested and what is not

| Heads | Tested how |
|---|---|
| 18/6 | everything: suites, all speed races, FA3 comparisons |
| 4/2 | quick suite (273 passed, 0 failed) and the 135M trainer run (same losses, MX kernel used on every forward); no speed race at 4/2 |
| 12/4, 16/4, 2/1, 6/6, 5/1 | only the CPU check of the work list (every head and tile computed exactly once); not run on a GPU |

So the logic is general, but on a GPU only 18/6 and 4/2 are proven. Before relying on it for a model with another ratio, I would run the suite once at that ratio (a few minutes).

## Where it does not apply at all

- **Other kernels:** MX is in the Hopper (H100/H200) forward kernel for head dim 128. The generic kernel for other GPUs does not use this work list, so nothing changes there.
- **Backward:** not changed, for any ratio.
- **Context parallelism:** the code passes each rank's own head counts, so the ratio stays the same; this path has not been run on GPUs with MX yet.

No, that check was not md5sum. It was a line-by-line comparison of the compiled instructions.

## How the machine code was compared

1. Compile the old source and the new source.
2. Dump the instructions of the compiled kernel from each object file with NVIDIA's tool (`cuobjdump -sass`).
3. Split the dump per kernel (pretraining kernel, packed kernel, new kernel copy) and remove the address column.
4. Compare old against new with `diff`, line by line.

Result: 0 lines differ for the pretraining kernel and for the packed kernel without shared halves. I did this twice, on the laptop (CUDA 13.0) and on P032 (CUDA 13.4). On P032 the pretraining kernel has 3,952 instructions and the packed one 3,552 in both builds.

## Where md5sum was used

Only for the source files: to prove that the files on the box, and later the files on the remote after your push, are the same files that were tested.

## Why md5sum would not work for the machine code

- The source file did change (the new code is in it), so its md5 differs even though these two kernels compile to the same instructions.
- The object file and the library also differ (they contain the new kernel copy too), so their md5 says nothing about one kernel inside them.

If you want the EOD sentence to say it exactly, use: "(i dumped the compiled instructions of both builds and compared them line by line , 0 lines differ)".

I could not open the Google Doc link: the Google Docs connector is not authorized in this session (it has to be authorized in the claude.ai connector settings). Everything below is from the local copy of that same document, [post_training_research_sft.md](work_docs(mark-down%20-%20(.md)%20files%20)/post_Training_research/post_training_research_sft.md), saved on 15/10/2026, so any edits you made in the Google Doc after that date are not included.

The research is in section 2.1 "Midtraining" of that document. It is research from two papers (OLMo 3 and OctoThinker); we did not run any of these experiments ourselves.

## What midtraining is

- Pipeline in the document: pretraining -> midtraining -> (long context) -> SFT -> DPO -> RL.
- Midtraining is more pretraining on a smaller, better data mix: more math, code, reasoning and QA, less generic web text.
- The loss is the same as in pretraining: every token is a target and there is no SFT-style mask.
- OLMo 3 midtrains on 100B tokens (the "Dolmino" mix) after 5.9T tokens of pretraining.
- That mix includes instruction chats sampled from the Tülu 3 SFT data, "to prime models for instruction-tuning", plus thinking traces.

## OLMo 3, finding 1: instruction and thinking data in midtraining helps

- They ran two 100B-token midtraining runs with the same total number of tokens.
- One run had instruction and thinking data mixed in; the other had only the standard midtraining text.
- The run with instruction and thinking data was better on every base-model evaluation.

## OLMo 3, finding 2: leave special tokens for SFT

They tested Tülu 3 SFT chats written three ways. Each test run was 5B tokens of the tested data plus 5B web tokens, trained while the learning rate falls to zero, one run each.

| How the chat was written | GSM8K | CruxEval |
|---|---|---|
| ChatML with the special ids (`<\|im_start\|>`, `<\|im_end\|>`) | 0 | 18.91 |
| Same template, markers written as ordinary text | 46.02 | 29.65 |
| No special tokens (messages joined by two newlines), the version they kept | 49.43 | 32.89 |

- **Why the special ids failed:** every token was a target, so the model learned to write the special ids itself. It printed them in its answers at test time and the answer extractor failed.
- **What broke:** the paper says the drop is "attributed primarily to disruption in answer parsing". The output format broke, not the math skill.
- **Their decision:** midtraining chats get no special tokens and no template. Special tokens are used only from SFT on.

## OctoThinker (arXiv 2506.20512): midtraining changes how well later RL works

- **Starting point:** the same RL (GRPO on MATH8K) worked on Qwen2.5-3B but not on Llama-3.2-3B. Llama repeated text until it hit 4,096 tokens and barely improved.
- **Method:** many midtraining runs on Llama-3.2-3B, 20B tokens each, changing one thing at a time, then the same RL on each.

| # | What changed in midtraining | Base-model test (before RL) | After RL |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Math web data: MegaMath-Web-Pro (high quality) | better than original Llama | big gains |
| 1 | Math web data: FineMath-4plus (weaker) | better than original Llama | small gains, still repeats until 4,096 tokens |
| 2 | + short reasoning QA (web:QA = 9:1) | small gains | no gain over web data alone |
| 3 | + long reasoning QA (web:QA = 9:1) | small gains | big gains, but RL unstable |
| 4 | + 1% instruction data, with short reasoning | MATH500 41.2%, GSM8K 71.8% | MATH500 52.4%, GSM8K 81.6%, answer length grows smoothly |
| 5 | + 1% instruction data, with long reasoning | MATH500 43.6%, GSM8K 73.2% | MATH500 58.8%, GSM8K 86.4%, but still collapses later |
| 6-8 | Budget: checkpoints at 20B / 70B / 100B of one run | 20B lowest; 70B clearly better; 100B about the same as 70B | 20B lowest; 70B better; 100B better than 70B |
| 9 | Final recipe: 200B at constant LR + 20B with decaying LR | 10-20% better than Llama | Long-3B on par with Qwen2.5-3B |

- **The 1% instruction data** is about 0.8B tokens from Tülu 3 persona IF, WildChat and UltraChat. It unlocked the gains of the short reasoning data.
- **For long reasoning data** they also needed a clearer RL prompt template and a max answer length raised in steps (2,048, then 4,096, then 8,192).
- **Budget finding:** from 70B to 100B the base-model tests showed no gain, but the RL result still improved. Their words: "Increasing the mid-training budget can improve RL performance, even if such gains are not evident in base model evaluations".
- **Final recipe ("Stable-then-Decay"):**
  - 200B tokens at constant LR: MegaMath-Web-Pro-Max 72.5%, DCLM web 10%, text-and-code 10%, QA 5%, code 2.5%.
  - 20B tokens with the LR decaying (2e-5 to 2e-6 for 3B), in three branches: long reasoning, short reasoning, hybrid.
  - The long branch is OpenR1 15%, AM-DeepSeek-Distilled 15%, instruction 10%, MegaMath-Web-Pro 55%.
- **Result:** every branch was 10-20% better than the original Llama on 13 math benchmarks. For example, the 1B model on GSM8K went from 7.66 to 44.88.

## What the document concludes for us

- How well RL works later depends a lot on what the base model saw in midtraining.
- A small amount of instruction data (about 1%, written as plain text) helps.
- Midtraining mixes should be compared by running RL on them, because base-model tests can miss the gain. OLMo 3 uses RL-Zero for this reason.
- Midtraining is a pretraining-side decision, not part of the SFT work.
- The one takeaway: if the team ever adds instruction data to pretraining or midtraining, write it as plain text and leave the special tokens to SFT.

## Related notes in our other docs

- **[plan_grid_search_sft.md](work_docs(mark-down%20-%20(.md)%20files%20)/plan_grid_search_sft.md) sections 4.16 and 4.23:**
  - Our 900B pretraining used ids 1 and 2 zero times, and our SFT is a separate stage with a mask, so nothing is needed for the current plan.
  - If the pretraining team plans a decay or midtraining phase with instruction data, they should use the no-marker format and never ids 1 and 2.
  - They should also tell us, because a base that has seen chat text changes the starting point of the SFT study (F4 would have to be re-run).
- **Same file, item X3:** the opposite direction, pretraining text mixed into the SFT data to reduce forgetting. It is noted as "to plan".
- **[sft_work_documentation.md](work_docs(mark-down%20-%20(.md)%20files%20)/sft_work_documentation.md) Part 3:** the general definition of mid-training, and a quote that Qwen2.5 used a lot of synthetic data during pretraining.

Our research document only had the one-line description of this mix. The table below is from the OLMo 3 paper itself (Table 5, arXiv 2512.13961), which I read just now.

## The full midtraining mix ("Dolma 3 Dolmino Mix", 100B tokens)

The share column is the percentage of the 100B tokens. Group shares are my sums of the paper's rows.

| Group | Source | Share |
|---|---|---|
| **Maths (19.2%)** | Dolmino Math (the maths set from OLMo 2) | 10.7% |
| | CraneMath | 5.63% |
| | MegaMatt | 1.73% |
| | TinyMATH Mind | 0.9% |
| | TinyMATH PoT | 0.24% |
| **Code (20%)** | StackEdu | 10.0% |
| | CraneCode (Python) | 10.0% |
| **Question-answer (13.9%)** | Reddit To Flashcards | 5.9% |
| | Nemotron Synth QA | 5.0% |
| | Wiki To RCQA | 3.0% |
| **Thinking traces (8.3%)** | QWQ Reasoning Traces | 1.87% |
| | General Reasoning Mix | 1.87% |
| | Llama Nemotron Reasoning Traces | 1.25% |
| | OpenThoughts2 Reasoning Traces | 1.25% |
| | OMR Rewrite FullThoughts | 0.85% |
| | Code Meta-Reasoning | 0.46% |
| | Math Meta-Reasoning | 0.38% |
| | Gemini Reasoning Traces | 0.25% |
| | Program-Verifiable | 0.16% |
| **Instruction data (6.1%)** | Flan (the subset used in OLMo 2) | 5.0% |
| | Tülu 3 SFT | 1.1% |
| **PDFs (5%)** | olmOCR science PDFs, high-quality subset | 5.0% |
| **Web pages (27.5%)** | Common Crawl, high-quality subset | 22.5% |
| | STEM-heavy crawl | 5.0% |

## The SFT data part

- **Size:** Tülu 3 SFT is 1.1B tokens, 1.45M chats. That is 1.1% of the mix.
- **Domain:** it is cross-domain, not maths only. The paper calls it "cross-domain instruction datasets to prime models for instruction-tuning".
- **What Tülu 3 SFT contains:** the paper does not break the 1.1% down by domain. From what I know of the Tülu 3 mix, it covers general chat, maths, code, precise instruction following, knowledge recall, safety, multilingual, tables and science. Our document's section 5.2 has the Tülu 3 table to check this against.
- **Which chats they took:** an expanded set, including examples that were created for Tülu 3 but filtered out of its final release.
- **How it is written:** no `<|im_start|>` / `<|im_end|>`; the messages are joined by two newlines. This is the "no special tokens" result from before.
- **Flan** is the other instruction set (5.0%). The paper says it was included because it improved question-answer tasks in their small test runs.

## Why they built it this way

- The paper names five targets for midtraining: better maths, better code, better knowledge recall through question-answer data, and a first start on instruction following and on reasoning before post-training.
- The web and PDF data are kept from pretraining (filtered for quality) so the data does not shift too far from what the model saw before.

If you want, I can add this table to section 2.1 of our local copy of the research document; the Google Doc itself I cannot edit from here.

> tool `Bash`: Read the model size and architecture details from the downloaded OLMo 3 paper text

The OLMo 3 base models that this midtraining mix was used on come in two sizes: 7B and 32B parameters. These numbers are from the OLMo 3 paper (Tables 33 and 35, arXiv 2512.13961), not from our document.

## Model size

| | OLMo 3 7B | OLMo 3 32B |
|---|---|---|
| Layers | 32 | 64 |
| Hidden size | 4,096 | 5,120 |
| Query heads | 32 | 40 |
| KV heads | 32 (multi-head attention) | 8 (grouped-query attention) |
| Context window in pretraining and midtraining | 8,192 tokens | 8,192 tokens |

Both use sliding-window attention (window 4,096) on 3 of every 4 layers, SwiGLU, RMSNorm, RoPE, and bf16 throughout.

## Training size per stage

| | 7B pretraining | 7B midtraining | 7B long context | 32B pretraining | 32B midtraining | 32B long context |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Total tokens | 5.93T | 100B | 50B | 5.5T | 100B, run twice | 100B |
| Sequence length | 8,192 | 8,192 | 65,536 | 8,192 | 8,192 | 65,536 |
| Rows per batch | 512 | 256 | 64 | 1,024 | 512 | 128 |
| Tokens per batch | 4.19M | 2.10M | 4.19M | 8.39M | 4.19M | 8.39M |
| LR schedule | modified cosine | linear decay to 0 | linear decay to 0 | cosine, cut at 5.5T | linear decay to 0 | linear decay to 0 |

### CLAUDE [2026-11-14 11:11 IST]
> tool `Bash`: Read our notes on the Tülu 3 and OLMo 3 SFT mixes and locate where the paper mentions Tülu 3 data
> tool `Bash`: Read the paper passages that say how the SFT stage data relates to Tülu 3 data

Short answer: yes, the two stages overlap. The chats put into midtraining come from the Tülu 3 SFT data, and the SFT stage later trains on many of the same Tülu 3 datasets again. The paper does not say they removed the midtraining chats from the SFT data. The SFT stage also adds a lot of new data that midtraining never saw.

The numbers are from the OLMo 3 paper (Tables 5 and 30, arXiv 2512.13961) and from section 5.2 of our research document.

## 1. What SFT data went into midtraining

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Source | Tülu 3 SFT data |
| Pool they had | 1.61B tokens, 1.95M chats |
| Used in midtraining | 1.1B tokens, 1.45M chats |
| Share of the 100B midtraining mix | 1.1% |
| Format | plain text: no special tokens, messages joined by two newlines |
| Loss | on every token (question and answer), no mask |

- The pool is bigger than the released Tülu 3 mix (939,344 chats) because they also took chats that were created for Tülu 3 but filtered out of its final release.
- The paper does not give a per-domain split of the 1.45M chats they used.

## 2. Which domains that data covers

It covers all domains, not only maths. This is the released Tülu 3 mix (939,344 chats), which is the base of that pool:

| Domain | Datasets | Chats |
|---|---|---|
| Maths | Persona MATH, Persona GSM, Persona Algebra, OpenMathInstruct 2, NuminaMath-TIR | 334,252 |
| Safety | CoCoNot, WildJailbreak, WildGuardMix | 110,983 |
| Code | Persona Python, Evol CodeAlpaca | 142,275 |
| General chat | WildChat, OpenAssistant, No Robots, hardcoded identity questions | 116,872 |
| Knowledge | FLAN v2, SciRIFF (science), TableGPT (tables) | 104,982 |
| Multilingual | Aya | 100,000 |
| Precise instruction following | Persona IF | 29,980 |

Maths is the largest single part (about 36%), but the rest is spread over six other domains.

## 3. What the SFT stage trains on

OLMo 3 has two SFT mixes, one per model type.

**Instruct SFT ("Dolci Instruct SFT", 2,152,112 chats).** The paper says it is built on their OLMo 2 Instruct mixture. It has two kinds of data:

- **Same Tülu 3 datasets as midtraining, with almost the same counts:**

| Dataset | In Tülu 3 mix | In Instruct SFT |
|---|---|---|
| Persona MATH | 149,960 | 149,958 |
| Persona GSM | 49,980 | 49,980 |
| Persona Algebra | 20,000 | 19,999 |
| OpenMathInstruct 2 | 50,000 | 50,000 |
| Persona Python | 34,999 | 34,999 |
| Evol CodeAlpaca | 107,276 | 107,270 |
| CoCoNot | 10,983 | 10,957 |
| WildGuardMix | 50,000 | 49,373 |
| WildJailbreak | 50,000 | 49,965 |
| OpenAssistant | 7,132 | 7,132 |

- **New data not in midtraining:** tool use (227,579), verifiable reasoning (310,572), logic puzzles (159,882), new Python algorithms (186,345), new precise instruction following (136,833), and more WildChat (302,406 against 100,000 in Tülu 3).

**Think SFT ("Dolci Think SFT", 2,268,468 chats for 7B).** Here the overlap is mostly in the questions, not the answers:

- The prompts for chat, safety, precise instruction following, tables and Aya are taken from Tülu 3.
- The answers are generated again with thinking traces (from DeepSeek R1 or QwQ-32B), so the text is different from what midtraining saw.
- The largest parts are new: OpenThoughts3 maths (752,997), Python algorithms (466,677), OpenThoughts3 science and code.

## 4. So what is the difference between the two passes

| | Midtraining | SFT stage |
|---|---|---|
| Amount of chat data | 1.1B tokens, 1.1% of the mix | the whole stage (Instruct 3.4B tokens, Think 45.4B tokens) |
| Format | plain text, no template | ChatML with special tokens |
| Loss | every token | answer tokens only |
| Purpose (paper's words) | "to prime models for instruction-tuning" | teach the chat format and the skills |

The model sees many of the same chats twice. The first time they are ordinary text mixed with maths, code and web data. The second time they are in the chat template with the loss on the answers only.

That the Instruct SFT counts match Tülu 3 almost exactly is my reading of the two tables. The paper does not state "we reuse the same chats", and it does not state that they deduplicated between the stages.

### CLAUDE [2026-11-14 11:24 IST]
> tool `Bash`: Read the paper's results for midtraining with and without instruction and thinking data

They measured it with two 100B-token midtraining runs with the same total number of tokens. The run with the instruction and thinking data scored 50.7 on average and the run without it scored 48.8, so adding it gave +1.9 points on average. It was better on every measure.

These are base-model scores (right after midtraining, before any SFT), from the OLMo 3 paper, Table 10. Each column is a group of benchmarks.

| Midtraining mix | Average | Multiple choice 1 | Multiple choice 2 | Generative QA | Maths | Code | Code fill-in-the-middle |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Without instruction and thinking data | 48.8 | 63.6 | 74.0 | 66.7 | 43.1 | 23.3 | 29.2 |
| With it (full mix) | 50.7 | 64.9 | 75.7 | 68.1 | 48.7 | 24.4 | 31.9 |
| Gain | +1.9 | +1.3 | +1.7 | +1.4 | +5.6 | +1.1 | +2.7 |

The biggest gain is in maths (+5.6). The names of the two multiple-choice columns did not come through in the page text I downloaded, so I have labelled them 1 and 2.

Three limits on what this result shows:

- **It is not the SFT chats alone.** The "without" run removed the instruction data (Tülu 3 SFT + Flan) and all the thinking traces together. That is about 14% of the mix, of which the Tülu 3 SFT chats are only 1.1%. The paper gives no number for removing the SFT chats alone.
- **It was run on an intermediate mix.** The "full mix" here is their round 3 candidate, not the final mix, and it started from an earlier pretraining checkpoint.
- **There is no after-SFT number for this comparison.** The table shows only base-model scores. So the paper does not show how much the final chat model gains from having seen SFT data in midtraining.

The only other direct number on the SFT chats is the small format test from before: 5B tokens of Tülu 3 SFT chats plus 5B web tokens gave GSM8K 49.43 with no special tokens, 46.02 with the template as plain text, and 0 with the special tokens.

> tool `Bash`: Find in the paper and in our docs the result on training Instruct SFT starting from the Think SFT model

Yes, that is OLMo 3 itself. They trained the Instruct SFT stage starting from the Think SFT model instead of from the base model, and it gave +3.3 points on average (44.5 -> 47.8).

This is in the OLMo 3 paper, section 5.2.2 "Starting from Olmo 3 Think SFT", Table 29. The model is an intermediate OLMo 3 Instruct 7B checkpoint.

| Benchmark | Instruct SFT from the base | Think SFT first, then Instruct SFT | Gain |
|---|---|---|---|
| Average | 44.5 | 47.8 | +3.3 |
| BBH | 46.5 | 46.6 | +0.1 |
| GPQA | 29.7 | 34.4 | +4.7 |
| MATH | 60.3 | 65.9 | +5.6 |
| GSM8K | 87.6 | 91.1 | +3.5 |
| OMEGA | 8.6 | 12.2 | +3.6 |
| HumanEval+ | 63.8 | 68.7 | +4.9 |
| MBPP | 54.1 | 57.1 | +3.0 |
| LiveCodeBench | 13.0 | 17.1 | +4.0 |
| AlpacaEval | 27.0 | 27.1 | +0.1 |
| IFEval | 81.0 | 84.7 | +3.7 |

- The gain is mostly in maths, code and science; BBH and chat quality (AlpacaEval) are almost unchanged.
- The paper's words: starting from the Think SFT model "significantly improves the performance of the Instruct model".

We already have this noted in two places:

- Our research document, section 2.6 (the order table): "think SFT, then instruct SFT | OLMo 3 Instruct | +3.3 average".
- [plan_grid_search_sft.md](work_docs(mark-down%20-%20(.md)%20files%20)/plan_grid_search_sft.md), item X1 "Think-SFT warm start (factor 13)", marked "noted, to plan". It also notes that if we use it, both SFT stages must use the same chat format.

**Your questions**

- **Can she modify with our token:** yes. It is the same token you push with, and it is a classic token, so read and write come together and it cannot be made read-only. She could push to every repo your account can push to, and GitHub would record it under your account.
- **Submodules:** yes, all three; the trainer build needs them. One flag in the clone command fetches them.

**The text to send her**, with the token already filled in, is in a file. Run this in a terminal, copy the output and send it:

```
SFT code: how to get it (branch dist_side_gautam_lottn, about 300 MB, under a minute)

1) Run this once. It gives git the access token for our private repos:

git config --global url."https://<TOKEN>@github.com/".insteadOf "https://github.com/"

2) Get the code with all 3 submodules (Tensor-Implementations, BluBridge-BLAS, Context_Parallelism):

git clone --recurse-submodules -b dist_side_gautam_lottn https://github.com/BlubridgeAI/BluTrain.git

Later, to get my new changes:

git pull
git submodule update --init --recursive

Please note:
- This is my personal token. Use it only to clone and pull. Please do not push with it and do not pass it on.
- Run step 1 on your own laptop or your own login, not on a shared login of a GPU box: git keeps the token in ~/.gitconfig of that login. To have the code on a box, copy the BluTrain folder there with scp or rsync.
- The steps to build and run are in BluTrain/sft/README.md.
```

I ran these exact commands on the laptop as a brand-new machine. In 19 seconds all four repos came at the pushed commits, all 5,068 files matched the pushed tree, and the update commands worked.

> tool `Bash`: Check which branch of BluTrain a clone gives when no branch is named

`-b` names the branch to check out: `-b dist_side_gautam_lottn` gives her our branch.

Without it, git gives the repo's default branch. I checked just now: BluTrain's default is `master` (commit 0095fee), not ours (commit d9606c2), so she would get code without our SFT work. BluTrain has 57 branches, so the name is needed to land on the right one.

### CLAUDE [2026-11-14 15:14 IST]
> tool `Bash`: Try the clone command with -b removed but the branch name left in, to see git's exact message

Right: the branch name can only be given through `-b`. `-b` and `dist_side_gautam_lottn` are one pair, and the name must come directly after the flag.

If `-b` is removed and the name is left in, git stops with an error and clones nothing. I tried both cases:

| Command without `-b` | What git says |
|---|---|
| name left in, folder given at the end | `fatal: Too many arguments.` |
| name left in, no folder | `fatal: repository 'dist_side_gautam_lottn' does not exist` |

In the second case git reads the branch name as the repo address, because the first plain word after the options is always taken as the repo.

If both `-b` and the name are removed, the command is valid, but she gets `master`, which is not our code.

So the line in the file stays as it is: `-b dist_side_gautam_lottn`, then the repo address, then the folder.

**One check failed on GPU 3, and I need your OK for a 7-minute control run to settle it.**

**What failed:** the quick suite of the pushed build at heads 12/4, with mixing forced everywhere, passed 272 checks and failed 1. The failing check is the value gradient (dV) of one 128-token chat, in the layout of 64 chats of 64 tokens plus 32 chats of 128 tokens. Its error is 0.0451 against an allowed 0.0444, so it is 1.5% over the limit.

**Why I think the pushed change is not the cause:**
- The backward kernel, which computes dV, is not part of the pushed change.
- This chat has 2 tiles, an even count, so mixing does not touch it.
- The same log shows the packed results equal the dense kernels' results element for element, dV included.

**What is not proven:** the old tree has never been run through this suite at 12/4, so I cannot yet say it fails the same way. Yesterday's suites were at 18/6 and 4/2 only.

**The control I want to run:** the same quick suite at 12/4 on the old tree, and on the pushed build with mixing switched off. That is about 3.5 minutes each, on GPU 3 after its stream ends (around 17:15 IST), and it does not disturb the other runs. If any other head setting fails, the same two runs for it.

**GPU status (19:06 IST):**
- **GPU 2:** started now with the smoke and then the full suite at 4/2 (about 40 minutes). Nothing of ours is on GPU 3 and no waiter is there; Dhanakumar's benchmark is running on it.
- **GPU 1:** still running our default-rule suites (12/4 has the same single failed check, 16/4 is clean), then the long rows; about 20 more minutes.

One thing to confirm: I read "leave 1" as "leave it (GPU 3) for now". If you meant GPU 1, say so and I stop it at once.

**Backward kernel, CPU work so far: the count is done.** This is an estimate from the chat lengths and today's measured times, not a GPU measurement.

**How the backward cuts a chat today (read from the code):**
- **Blocks:** one block per 128 keys of a chat and per query head. A block has two compute groups, each owning 64 of those keys.
- **The waste:** a chat with an odd number of 64-token tiles ends in a block with a single step, where the second group has no key of the chat. It still does the full math and stores nothing.
- **Sharing:** that idle group does the same tile for another query head of the same KV head. Two heads' last blocks become one.

**Estimated change of the backward time** (8 rows × 4,096). The first value assumes a shared block costs what a block costs today; the second assumes 20% more.

| Layout | Heads 4/2 | Heads 18/6 |
|---|---|---|
| every chat 16 tokens | −43% to −34% | −30% to −24% |
| every chat 64 tokens | −30% to −24% | −22% to −18% |
| every chat 160 to 192 | −11% to −9% | −8% to −6% |
| every chat 320 | −5.7% to −4.5% | −4.1% to −3.3% |
| every chat 704 | −2.5% to −2.0% | −1.7% to −1.4% |
| chats of 32-160 mixed | −10.3% to −8.2% | about −7.5% to −6% |
| chats of 300-1,500 | −1.2% to −0.9% | not estimated |
| real rows (3 groups) | −1.1%, −0.9%, −0.3% | −0.7%, −0.6%, −0.2% |
| even tile counts, one long chat | 0 | 0 |

- **Why it fades faster than the forward on long chats:** in the forward the half-empty unit was the chat's most expensive one; in the backward it is the cheapest block (one step).
- **In absolute time it is still the bigger win on short chats:** at 4/2 on chats of 32-160, the forward change saved 0.0076 ms, and this would save about 0.020 to 0.025 ms. Forward plus backward together would go from −2.5% now to about −10%.
- **Real SFT rows gain about 1% or less.**

**What the change needs; it is larger than the forward change:**
1. **Plan builder:** shared blocks in the backward's block list (each entry has two unused numbers, so there is room).
2. **Kernel:** a new variant for shared one-step blocks. It loads the queries of two heads, both groups use the same 64 keys, and each group writes its own head's gradients. The dQ part needs new code, because today the two groups split one head's dQ between them.
3. **Existing kernels stay untouched**, with a switch and the old code kept.
4. **GPU tests afterwards:** the suite at all head settings, a race against today's backward, and the trainer comparison.

**Decision for you:** the gain is real for data with many short chats (up to about 200 tokens) and small for our current real rows. Do you want me to go on with the code on the CPU side (plan builder first, then the kernel variant), or stop at this count?

The script and its two result files are in [bwd_share_study](profiling_reports/attn_mx_followup_2026_11_14/bwd_share_study/).

**GPU runs at 19:15 IST: two of three are done or nearly done; everything ends by about 19:45.**

| GPU | Run | State | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Default-rule suites at five head settings, then long rows at 32,768 | **done 19:14, GPU 1 is free now** | 16/4, 2/1, 5/1, 6/6: 273 of 273 each; 12/4: the same single failed check; long rows: 69 of 69 passed |

| 2 | Full suite at heads 4/2 | running, about 25 more minutes | 152 checks passed, 0 failed so far |

The control settles the open finding: the 12/4 failure is in the old tree too, so it does not come from our pushed change.

**Backward kernel: where we stand.** Yes, Vj2 is ours and it is the current default and best. From our records it has no lag:

| Backward, heads 18/6, 8 rows × 4,096 | Ours (Vj2) | FA3 | FA4 | cuDNN |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| dense (16/10) | 3.072 ms | 3.073 ms | 3.042 ms | 3.632 ms |
| packed real rows (16/10) | 1.511 ms | 1.560 ms | 1.539 ms | 1.730 ms |
| packed chats of 32-160 (13/11) | 0.947 ms | 1.634 ms | not in my notes | not in my notes |

- **Dense:** level with FA3 and FA4, ahead of cuDNN.
- **Packed:** ahead of all three; on short chats far ahead of FA3.
- **Small losses exist** on a few shapes: dense with 24/8 heads was 1.10× FA3, and packed rows of long chats about 1.02×.

**Where the backward's time goes** (profiler run of 16/10, packed real rows at 18/6): the call takes 1,495 µs, of which the main kernel is 1,103 µs and three helper kernels are 387 µs. The helpers are the preparation step (174 µs), the dQ conversion (106 µs) and the dK/dV sums over query heads (107 µs). That is 26% of a packed call, and every library pays about the same there.

**What could be applied, in my current order of promise:**
1. **Sum the query heads of one KV head inside the block.** This removes the per-head partial results and the head-sum kernels, loads K/V once per KV head, and makes blocks longer so their start-up cost is shared. It should help every layout, real rows included, but it is the largest change and I have no measured estimate yet.
2. **Sharing of one-step blocks** (yesterday's idea): about −8 to −10% on short chats, about −1% on real rows, as counted earlier.
3. **Skip the group whose keys are all masked.** In the first step of every block the second group runs four of its five multiplications on keys that come after all the queries. The code change is small; the gain is unknown because the two groups move in step.
4. **The preparation and dQ-conversion helpers** (280 µs together): memory-bound; I have not studied them yet.

**Yesterday's lessons that carry over:** gains from sharing sit on short chats and stay small on real rows; a changed plan costs every block a little, so it needs a threshold rule; and the trainer step barely moves because attention is a small part of it.

**For the deep research I need two short measurements before choosing what to build:**
- a per-kernel breakdown of the backward on today's six layouts at 4/2 and 18/6 (the 16/10 one covers only real rows at 18/6);
- a quick test that switches off the masked group's work, to see whether item 3 is worth anything.

That is about 15 to 20 minutes on one GPU. GPU 1 is free now: may I run these there?

**Backward research, progress while GPU 2 finishes its full suite:**

**One correction to my earlier sharing estimate.** The cost I fitted per one-step block includes helper work that sharing would not remove, so the figures I gave (for example −8 to −10% on chats of 32-160 at 4/2) are an upper bound. My rough guess is that the real figure is 0.6 to 0.8 of that; only the per-kernel measurement can say.

**What I found reading the three helper kernels:**
- **Padding cost on packed rows:** every tile of a chat gets a full 64-row dQ buffer per query head, even when the chat has only 16 tokens. That buffer is zeroed by the preparation step, added to by the main kernel and read again by the conversion. On rows of 16-token chats this is 4 times more rows than the real ones.
- **A new idea from that:** the first two tiles of every chat receive dQ from only one block, so they need no shared buffer. The block could write them directly, and for chats up to 128 tokens the zeroing and the conversion would disappear completely. On short chats this may matter more than sharing; on real rows it covers about 2 of every 13 tiles.

**Candidates so far:** head sums inside the block, sharing of one-step blocks, skipping the masked group, and now direct dQ writes for a chat's first two tiles.

**Ready to run on your word:** I wrote the measurement that splits a backward call kernel by kernel on four layout sets (short chats, real rows, and the 16-to-192-token sweep rows) at heads 4/2 and 18/6. It is 8 profiler runs, about 16 to 20 minutes on one GPU, and touches nothing else. GPU 0 and GPU 1 are free; tell me which one I may use, or that I should wait.

**While that runs, I am preparing the first kernel experiment: skipping the masked group.**
- **What it is:** in the first step of every block, the second compute group's keys all come after the step's queries. Today it still runs its four multiplications, and the results are exact zeros.
- **The change:** on that step the group skips those four and does only its dQ part. The results stay identical, because only zero work is removed.
- **Why first:** it is small, it applies to every block of every layout (not only odd-length chats), and it needs no change to the plan. A one-step block would do 80% less work in that group; whether the block gets faster is what the race will show.
- **How I will test it:** a separate copy of the tree on the box with the change behind a build switch, the suite for correctness, then a race against the current backward.

| one chat of 4,096 | 18/6 | 3,066 µs | 2,680 | 169 | 106 | 106 | 12% |

The helper kernels are a quarter of the call on real rows and close to half on short chats. That is where the room is.

**What it says about the four ideas** (estimates from these numbers; nothing is built):

| Idea | Chats of 32-160 | Real rows | Size of change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sum the query heads inside the block (no head-sum kernels) | −10 to −13% | −6 to −10% | largest |
| Write dQ directly for a chat's first two tiles | −17 to −19% | about −1.6% | medium |
| Sharing of one-step blocks | −5 to −7% | under 1% | medium to large |
| Skip the masked group | unknown | unknown | small |

- **Sharing is the weakest of the four.** My first figure for it (−8 to −10%) was too high: it counted helper work that sharing does not remove.
- **One reality check:** by my arithmetic from today's times, the attention backward is about 5% of a 1.6B training step, so even −9% of it is under half a percent of the step.

The full tables are in work log section 45.197.

Your first `kill 2565658` did work. The GPU got busy again for a different reason.

**What happened, from our log on the box:**

| Time (IST) | What |
|---|---|
| 18:27:56 | our chain started the full suite at heads 4/2; its test program was pid 2565658 |
| 18:30:53 | your `kill 2565658` ended it (the log shows "Terminated", exit code 143 = ended by a kill) |
| 18:30:59 | the chain script was still alive and started the next test, the full suite at 18/6 (a new pid, 2581035) |
| 18:31:55 | my pause ended that one; the stop file kept the chain from starting anything more |

So 2565658 was only one test, not the chain that starts the tests. Killing it made the chain move on to its next test within seconds.

**Why `kill -f` gave an error:** `kill` has no `-f` option. Whatever comes after the `-` is read as a signal name, and there is no signal called "f". You may be thinking of `pkill -f`, which matches by command line; avoid that on P032, because it can hit a colleague's process.

**Yes, you can kill any process on P032.** Everyone there is the same Unix user `operator`, so `kill` works on ours and on colleagues' processes alike. That is also why it is worth checking the pid first.

**To stop our work by hand next time, stop the chain first, then the running test:**
```
touch /localstorage/gautam_k/attn_1113/pkg14/STOP
nvidia-smi -i 5 --query-compute-apps=pid,process_name --format=csv
ps -o pid,etime,args -p <pid>
kill <pid>
```
- **The first line** stops the chain: nothing new starts.
- **The next two** show the pid on the GPU and confirm it is ours (its path is under `/localstorage/gautam_k`).
- **`kill <pid>`** ends it. If it is still there after about 10 seconds, use `kill -9 <pid>`.

Or just tell me "pause"; that does the same thing.

**Answer for the 350M model's SFT, worked out from measured memory (not yet run on a GPU):**

| Row length (tokens) | One GPU (H200, 141 GB) | Context parallelism, 2 GPUs (per GPU) |
|---|---|---|
| 16,384 | 31.7 GB, fits | 22.6 GB |
| 65,536 | 83.2 GB, fits | 49.5 GB |
| 98,304 | 117.6 GB, fits | 67.5 GB |
| 114,688 | 134.8 GB, fits (about 7 GB spare) | 76.4 GB |
| 122,880 | 143.3 GB, **does not fit** | 80.9 GB |
| 131,072 | 151.9 GB, **does not fit** | 85.4 GB |

- **Context parallelism is not needed up to about 120,000 tokens per row.** Above that, the model needs 2 GPUs; with 2 GPUs it fits up to about 234,000 tokens.
- **Compared with the 135M model:** that one fits up to about 173,000 tokens on one GPU, which is why 131k worked without context parallelism.
- **Sliding window does not change this:** the backward still keeps Q, K, V and the output for every token, so the memory per token is the same.
- **Our SFT trainer and kernels do not support sliding window yet.** If the 350M model was pretrained with it, SFT would need that support added.

**How this was calculated (the proof):**
- **Two measured models:** I used the peak memory of our own SFT trainer from the 07/11 tests. The 135M model took 61.5 GB at 65,536 tokens and 111.0 GB at 131,072 tokens, which is 0.755 MB per token. The 1.6B shape, from its context-parallel pair, comes to 2.11 MB per token.
- **One formula for both:** counting the tensors each layer keeps per token explains both measurements with nearly the same correction factor (1.17 and 1.19).
- **Applied to 350M:** that formula gives 1.05 MB per token, plus 14.6 GB for the weights, optimizer state and fixed buffers. The 14.6 GB fits the same two measurements (14.5 bytes per parameter plus 9.6 GB).

**Ready to confirm on a GPU:** real SFT data is prepared on P035 with our own prep script at nine row lengths, from 16,384 to 131,072 tokens. The run script tries each length on one GPU and stops at the first out-of-memory. It needs about 15 minutes on one GPU once you say a GPU is ours.

**1. Context parallelism: yes, we have it, and it works.** Our SFT trainer has it, and it was tested twice (07/11 and 16/11) with identical losses. For the 350M model, 2 GPUs cover about 234,000 tokens per row by the calculation. Two caveats:
- **Prep limit:** our data prep currently refuses rows longer than 131,072 tokens, so longer rows need that limit lifted.
- **No sliding-window conflict:** our type of context parallelism gives each GPU the whole row for some of the heads, so a sliding window needs no change there.

**2. The open issue is the sliding window, and right now it is only local.** It exists only as one commit by Navin (`b913f32`, 04/11) in `/localstorage/test/BluTrain` on P015, on branch `swa-135m`:
- **Not on GitHub:** a search of the company GitHub repositories finds no sliding-window code, there is no such branch on the remote, and it is not in preproduction.
- **Old base:** it is built on code from 29/10, before our forward change of 13/11.
- **Pretraining only:** it works only for plain rows; for packed rows, which SFT uses, it stops with an error.

**3. Can we do SFT with normal attention on a model pretrained with a sliding window?**
- **Loading works:** the sliding window adds no weights, so the tensor shapes are identical, and the checkpoint loads into our SFT trainer unchanged.
- **The results differ for every chat longer than 1,024 tokens.** In 3 of every 4 layers, the model never learned to look further back than 1,024 tokens, and normal attention would let it.
- **That is a large part of our data:**

| Our SFT data | Chats longer than 1,024 tokens | Share of all tokens in those chats |
|---|---|---|
| m1 smol | 42.8% | 66.2% |
| m2 tulu | 17.8% | 44.8% |
| d8 all | 27.9% | 53.2% |

So yes, it needs a test, and the test is cheap. Take their sliding-window checkpoint and measure its loss on our SFT validation data twice, once with the sliding window and once with normal attention, with no training. If normal attention is clearly worse, SFT must use the sliding window. Inference must then use the same attention as SFT. For this I need the path of their pretrained 350M checkpoint, and about 15 minutes on one GPU.

**4. Is the formula correct? Yes.** Their rule is that each query sees the last 1,024 keys, itself included. I compared it with the public code:

| Source | Rule | Same as theirs? |
|---|---|---|
| Hugging Face transformers | `kv_idx > q_idx - sliding_window` | yes |
| HF passing it to FlashAttention | `window_size = (W - 1, W - 1)`, with causal | yes |
| FlashAttention | keys `[i - left, i + right]`, inclusive | yes, with (W − 1, 0) |
| Ram's PyTorch script | `q_idx - kv_idx < window` | yes |
| PyTorch attention-gym example | `q_idx - kv_idx <= window` | **no**: one extra key |

Which layers stay global is also the same in all the scripts: every 4th layer, so 7 of the 28.

**5. Is the kernel correct? By reading the code, yes, for plain rows.**
- **Forward:** each block of 128 queries reads only the key tiles inside its window, and masks the window's lower edge in the first tile. It also handles rows that are fully masked in that tile, the same way FlashAttention-3 does.
- **Backward:** each key block visits only the query steps that can see it, and masks the edge steps.
- **Their test:** they wrote one with an exact fp64 reference. I have not run it yet; that is a short GPU run.
- **Limits:** plain rows only, the window must be a multiple of 128, and H100/H200 only.

**6. What adding support for SFT means:** yes, as you said.
1. Bring their commit onto our branch. It touches the same two kernel files as our forward and backward changes, so it needs a careful merge.
2. Add the packed-row version: the window counted inside each chat, in the forward work list and in the backward block list.
3. Run the full test set, then races against FlashAttention-3 (which has a window option for packed rows), FlashAttention-4 and FlexAttention, then optimize.

**My suggestion:** run the cheap test in point 3 first, because it tells us whether SFT needs the sliding window at all. Please get the checkpoint path from Navin or Ram. Everything is ready on P035; I start only when you give a GPU.

You are right on part of this, and I should have explained it properly instead of only listing steps. Let me check the published sources so the answer rests on evidence, not on my word.
> tool `Bash`: Download the public papers and model configs on sliding-window attention (Mistral 7B, Gemma 2, Gemma 3, gpt-oss) for exact quotes

You are right on one point and I explained it badly. I'll start with the mechanism, then the published sources.

**1. Which 1,024 tokens does a token see? No selection: always the 1,024 positions right before it.**
- Nothing is picked by importance. In a windowed layer, the token at position 32,000 sees positions 30,977 to 32,000, the nearest 1,024 counting itself. Everything earlier is masked.
- Choosing the "top" tokens by score would be a different method (block selection by relevance); it is not a sliding window.

**2. Where you are right:** in a windowed layer, a token at chat position 1,500 cannot directly see chat positions 0 to 476. That holds in SFT and in pretraining alike.

**3. Why the model still sees its whole chat: not every layer is windowed.**
- **Global layers:** in Ram's and Navin's 350M setup, every 4th layer is a normal full layer, 7 of the 28. In SFT those layers see every earlier token of the chat, from the first token on.
- **Stacking:** after the first global layer, the information from the start of the chat sits in the hidden state at every later position. The windowed layers above it read those nearby hidden states, so the far tokens' content still reaches them.

For a token at chat position 1,500 in SFT, with the chat mask and the window combined:

| Layer type | Sees |
|---|---|
| windowed layers (21 of 28) | chat positions 477 to 1,500 |
| global layers (7 of 28) | chat positions 0 to 1,500, the whole chat so far |

**4. Published models that use a sliding window keep it in post-training, unchanged.** Quotes from the papers and configs I just fetched:

| Model | Pretraining attention | Post-trained version |
|---|---|---|
| Mistral 7B (arXiv 2310.06825) | every layer windowed, W = 4,096; "SWA exploits the stacked layers of a transformer to attend information beyond the window size W", about 131K-token reach | "We also provide a model fine-tuned to follow instructions, Mistral 7B – Instruct"; its config has `sliding_window: 4096` |
| Gemma 2 (arXiv 2408.00118) | "local sliding window attention and global attention in every other layer", local 4,096 | Gemma 2 IT, same layers |
| Gemma 3 (arXiv 2503.19786) | "5 local layers for every global layer", local span 1,024; "only the global layers attend to long context" | Gemma 3 IT, same layers |
| gpt-oss (arXiv 2508.10925) | "alternate between banded window and fully dense patterns, where the bandwidth is 128 tokens" | the released gpt-oss-20b config alternates `sliding_attention` and `full_attention` |

So yes, people use a sliding window in post-training, and they keep exactly the pretraining pattern. That includes Gemma 3, whose window is the same 1,024 as ours.

**5. What this means for us:**
- **If the 350M model is pretrained with the window, SFT must use the same pattern:** the windowed layers windowed inside each chat, the global layers over the whole chat. Switching to full attention in all layers would change how the model works. No published model does that.
- **Our SFT trainer cannot do this yet.** The colleagues' kernel handles plain pretraining rows only and refuses packed chats. So the job is the packed-row version: each chat's window counted from its own start, with the global layers unchanged.
- **The test I suggested is no longer needed to decide.** Published practice already answers it.

The deep analysis is done and saved for the technical report: [sliding_window_attention_sft_analysis.md](<work_docs(mark-down - (.md) files ) /post_Training_research/sliding_window_attention_sft_analysis.md>). The short version:

**1. Published: every model pretrained with a sliding window keeps it in post-training.** Mistral 7B Instruct, Gemma 2 IT, Gemma 3 IT (same 1,024 window as ours) and gpt-oss all do. No published model switches to full attention for post-training.

**2. Published: switching the attention type after pretraining.**

| Direction | What was measured |
|---|---|
| full-attention model, then sliding window (SWAA, Qwen3-4B) | done naively, long-context results collapse; with some full layers kept plus a light fine-tune (LoRA), the gap closes |
| sliding-window model, then full-attention fine-tune (LASER, Gemma 3 270M to 12B) | full attention matched or beat the window, but on one narrow regression task, not chat SFT |
| sparse local attention in fine-tuning, full at inference (LongLoRA) | comparable results |

**3. Measured by our colleagues, which I found on P015.** These are pretraining runs, 5B tokens, 4,096-token rows, same start and same data, compared against full attention:

| Run | Validation loss against full attention | Speed |
|---|---|---|
| 135M, sliding window | 0.0025 lower | 12% faster |
| 350M, sliding window (every 4th layer global) | 0.0011 lower (seed-to-seed noise 0.0002) | 12% faster |
| 350M `kv4_swa3` (4 KV heads plus sliding window) | 0.0091 lower | |

`kv4_swa3` is the config their screen chose, so the 350M model will be pretrained with the window. And in pretraining, the window costs no loss.

**4. Not published anywhere, which our ablations will cover:**
- the 2×2 study (pretraining with full attention or the window, SFT with full attention or the window), measured on chat benchmarks;
- the window together with packed, chat-masked SFT rows;
- small models (135M, 350M) in post-training;
- DPO with the window;
- the effect split by chat length. In our data, 18% to 43% of chats are longer than 1,024 tokens.

**5. Ablation plan.** The starting checkpoints already exist and are paired: the colleagues' 350M full-attention `base` and window `swa3`, same data and same start.

| Arm | Pretraining | SFT | Question |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | full | full | baseline |
| B | full | window | does the window in SFT hurt a full-attention model? |
| C | window | window | the published practice |
| D | window | full | can we skip the window in SFT? |

A and C also get a second seed, for the noise level. Each arm is measured by:
- SFT train and validation loss, split by chat length and by position in the chat;
- our SFT eval suite;
- a test where the answer sits more than 1,024 tokens back in the same chat;
- each model evaluated with the other attention type as well;
- step time and memory.

**6. Order, my recommendation:**
1. **Window support for packed SFT rows, correct but not optimized.** Bring Navin's commit onto our branch, count the window from each chat's start, and check against the exact reference. Arms B and C cannot run without it.
2. **The ablations,** then decide.
3. **Optimize** (our backward ideas inside windows, races against FlashAttention-3, FlashAttention-4 and FlexAttention) only if the window stays in SFT. Then DPO uses it.

Doing the ablations before any support is not possible for arms B and C. Optimizing before the ablations could be wasted work.

## Sliding-window attention (SWA): your questions

1. **Node and GPUs:** yes, P015, and 2 GPUs are enough. The 350M checkpoints and Navin's SWA code are already on P015.

2. **350M only:** agreed. I'll use the colleagues' pair `kv4` (full attention) and `kv4_swa3` (window). Both start from the same weights and train on the same data for the same 5.0B tokens; the window is the only difference. `kv4_swa3` is the config chosen for the 350M, so no new pretraining is needed.

3. **The "131k limit" is really two separate things:**
   - **Code:** the old 4,096 limit is gone, but on 31/10 we left one check in [prepare_sft_data.py:697](../BluTrain_push/sft/prepare_sft_data.py#L697): the row length must be a multiple of 256 and at most 131,072, the longest length we had tested. It is one fixed cap, not one per case: you choose the length with `--seq-len`, and without it the default is 4,096 (line 668). The loader and trainer have no cap; they read the length from the data's `meta.json`. Removing the cap and the default is the future task you gave on 01/11. It is not done yet.
   - **GPU memory:** the 350M fits about 121,600 tokens per row on one H200. That number is calculated from measured runs; the GPU test is not run yet. Past it the run fails with out-of-memory, and then you need CP.
   - For the SWA tests neither matters: rows will be 4,096 tokens, the same as pretraining.

4. **Support first?** Only arms B and C need it (SWA in SFT). Arms A and D use full attention in SFT, which we already have, so they can start as soon as the checkpoints load correctly.

5. **DPO:** agreed, not our work. They need no kernel changes; they pass one extra value per layer (the window, 0 = full attention) in the same attention call, the way they pass the chat plan today.

6. **My boss:** I'm Claude, made by Anthropic. Dario Amodei is Anthropic's CEO and co-founder. Here I work on what you ask.

## SWA plan, step by step

The plan is saved in the analysis doc, section 6.1. Every arm uses the same settings; only the attention changes:
- data m1 smol (43% of its chats are longer than 1,024 tokens);
- template tulu-plain-v1, rows of 4,096 tokens, 1 epoch (~3,570 steps), 128 chats per step;
- LR 1e-4 (your 135M SFT screen LR), cosine schedule, warmup 3%, Muon (to confirm it matches the pretraining);
- the second seed is a second row order.

| Step | What | GPUs | Time (estimate) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | Check configs, tokenizer and optimizer on P015. Load the checkpoints into our trainer; it must match an independent numpy reference within 0.2%. Real data prep, val files split by chat length and position, 30-step smoke run | 1 (~30 min) | ~3 h |
| 1 | Arms A and D | 2 | ~1–1.5 h per arm |

- **Risk:** there are fewer blocks, each doing more work, so a small batch with one long chat may not fill the GPU. If that shows up, a rule set by tests keeps the old path for those cases.
- **Dense rows** get the same change, so pretraining benefits too.
- **Expected gain:** about 6–10% off the attention backward on real rows. That is an estimate from the profile, not a measurement, and it is under 0.5% of a 1.6B training step.

## SWA research

All of this is saved in the analysis doc, section 7.

**1. What the window does per chat.** In a packed row, a token already reads only earlier tokens of its own chat. The window adds one rule in the 21 windowed layers: the key must be among the last 1,024 positions of that chat, counted from the chat's first token.
- Nothing is cut or dropped. Every token still goes through every layer and gets its loss.
- A token at chat position 1,500 reads positions 477–1,500 in the windowed layers, and 0–1,500 in the 7 global layers.
- A token at position 1,024 or earlier gets exactly the full-attention result.
- A packed chat gives the same result as that chat alone in its own row. So a per-chat window isn't unusual; it's what the model computes on one chat without packing.

**2. Row length vs window (your 4,096 question).**
- 4,096 is the row length and 1,024 is the window. Pretraining rows were 4,096 tokens with the 1,024 window inside them, so the windowed layers never saw the whole row.
- The window equals full attention only when it is at least the row length (Navin's code then runs plain causal).
- Yes, SFT should use the same settings as pretraining: window 1,024, every 4th layer global. That is arm C, the default. The other arms only check whether changing it matters.

**3. Do others really use the window in post-training, per chat?** Yes:

| Stack | What it does |
|---|---|
| HF transformers | With packed sequences, it applies the window per sequence, on positions counted inside each sequence |
| TRL (packing, padding-free) | Uses the model's HF attention, which calls FlashAttention varlen with the window. So a Gemma or Mistral SFT in TRL gets per-chat windows by default |
| FlashAttention varlen | The window is relative to each sequence's own positions |
| PyTorch FlexAttention blog | Names "Sliding Window + Document Masking + Causal" as a combination people want, and shows how to apply any mask per document |
| TransformerEngine (Megatron, NeMo) | Supports the window with packed sequences |
| Released instruct models | Gemma 3 4B IT: window 1,024, 5 local layers per global. Mistral-7B-Instruct: window 4,096. gpt-oss (all its released models are post-trained): window 128 |

But nobody has published an SFT quality comparison of window versus full attention. They keep the model's architecture and the frameworks apply the config. Our arms C and D measure exactly that gap.

**4. How much it saves in our SFT.** Calculated from our real packed data, with the 350M model's 21 windowed and 7 global layers:

| Data (rows of 4,096) | Chats over 1,024 tokens | Tokens past chat position 1,024 | Attention work saved | Training compute saved |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| m1 smol | 42.8% | 12.9% | 3.6% | 0.33% |
| m2 tulu | 17.8% | 15.4% | 13.6% | 1.31% |

- You're right: it saves almost nothing today. Most chats over 1,024 are only a little over, and attention is only about 9–10% of the compute.
- For long chats it matters a lot. Attention work drops to 42.6% of full attention for a chat of 8,192 tokens, 29.6% at 32,768, and 26.2% at 131,072.

**5. So why keep the window in SFT?** For consistency, not for SFT speed.
- The 21 windowed layers were pretrained without ever seeing a key more than 1,023 positions back. Full attention in SFT would show them keys they never saw.
- The model is meant to be served with the window. Gemma 3 states its reason as KV-cache memory: with only full-attention layers the cache is 60% memory overhead, versus under 15% with windows of 1,024. vLLM keeps only the last W tokens for windowed layers.
- If SFT uses full attention, serving must also use full attention (losing the memory saving), or the model is served with a window it wasn't fine-tuned with.
- So your guess is right: if it matters, it's because of this pretraining → SFT → serving mismatch. Arms C and D measure it, with the 12.9–15.4% of tokens past position 1,024 reported as their own group.

**6. Row-length cap and default:** agreed, we remove both, as you decided on 01/11:
- `--seq-len` becomes required (no default);
- the 131,072 cap goes;
- the multiple-of-256 check stays.

Our kernels and trainer are proven only up to 131,072, so the test is a real data prep plus a trainer run past that length. I'll schedule it after the backward work and the SWA support.

The local window stays 1,024. When a model goes to long context, only the global layers change.

**First, the two terms:**
- **Local** = the 21 windowed layers. Their reach is fixed: 1,024 tokens back.
- **Global** is not a fixed size. A global layer reads the whole chat or row, so its reach is the row length: 4,096 in pretraining today, and 64k automatically if the rows are 64k.

**What every published model with a sliding window did at long context.** I checked the reports and the official config files:

| Model | Local window | Context | What they did |
|---|---|---|---|
| Gemma 3 | 1,024 (5 local : 1 global) | 128k | Pretrained on 32k rows, then extended to 128k at the end of pretraining by changing only the global layers' RoPE (base 10k → 1M, plus 8× scaling). Local layers kept base 10k and the 1,024 window. |
| gpt-oss | 128 | 131,072 | Pretrained at 4,096, then "extend the context length of dense layers to 131,072 tokens using YaRN" (32×). The window stayed 128. |
| Command A (Cohere, 111B) | 4,096 (3 local : 1 global) | 256k | Window 4,096 at 256k. The global layers use no positional encoding at all (no RoPE). |
| Llama 4 Scout | local chunks of 8,192 (3 local : 1 global) | 10M | Local chunk stays 8,192. 12 of 48 layers are global with no RoPE. |
| Mistral 7B | 4,096 (all layers) | 8k → 32k in v0.2 | The only exception: v0.2 removed the window entirely when it went to 32k. No official reason was given. |

No model grew the window along with the context. Gemma changed the window only between model generations (Gemma 2: 4,096, Gemma 3: 1,024), and that was decided before pretraining.

**Why the window doesn't need to change:**
1. A windowed layer never sees a key more than 1,023 positions back, whether the row is 4k or 64k. Nothing is new for it, so its RoPE stays as trained.
2. Only the global layers see new, longer distances (4k → 64k). So only they get the position extension: a bigger RoPE base, scaling, YaRN, or no positions at all. Then comes a short long-context training phase on long documents.
3. Memory: a windowed layer keeps the KV of only 1,024 tokens at any context length. Growing the window would give that saving back, and the saving is the reason SWA exists.

**For our 350M at 64k, the same recipe:**
- Keep the window at 1,024 and the local layers' RoPE base at 10,000.
- Extend only the 7 global layers (e.g. RoPE base 1M as Gemma 3 did, and/or 16× scaling for 4k → 64k).
- Then a long-context training phase. That is the colleagues' pretraining decision.
- Then long-context SFT with exactly those settings.

**What this means for our code:**
- Our trainer builds one RoPE table for all layers ([bluscript_sft.cpp:954](../BluTrain_push/train/production_zero/bluscript_sft.cpp#L954), one `BLU_ROPE_THETA`, no scaling). It needs a second table for the global layers, picked with the same layer rule as the window. That's a small change.
- The window kernels don't change, since the window stays 1,024.
- At 64k rows each windowed layer does about 3% of the full attention work, so long context is where SWA really pays off.
- A 64k row of the 350M fits on one GPU; CP is only needed above about 121k tokens.

## Research: how other kernel libraries do packed SFT + sliding window

Done; it's in the analysis doc, section 9. I read the actual source code:

| Library | Packed rows + window? | How the kernel does it |
|---|---|---|
| FlashAttention 2 / 3 / 4 | Yes | Forward: each query block starts its key loop at "query block − window" instead of the sequence start. Backward: each key block stops its query loop at "key block + window". Element masks only on the edge blocks. Lengths come from each sequence, so it is per chat. |
| cuDNN | Yes | Its feature table lists packed ("ragged") layouts and "Sliding window" masking for Hopper forward and backward |
| FlexAttention | Yes | A precomputed list of key blocks per query block. Blocks fully inside the window skip the mask. |
| xformers | Yes | A ready-made mask type for packed + causal + window sequences |
| FlashInfer | Forward only | A window setting for packed batches (inference) |

They all use the same design, and it's the one already planned for our packed SWA:
- the forward reads key tiles from max(chat start, tile − 1,024) to the diagonal;
- the backward caps each key tile at min(chat end, tile + 1,024);
- masks run on just two tiles per query tile: the window edge and the diagonal.

Navin's kernel already does this for plain rows. For packed rows we only replace "row start" with "chat start".

Sources (read directly):
- [FlashAttention 2 forward kernel](https://github.com/Dao-AILab/flash-attention/blob/main/csrc/flash_attn/src/flash_fwd_kernel.h), [backward kernel](https://github.com/Dao-AILab/flash-attention/blob/main/csrc/flash_attn/src/flash_bwd_kernel.h), [mask.h](https://github.com/Dao-AILab/flash-attention/blob/main/csrc/flash_attn/src/mask.h)

What he described is exactly how Qwen does it. Two different numbers:

| | What it means | Qwen3 |
|---|---|---|
| **Training context** | The row length the model was actually trained on. This sets memory use and whether training needs CP. | The last pretraining stage trains on 32,768-token rows and raises the RoPE base from 10,000 to 1,000,000. |
| **Inference context** | How much the model can read when serving | 131,072 = 32,768 × 4, using YaRN with factor 4 |

- **"131k in inference"** means you add a YaRN entry to the model's config when serving, and the model can then read 4× its trained length, with no extra training. The Qwen3-4B and 8B model cards say: "32,768 natively and 131,072 tokens with YaRN". Qwen3-0.6B lists 32,768.
- **YaRN in one line:** it keeps the RoPE parts that encode short distances as trained, and stretches the parts that encode long distances so 4× longer positions fit into the trained range.
- **Practical notes from Qwen's own card:**
  - Turn YaRN on only when long inputs are needed. The fixed setting applies to every input and can slightly hurt short texts.
  - About 4× is what they use this way. Gemma 3 instead trained its 8× extension at the end of pretraining.

**For our 350M with 32k pretraining:**
- **Training:** SFT rows up to 32k need no CP, since one H200 holds about 121k tokens per row.
- **Serving at 131k:** YaRN ×4 goes on the global layers only. The windowed layers keep the 1,024 window and their RoPE as is, the same way gpt-oss applied YaRN to its dense layers only.
- **Our side:** the export and trainer need per-layer RoPE settings. That is the one code item from before.
