**YaRN: what it is, what it does, why it's used**

**The starting point is RoPE (how the model knows distances):**
- Each attention head's 128 numbers are treated as 64 pairs. RoPE turns each pair by an angle equal to position × that pair's speed.
- Pair 0 is fast: one full turn every 6.3 tokens. Pair 63 is slow: one full turn every 54,410 tokens (our 350M, RoPE base 10,000).
- When two tokens meet in attention, the model sees the difference of their angles. Fast pairs tell it exact short distances; slow pairs tell it long distances.

**The problem past the training length:**
- A model trained on 32k rows has only ever seen angle differences for tokens up to 32k apart.
- At 131k apart, the slow pairs produce angles it never saw in training. Its attention scores there can't be trusted, and quality drops fast past the trained length. Gemma 3's report shows this: its models "rapidly degrade" past their extended length.

**What YaRN changes.** It is one config entry read at load time; the weights don't change. It changes the speed of each pair:
- **Fast pairs** (more than 32 full turns inside the training length) are left unchanged, so short-distance detail stays exactly as trained.
- **Slow pairs** (less than 1 full turn in training) are slowed down by the factor, e.g. 4×. A 131k distance then gives the same angle a 32k distance gave in training, which the model has seen.
- **Pairs in between** get a smooth mix of the two.
- **One small fixed sharpening of the attention scores.** Stretching otherwise makes attention flatter than in training.

For our settings (factor 4):

| RoPE base | Trained length | Reads up to | Pairs unchanged | Pairs slowed 4× | Mixed |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 10,000 (our 350M today) | 4,096 | 16,384 | 21 | 18 | 25 |
| 10,000 | 32,768 | 131,072 | 36 | 4 | 24 |
| 1,000,000 (Qwen3's choice) | 32,768 | 131,072 | 24 | 24 | 16 |

**What it's for:**
- Train at 32k, which is cheaper: 4× fewer tokens per row, much less attention work, no CP needed.
- Still serve 131k-token inputs (long documents, long chats, retrieval, long agent histories) by switching YaRN on at inference.
- That is exactly Qwen3's approach: trained at 32k, served at 131k with YaRN ×4.

**Its limits:**
- About 4× works well without extra training, as Qwen shows. Bigger jumps need some training with the stretched positions: Gemma 3 trained its 8× extension at the end of pretraining.
- A fixed YaRN setting applies to every input, so short texts lose a little. Qwen advises turning it on only for long inputs.
- In our sliding-window model, the windowed layers never see distances over 1,023, so they need no YaRN. Only the 7 global layers get it.

one-list ordermeans ? hwdiffertnfromdefaultorfder andwhat are these, explainminimallya nd simnply

### CLAUDE [2026-11-17 20:38 IST]

These are three ways of ordering the backward's work list. The kernel math is identical in all three; only the order the GPU runs the blocks in changes.

**Setup:**
- The backward is cut into blocks. One block = one 128-key tile of one chat, for one KV head.
- The GPU starts the blocks in the order of a list.
- The order matters for two things:
  1. **Balance:** the longest blocks should start first. Otherwise a few long blocks run at the end while the rest of the GPU sits idle.
  2. **Cache reuse:** blocks of the same row and KV head read the same data. If they run close together in time, that data stays in the GPU's cache, which is faster.

**The three orders:**

| Order | How the list is made | Result |
|---|---|---|
| **Default** | cut into small groups of 1–2 (row, KV head) pairs; longest-first only inside each group | good cache reuse, but long blocks of the last groups finish late |
| **One-list** | no groups: every block in one list, longest-first | best balance, but rows and heads get mixed and the data falls out of the cache; with many heads (18/6) it was 5–8% slower |
| **Whole rows** (final) | groups of whole rows (all KV heads of a row), as many rows per group as fit about 80 MB of cache (4 rows at 4/2, 1 row at 18/6); longest-first inside each group | keeps the cache reuse and balances better |

**Trainer result (step time vs the pushed code):**

| Order | 135M | 1.6B |
|---|---|---|
| Default | −1.3% | −0.5% |
| One-list | −2.0% | −0.1% |
| Whole rows (final) | −1.7% | −0.7% |

One-list helps the small model but loses the big one. Whole rows is good on both, so it's the one in the final version.

I'd go with **"only when off"**: print one line, once per process, whenever idea 4 is *not* used, for either reason:
- someone switched it off (`BLU_VJ2_HSUM=0`), or
- the automatic rule turned it off because the GPU has only 1 KV head (as in the 135M with CP).

When idea 4 runs, which is the default, nothing is printed.

Why:
1. **Same as our other switches.** `BLU_VJ2_DKDV_F32` also prints only when it changes the default path. A silent log then always means "default path".
2. **The non-obvious case gets a line.** Someone running CP with 1 KV head per GPU would otherwise not know idea 4 was skipped. One line per process tells them.
3. **No noise.** Normal runs, which are most runs, stay clean, and the lines that do appear always mean something.

If you'd rather see the state in every run's log anyway, printing both is a one-line change.

**Short answers:**
- **dK outlier:** not a wrong value. It doesn't change training, speed, or overall precision.
- **Benchmark:** you're right, it was wasteful. Only about 4 of the 89 GPU-minutes last night were real measuring. The time went to profiler start-up, not to CPU work.

## 1. The dK outlier

**What the test checks:** for every chat, it compares our gradient with an exact answer computed in fp64. Our largest error in that chat may be at most 2× the error of plain bf16 PyTorch math on the same chat. FA3's and PyTorch's own tests use the same rule.

**What failed:** 1 piece out of 5,304, the 2-token padding piece at the end of row 1444 (tokens 4094–4095). The columns below are: our largest error in that piece, the limit, and the ratio of the two.

| Build | Our largest error | Limit (2× plain bf16) | Ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| Final code (idea 4 on) | 0.01765 | 0.01553 | 1.136, fail (13.6% over the limit) |
| Idea 4 off (same as pushed) | 0.01427 | 0.01553 | 0.919, pass |

**Why this piece:**
- In a 2-token piece, the first token's share of dK is exactly 0.
- The second token's share comes from subtracting two nearly equal numbers (dP − D). The rounding error stays while the result shrinks, so the error looks large next to the value.
- The test already has a separate rule for 1-token pieces for this kind of reason. A 2-token padding piece also needed a recorded exception in October (dQ, "pad row 492 @4094 L=2").

**Why idea 4 moved it:**
- Before idea 4, each query head's dK was rounded to bf16, then the 3 heads were added and rounded again.
- With idea 4, the 3 heads are added in fp32 and rounded once. This is the same way FA3 does it (our kernel also computes dS the FA3 way).
- On this one piece, the old double rounding happened to land closer to the exact value. Everywhere else, rounding once is better (compared with idea 4 off):
  - dK: median ratio 0.383 → 0.314 (−18%), 99th percentile 0.609 → 0.518 (−15%).
  - dV: median 0.487 → 0.354 (−27%), worst 1.171 → 0.711. The 4 old recorded dV failures are gone.

**Your questions:**
- **Wrong values?** No.
  - The piece is bit-identical whether it runs packed in a row or alone.
  - 1000 repeated runs are bit-identical, so there is no race.
  - Trainer A/B: same step-0 loss. Gradient norm within 0.01%, the same size as the old code's own run-to-run difference.
- **Training?** No effect. Padding tokens have no loss, so their gradient is exactly 0, and dK there is exactly 0 in both versions. The test puts random gradients on padding on purpose, as a stress test. Training never does that.
- **Speed?** None. This is a precision check only.

**Best thing to do:**
- Record it as a known case with its measured bound of 1.136, as the October cases were.
- Before that, run FA3 on the exact same 2 tokens, so this becomes a measured fact and not just my reasoning. The test can already save one piece to a file, and FA3 is installed.
  - Cost: a small test change, a rebuild on CPU, and about 3 min of GPU.
  - My expectation is that FA3 gets about the same ratio, because with idea 4 our arithmetic here is FA3's.
  - If FA3 passes clearly, we have a real gap, and we fix it before pushing.

## 2. Why the benchmark was so slow

I measured last night's runs from the clock log each run records every 100 ms:

| Part of one run | Time |
|---|---|
| Waiting before the GPU does anything (profiler start-up) | 65–130 s |
| GPU actually measuring | 5–12 s |
| After the run: profiler finishing + export (CPU) | ~10 s |

- The same binary without the profiler (the calibration step) finished 3 layouts in 10 s in total.
- Under the profiler, the GPU stayed idle at its lowest clock for the first 64 s (ours) or 82 s (FA3) of each run. 75 of 80 run outputs show the profiler warning "GPU initialization took too long".
- So the waste was starting a fresh profiled process 43 times, about 1–2 min each, before the GPU did anything. The CPU export work after each run was only about 10 s.

**Fix:**
1. **CPU first, no GPU:** remove the duplicate layout lines and check every layout with the rivals' own rule. That check would have caught last night's crash in one second.
2. **3-min probe on 1 GPU:** find out exactly what the profiler waits for, then pick the cheapest start-up.
3. **New runner:**
   - Start each contender once per round, with all its layouts inside that one process. If the probe allows it, use one profiler session for everything.
   - Keep the same contenders, the same order, the same kernel-time method and the same summary tables.
   - Exports run in the background. Each run is saved the moment it ends, so a stop never loses finished work.
4. **Validation:** re-measure one finished layout (real rows 0-7, 18/6) with the new runner. It must match last night's ratios within about 1% before we trust it.

**Time for what's left** (18/6 rows 16-23, and all of 4/2), on 2 GPUs:
- Old way: about 62 min.
- New way: about 35 min in the worst case, or about 10–15 min if the probe finds the start-up cause.
- Option: run one round instead of two to halve that again. Last night the two rounds agreed within 0.3%.

## 3. Temp folder: not needed

- It holds raw trace tables from last night's GPU 1 runs. It is 170 MB and sits in `/dev/shm`, which is the box's RAM.
- Our script deletes these after writing each summary, but the 22:50 stop came before that step.
- The summaries are already saved on the box and on the laptop. The only other content is half of one unfinished layout, which will be measured again anyway.

Everything about our code was checked in the code: our SFT trainer, its README, and Adhitya's submodule at `cf1372d`. Calculated numbers are marked as calculated.

**Short answers to your doubts:**
- **Ring attention and Ulysses are two ways to do context parallelism.** The hybrid (Ulysses inside a group of GPUs, ring between the groups) is real too: Adhitya's library has all three.
- **Our SFT trainer uses Ulysses only** (`BLU_SFT_CP=U`). Ring and hybrid are not wired in.
- **Ring attention can do GQA.** Adhitya's ring kernels are GQA kernels, and GQA even makes ring send less data, because ring sends only K and V. So it's not true that only Ulysses works for GQA.
- **We chose Ulysses because of our packed chats.** After its swap, every GPU has whole rows, so our own attention kernels run unchanged. Ring needs a kernel that runs queries from one piece of the row against keys from another piece, with chat boundaries and positions handled across the cuts. Our current kernels don't have that.
- **Ulysses's limit:** the number of GPUs per row must divide the number of KV heads.
  - 135M: 2 GPUs.
  - 350M: 2 or 4.
  - 1.6B: 2, 3 or 6.
  - Beyond that you need copies of the KV heads (Adhitya's version can do this, ours doesn't), ring, or the hybrid.

**What's inside the file:**
1. Why one GPU runs out of memory on long rows, with our measured memory per token.
2. Which parts of a layer need other GPUs (only attention).
3. Ulysses step by step on an 8-token example, the real tensor shapes, the backward pass, the rules, and how much data it moves.
4. Ring step by step, with a worked numeric example showing the merge gives exactly the one-GPU result.
5. The causal work imbalance in ring (one GPU does 3× the other) and the fix that makes it equal.
6. Ring with packed chats and with GQA.
7. The hybrid.
8. A side-by-side table of the three methods.
9. What we use and the measured results from 07/11: CP=2 trains the same as one GPU, the 135M at 128k is 1.65× faster using 56% of the memory per GPU, and the 1.6B at 64k only fits with CP.
10. When to use CP for each model, and what depends on what.

The first results are in. They come from session 1 of 4.

**Setup:**
- **Data:** the mix set (chats of mixed lengths), heads 18/6. Each call is 8 packed rows of 4,096 tokens.
- **Measurement:** kernel times from nsys, with free clocks, averaged over the 2 rounds; each round runs all 5 contenders, the second in reverse order.
- **How to read the numbers:** each one is our final code's time divided by the other's time, for one forward + backward call. Below 1.00 means ours is faster.

| Layout | vs FA3 | vs FA4 | vs cuDNN | Final vs our pushed code |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| rows 0-7 (353 chats, mostly short) | **0.428** | 0.402 | 0.424 | 0.570 |
| rows 8-15 (42 chats) | **0.795** | 0.787 | 0.771 | 0.865 |
| rows 16-23 (8 long chats) | **0.928** | 0.907 | 0.812 | 0.964 |

So on rows 0-7 our final code takes 57% less time than FA3 and 43% less than our pushed code. On rows 8-15 it takes 20% less than FA3, and on the long chats 7% less. The forward alone is also faster than all three rivals on all 3 layouts (0.816 / 0.916 / 0.966 of FA3's time).

**It matches the past records** (forward + backward vs FA3):
- **rows 0-7:** 17/11 gave 0.425 and today gives 0.428. Our pushed code gave 0.752 on 13/11 and 0.751 today.
- **rows 8-15:** 0.792 then and 0.795 now. Our pushed code gave 0.920 then and 0.919 now.
- **rows 16-23:** measured for the first time (on 17/11 the rivals crashed on these rows).

**Forward 1–2% slower than our pushed code: this is the clock, not the code.**
- The forward kernel did not change. Only CPU-side plan code changed in that file.
- All runs hit the ~694 W power limit. The final backward keeps the tensor cores busier, so the GPU lowers its clock:
  - rows 0-7: 1,920 MHz vs 1,980 MHz for the pushed code;
  - rows 8-15: about 1,657 vs 1,702 MHz.
- The unchanged forward follows the clock.
- Ours even runs at a lower clock than the rivals (rows 8-15: ~1,657 vs ~1,808 MHz) and still wins.

**A small detail:** on rows 16-23 our test program ran the layout twice, because the layout list holds it twice. Both passes gave the same times (forward 1.015 ms, backward 2.990 / 2.991 ms), so the result is not affected.

Session 2 (real set, 18/6) is running. The campaign should end around 16:01 IST and the push-tree checks around 16:13.

Yes. I re-checked every run, and the comparison is apples to apples. The gains are real, but **the big ones are only on short chats**, where every library is very inefficient and ours is less so. On long chats ours is only 4–9% ahead of FA3. Everything below was done on the CPU, from the 120 runs' own kernel traces.

**1. Same problem for every contender (checked in the scripts)**
- **Shape:** head size 128, bf16, causal, 8 rows × 4,096 tokens, heads 18/6 or 4/2.
- **GQA:** K and V really have 6 (or 2) heads for every contender; they are not copied up to the query heads.
- **Chats:** exactly the same ones. The rivals read the chat list our test program exported, and each list is checked to cover every row with no gaps.
- **Conditions:** same GPU, same session, 2 rounds in opposite order.

**2. Nothing hidden in the counting**

I counted each iteration (forward + backward) three ways:
- **A:** what I reported.
- **B:** every kernel added up, whatever its name.
- **C:** the GPU timeline including every idle gap. This is the worst case for ours, because our test program waits after each call and the rivals' loop does not.

| Ours vs | A (reported) | B (all kernels) | C (with all gaps) |
|---|---|---|---|
| FA3 | 0.403–0.928 | 0.400–0.928 | 0.453–0.938 |
| FA4 | 0.383–0.907 | 0.347–0.910 | 0.397–0.920 |
| cuDNN | 0.235–0.812 | 0.230–0.824 | 0.269–0.830 |
| Our pushed code | 0.570–0.980 | 0.575–0.980 | 0.587–0.974 |

- B matches A within 1–2%. We launch **zero** kernels outside A.
- FA4 and cuDNN each have about 8 µs of small extra kernels that A did **not** count against them.
- Ours wins all 48 comparisons under all three counts.

**3. The numbers are physically possible.** This is useful work per second, measured in TFLOPS; the H200's peak is 989.

| Case | Ours fwd | FA3 fwd | Ours bwd | FA3 bwd |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Long chats (8 × 4,096) | 615 | 594 | 519 | 475 |
| Real chats (average 800–1,400 tokens) | 448–520 | 425–486 | 371–419 | 289–352 |
| Short chats (average 93 tokens) | 92 | 75 | 85 | 31 |

- **On long chats FA3 reaches 594 TFLOPS, its normal level.** So it was set up correctly and not slowed down by our setup. Ours is only about 4% (forward) and 9% (backward) faster there.
- **On short chats every library runs at 3–9% of peak.** FA3's backward does only 31 TFLOPS of useful work, and that is where the big ratios come from.

**4. Why ours is faster on short chats.** Time per iteration in µs, mix 18/6 rows 0-7:

| | Ours | Our pushed | FA3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| forward | 180 | 175 | 219 |
| backward main kernel | **311** | 560 | 801 |
| zero-fill of fp32 buffers | 0 | 0 | 105 |
| prep (row sums of dO·O) | 159 | 196 | 182 |
| dQ fp32 → bf16 convert | **19** | 128 | 131 |
| dK/dV head sum or convert | **0** | 105 | 108 |
| **total** (FA3 also has a 6 µs scheduler kernel) | **669** | 1,164 | 1,552 |

- **Idea 4:** one block handles all 3 query heads of a KV head. It loads K and V once, adds the 3 heads' dK/dV in its registers, and writes the final dK/dV once.
  - FA3 and our pushed code work one query head at a time, so they must add the 3 heads in fp32 buffers afterwards.
  - FA3 has to zero those buffers first and convert them at the end (105 + 108 µs). Our pushed code ran separate head-sum kernels (105 µs). Ours needs none of that.
- **Ideas 1 + 2:** with chats of about 93 tokens, almost every dQ tile is one of a chat's first two tiles, which only one block writes. So ours writes dQ directly in bf16, and the convert step drops from about 130 µs to 19.

**5. What it means for training.** On 17/11 the whole training step, measured against our pushed code, was 1.7% faster for the 135M model and 0.7% faster for the 1.6B. That's small, because attention is only part of each step. The big gains are at kernel level, not in step time.

**Honest caveats:**
- **Loop difference:** our test program waits after each call and the rivals' loop doesn't. Count C covers that, and ours still wins.
- **Inputs:** the random input values differ between our program and the rivals'. Speed does not depend on the values.
- **Plan building:** our chat plan is built once per batch on the CPU and isn't in these kernel times. In training it is built once per step for all layers, and the 17/11 trainer test includes it.
- **Clocks:** ours ran at a lower clock than the rivals in most cases, so the time ratios are, if anything, cautious.

The check script is `dk18/apples20.py`. Its outputs are in `dk18/box_results/apples20_all.txt`, `apples20_kernels.txt` and `apples20_tflops.txt`.

## The 3 files, line by line

The line numbers below are lines of [the patch](work_docs(mark-down%20-%20(.md)%20files%20)%20/gqa_backward_ideas_1_2_4_vs_TI_f1a7d98.patch).

### File 1: `GQA_bwd_vj2_sm90.cu` (the backward kernel and its launcher)

**Before:**
- One block = 128 keys of one chat for ONE query head.
- Compute group 0 owns keys 0–63 of the block, group 1 owns keys 64–127.
- One step = one 64-row query tile. Warp 0 (the loader) loads each step's Q, dO, LSE and D.
- Warp 1 (the dQ writer) reduce-adds each step's fp32 dQ into an fp32 buffer; a conversion kernel turns it into bf16 at the end.
- Each query head writes a bf16 dK/dV partial, and 2 head-sum kernels add the G partials.

| Patch lines | What changes |
|---|---|
| 7–8 | Declares `gqa_vj2_hsum_list` (defined in file 2). The launcher uses it to get the plan's per-KV-head block list. |
| 12–27 | Prep kernel: it zeroes the fp32 dQ buffer. Now it skips tiles marked "direct" (`dt.w == 1`), because the main kernel writes those straight to bf16 (idea 2). |
| 28–45 | New template flag `HSUM` (the idea-4 kernel variant) and a new last argument `dQout` (the bf16 dQ output for idea 2). It goes last so the old arguments keep their places. |
| 46–67 | Which work a block takes. Packed rows: it reads `hst`, the slot step from one query head to the next (7th number of the new list entry). Dense rows with `HSUM`: the grid pairs become (row, KV head), and `hq` = the group's first query head. |
| 70–84 | `NT` = G × steps with `HSUM`, otherwise just the steps. `nDirect` = 2 in key block 0 of a chat (1 if the chat has one query tile), 0 everywhere else, 0 on dense rows. |
| 88–118 | Loader: loops over all `NT` steps. `ii` = step inside the current head, `g` = head offset. It loads Q and dO of head `hq + g` and that head's LSE/D slot (`dqt0 + g × hst + ii`). The double-buffer stage (`i & 1`) and the barrier phases keep counting across the head boundary. |
| 121–149 | dQ writer: direct steps have nothing to reduce-add, so it skips them (with `HSUM`, each head's first `nDirect` steps). The tile address is for head `hq + g`. |
| 150–211 | **Idea 1** (path without `HSUM`). In a block's first step, every key of group 1 comes after every query of the step, so the causal mask makes its whole P zero. Group 1 now only: writes zeros into its 64 dS rows; meets group 0 at BAR_PDS; runs its dQ GEMM (head columns 64–127) from group 0's dS rows; then stores that dQ directly (idea 2) or hands it to the writer. It no longer runs the S and dP GEMMs, the 2,048 exps, or the dV/dK GEMMs, which all produced exact zeros. Its loop then starts at step 1. |
| 212–273 | The step loop now runs `NT` steps. With `HSUM`, idea 1 happens at the first step of every head (`ii == 0`). `pend` means "the writer may still be reading my last hand-off": the group waits for it before reusing the staging buffer. |
| 277–313 | **Idea 2** inside the step. On a direct step, the group converts its dQ to bf16 with the softmax scale (the same rounding the conversion kernel does), syncs, and every thread stores 16-byte pieces of the rows that lie inside the chat. Other steps hand off to the writer as before. |
| 316–358 | End of block. With `HSUM`, dK/dV hold the fp32 sum over all G heads, so the block writes the **final** rows of the KV head (row `b × Hkv + hkv`) instead of a per-head partial (`b × Hq + hq`). The same change is made in all 4 store places. A `static_assert` stops `HSUM` being combined with fp32 partials. |
| 359–369 | Conversion kernel: returns at once for direct tiles. |
| 370–387 | The empty stand-in versions (builds without sm_90) get the same new flag and argument, so the file still compiles everywhere. |
| 388–435 | Launcher, the idea-4 decision, in this order: `BLU_VJ2_HSUM` (default 1); off with `BLU_VJ2_DKDV_F32=1`; packed rows with G ≥ 2 need the plan's per-KV-head list; **rule 2b**: off when the call has fewer than `BLU_VJ2_HSUM_MINKV` (default 2) KV heads. The decision uses the shape only, so a chat packed and the same chat alone always take the same path, which keeps their results bit-identical. Each OFF reason prints one line, once per process. Nothing prints while idea 4 runs. |
| 436–455 | With idea 4: no partial buffers are allocated, and the TMA store maps point at the final dV/dK. |
| 456–487 | The idea-4 launch. Packed rows: one block per entry of the per-KV-head list. Dense rows: (S / 128) × B × Hkv blocks. The section size follows **rule 1** (as many whole rows as fit in about 80 MB, rounded down to a power of 2) unless `BLU_VJ2_HSUM_SECT` sets it. |
| 488–507 | The old launches, unchanged except for the new last argument (packed: `d_dQ`; dense: `nullptr`). |
| 508–517 | The 2 head-sum kernels run only when idea 4 is off. |

### File 2: `GQA_fwd_generic.cu` (plan builder, host code only; no forward kernel changes)

| Patch lines | What changes |
|---|---|
| 527–529 | 3 includes: a lock, a hash table, and printing. |
| 537–566 | A small table that maps the plan's `vj2_blocks` pointer to (per-KV-head list, entry count, G), protected by a lock; `gqa_vj2_hsum_list` looks it up. It is not a new field in `GqaChatPlan` because programs that hold that struct by value (the test program does) would break. `vj2_hsum_sect()` reads `BLU_VJ2_HSUM_SECT` once. |
| 571–581 | dQ tile list: the 4th number is now 1 for a chat's first two query tiles (direct, idea 2). It used to be always 0. |
| 586–614 | The per-KV-head list, built only when the plan knows Hkv and G ≥ 2. Sections follow rule 1. There is one entry per (row, KV head) pair × chat × 128-key tile: {row, start, length, key tile, first query head, its dQ slot, slot step per head, G}. Inside a section the longest work goes first. |
| 621–628 | The list goes last in the plan's single GPU allocation, so every other list keeps its place. |
| 636, 642 | The build registers the list in the table after the upload; `gqa_chat_plan_free` removes it. |

### File 3: `test_varlen_attention.cu` (test only)

| Patch lines | What changes |
|---|---|
| 652–654 | Comment: the 4 old dV KNOWN entries come from the per-head path. With idea 4 they no longer occur; they stay because `BLU_VJ2_HSUM=0` brings that path back. |
| 662–670 | New KNOWN entry: G11 D10 dK, the 2-token pad piece (row 1444 @4094), limit 1.136 × 1.01. The reason is written next to it: FA3 and FA4 give a bit-identical dK on the same bytes, and training never sees this case because pad tails get dO = 0. |

**What stays the same:**
- Every forward kernel and the trainer.
- The per-query-head path is still there. It runs with `BLU_VJ2_HSUM=0`, with fp32 partials, or with 1 KV head. It now includes ideas 1 + 2, which have no switch, so it is not the 13/11 code.
